articles.title: South Korea’s Ruling Democratic Party Is Tumbling in the Polls
articles.full_text:
Its in-house gaffes and disputes are largely to blame for the DP’s plummeting approval ratings.
On October 19, Gyeonggi, South Korea’s most populous province, held a post-funeral ceremony ahead of a firefighter’s internment. More than 2,700 people filled the indoor stadium. Choo Mi-ae, the provincial governor, stood on the green sports surfacing, tears streaming down her face. File after file of uniformed firefighters weaved around her amid dirgeful tributes.
Of course, the firefighter’s burial signified the loss and sacrifice of a serviceman who braved a conflagration to save lives. Yet, it also rang the death knell for the ruling Democratic Party’s approval ratings. 
The same day, Realmeter, an authoritative pollster, released a poll. The DP’s approval rating, at 36.2 percent, was lower than the opposition People Power Party’s 40.9 percent. It was the first time since the June local elections that the PPP had outpolled the DP. 
The alienation of DP supporters happened fast. Less than five months ago, the June local elections handed the DP a resounding victory. Since then, the DP has registered a double-digit plunge in approval ratings.
The party’s fall was particularly steep in Seoul, with the DP polling at 26.7 percent as opposed to the PPP’s 45.7 percent. One-fifth of South Koreans live in Seoul; track records in the capital thus tend to reflect where the swing voters stand. Oh Se-hoon, its current mayor, may lose the post should the Supreme Court uphold the special counsel’s charge that Oh allegedly paid a pollster to rig polls in his favor. (On October 23, the appellate court overturned his guilty verdict. The Supreme Court will rule on the case early next year.) The DP hopes to retake Seoul in a potential by-election, but with these poll numbers success is far from assured. 
The DP’s popularity may still crater further. Given the touchy nature of the reform agenda still ahead for the Lee Jae-myung administration, the rest of this year and next year may not really be a rosy picture for the party. And then it will already be time for the 2028 general elections.
The party’s poor polling performance is of its own making, though. Choo, the governor of Gyeonggi-do, dealt the most immediate damage in a controversy that preceded the firefighter’s funeral.
On October 13, during a parliamentary audit, Choo said that “firefighting is like a financial straw, causing the biggest headache.” She then elaborated on how much firefighters are setting back the province’s coffers. Firefighters’ unions went up in arms, wondering how the sacrifice of constantly putting their lives in jeopardy could be reduced to a budgetary complaint. 
Choo ignored their calls for an apology. The province explained that her remark was in reference to the ballooning budgetary burden on the local government due to decreasing financial contributions from the central government – even though the firefighters are directly employed by the central government. Despite her true intention, Choo’s phrasing was no doubt inappropriate and hurtful. She was already facing steep criticism. Then October 16 changed everything. 
A fire erupted in a metal printing factory in a town in Gyeonggi. Flames engulfed firefighter Kim Jin-seok, who passed away in the line of duty. The nation became even more infuriated with Choo’s callous analogy earlier. 
The next day, Choo attended Kim’s funeral, where she finally apologized: “Since you want an apology, I wholeheartedly apologize.” You have to want to apologize for an apology to feel sincere. But she made it clear she was forced. Her apology duly backfired, to the point where she might have been better off not apologizing at all. 
Making matters worse, when Kim Min-seok, the DP’s leader, arrived at the funeral his car parked in a spot reserved for emergency patients. It was a collective PR disaster for the party.
Choo has also been stirring the pot within the DP. She openly clashed with President Lee Jae-myung on the latter’s choice for head of the Serious Crime Investigation Agency (SCIA). It’s a new institution born out of abolishing the prosecutor’s office. The prosecutor’s office used to wield unchecked political powers through its dual authority to investigate and indict. Lee’s criminal justice reform and the DP’s legislation kiboshed this practice by distributing investigatory powers to the police and the SCIA, and indictment authority to the Prosecution Service, also a new body. 
In September, when Lee picked Kim Ji-yong, a former prosecutor, to lead the SCIA, Choo maligned Lee by wondering out loud, “Why is he shivering before the insurrection forces?” Kim Yong-min, a popular hard-line DP legislator, joined forces with Choo. They believe Kim Ji-yong huddled around former President Yoon Suk-yeol when Yoon was chief prosecutor and that appointing Kim means giving in to the prosecutors and insurrection forces that aided and protected Yoon for his authoritarian practices and failed self-coup. For his part, Lee maintains that Kim was anti-Yoon. 
Their public disagreement continued into this month. “Why appoint someone who can turn their back to the people and justice as the captain of our reform ship?” Choo wrote on October 2. On the same day, Kim Yong-min held a press conference publicly denouncing Kim Ji-yong for having always opposed prosecutorial reform. Meanwhile, Lee made repeated social media posts and a parliamentary submission arguing that the nominee had appropriate qualities needed to establish a trustworthy criminal justice system.
Voices in and out of the DP expressed concerns that such open defiance seemed to challenge Lee’s authority over personnel. The spat peaked in rhetoric on October 9, when Lee made a social media post maligning “those incompetents … who stage internal attacks purportedly for radical reform as a noble cause” when in fact they were complaining because “personnel and national policy didn’t go the way they wanted.”
Separately, the president’s online spat with Cho Kuk, a former justice minister who founded the Rebuilding Korea Party (RKP), further fractured the support for the DP. With 12 legislators in the National Assembly, Cho’s RKP is the third largest party after the DP and the PPP. Cho is also frequently mentioned as a strong contender for the next presidency. The RKP collaborated with the DP to boost liberal voters’ turnout during the 2024 April general elections. 
The DP-RKP alliance became uncomfortable in June, however. When Cho ran for a parliamentary by-election, the DP fielded a candidate of its own – a choice many questioned. Liberal votes naturally split, and the PPP easily nabbed the seat. 
Ever since, talk of merging the two parties has become fraught with grudges. Cho and Lee have also exchanged criticisms over each other’s stance on the extent of prosecutorial reform. Lee must have targeted Cho as well when he wrote on October 5 that his detractors “shouldn’t try to influence personnel choices and specific affairs of investigation and indictment in the name of prosecutorial reform and for selfish reasons.” (Cho and his wife served prison time after the prosecutors dug every dirt on them to stem former President Moon Jae-in’s and Cho’s effort to curtail the prosecutor’s office’s undue investigative and political powers.) Cho retorted that “the sense of crisis over the dissolution of our alliance has reached the boiling point.”
The past couple of months has seen Lee devoting a large portion of his time and energy to putting in place vociferous elements within the liberal camp. There are two reasons the president rolled up his sleeves to personally engage with critics. 
First, Lee must be feeling isolated and betrayed. In September, he shared someone else’s post: “What hurts more are words from within than foes from without … In this chess game, we need to protect the queen that is Lee Jae-myung.” Second, Kim Min-seok, the DP leader who had Lee’s support in the August chair election, has failed to set the party’s house in order. He is kind and voluble but ineffective in quelling the internal unrest. His frequent warnings against those critical of Lee have fallen flat. 
While the DP’s big shots are preoccupied with aggrandizing their own presence, the RPK’s support rating reached 9 percent, its highest since the onset of the Lee administration, according to the October 22 figures released by Media Tomato, another major pollster. On the one hand, it indicates the degree to which the DP let down even its core supporters. On the other hand, at least the overall support for the liberal bloc is still more robust than for the PPP. The most pressing thing would be learning how to coalesce at critical moments.

articles.title: Xi Jinping May Have His Own Reasons to Avert a China-Russia-US Summit
articles.full_text:
A formal trilateral could raise strategic questions that are awkward for the EU, Ukraine – and China itself.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin have put Xi Jinping in an unusual position by expressing interest in a trilateral summit with the Chinese leader at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen mid-November. Xi’s cautious response so far – Moscow and Washington have confirmed discussion, while Beijing has yet to commit publicly – could help Europe and Ukraine avoid the worst: major powers making decisions about the region in their absence.
The idea for a meeting came from Russia and it’s not hard to see why. Moscow’s ideal outcome would reportedly be a “Yalta-style” agreement on Ukraine, echoing the 1945 conference at which the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union discussed the post-war order in Europe. But even much more modest results would count as a success. Simply taking part in such a summit would elevate Russia’s status alongside the U.S. and China, help break its diplomatic isolation, potentially drive a further wedge between the U.S. and Europe, and provide an important platform for its narrative of Western threats to Russia.  
A three-way meeting would play to Trump’s self-regard as a dealmaker and peacemaker – and quite possibly his appetite for economic gain. The United States recently eased sanctions on Russian diesel fuel exports, with an initial shipment of 40,000 tonnes reportedly on its way to the U.S. Moscow has also offered to increase fertilizer exports amid shortages caused by the Middle East crisis. But Trump may also have a larger strategic motivation. He has said that nuclear disarmament, not Ukraine, should be at the top of the agenda.
With the APEC summit in China being discussed as the venue, Xi would surely welcome the huge symbolic win of being seen as the world leader capable of hosting such an important gathering – while possibly helping to widen the divide between the U.S. and Europe. But Xi also has very good reasons to avoid such a meeting. China has benefited from dealing with Washington and Moscow separately, and it has in the past insisted that both Russia and Ukraine must be involved in any peace process. A China-Russia-U.S. summit to discuss Ukraine’s future without Kyiv would undermine both those positions.
A high-profile trilateral could overshadow the APEC summit, which Beijing wants to use to showcase its economic leadership and promote openness, innovation, and cooperation. A highly publicized gathering of three major powers also would sit uneasily with Beijing’s repeated calls for inclusive multilateralism, particularly at a forum intended to promote regional economic cooperation. 
A successful trilateral might make the risk worthwhile. But such an outcome is uncertain – not least because of the unpredictability of Trump and Putin. The meeting could end up dominating APEC at the expense of Beijing’s economic agenda, without producing any significant outcomes. 
Lastly, while Putin and Trump have major strategic incentives to meet, Xi has a strategic reason to avoid doing so. Trump’s insistence on putting nuclear arms reduction at the top of the agenda is problematic for China. Beijing has long emphasized that its nuclear arsenal is far smaller than those of the United States and Russia – and that Washington and Moscow must make substantial reductions before China joins any talks. Abandoning this position would risk China being bound by the same rules as Russia and the U.S., despite the gap in nuclear capabilities. 
But Xi may recognize that he cannot dismiss the idea of a meeting altogether. Chinese diplomats have reportedly indicated that they would not rule out a trilateral. If Xi cannot prevent such a meeting, he could at least use his position as host to shape it – a less prominent, more informal encounter with a loose agenda focused on major power relations or the global economy, rather than a formal summit focused on Ukraine or nuclear arms control that would raise public expectations. Xi could even cast himself as the host of a Trump-Putin meeting rather than a participant in three-way talks. 
Such stage-management would not protect Europe and Ukraine from the United States, Russia, and China talking about them behind their backs. But it would allow European governments to frame such a meeting as nothing more than an exchange of views. A formal summit explicitly devoted to Ukraine, by contrast, would risk signaling to the world that the three leaders are entitled – by right or by force – to make strategic decisions about Europe in Europe’s absence. That alone would send a terrible precedent for the continent. 
Much can still happen until the APEC summit next month. Another round of U.S.-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi are reportedly under discussion, while Trump’s views on Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy continue to shift. But whatever summitry emerges in Shenzhen, European governments must continue to insist on Ukrainian participation in any talks about the country’s future. Apart from pressing Washington to take them into account, Kyiv and European capitals should also appeal to Xi’s own reservations about a trilateral summit that also carries many risks for Beijing.

articles.title: The China-Taiwan Diplomatic War Is More About Politics Than Economics
articles.full_text:
Taiwan’s formal relationships in Africa and Latin America point to the real factors driving recognition decisions – and it’s not “dollar diplomacy.”
An honor guard stands at attention with flags of Taiwan and Paraguay during a welcome ceremony for Paraguayan President Santiago Peña in Taipei, Taiwan, May 8, 2026.
Since the Chinese Civil War concluded in 1949, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and the Republic of China (ROC) have battled endlessly for diplomatic recognition. Due to Beijing’s “One China” principle, states are forced to either pick one side or pick neither. 
The ROC, now colloquially better known as Taiwan, initially enjoyed an advantage in international recognition due to U.S. anti-communist messaging and generous economic assistance programs. After U.N. Resolution 2758 admitted the PRC to the United Nations and expelled the ROC, the battle for international recognition has tilted increasingly in Beijing’s favor.
Nevertheless, Taiwan still holds formal diplomatic relations across the globe. Three Pacific island-nations – the Marshall Islands, Palau, and Tuvalu – recognize the ROC over the PRC, receiving major financial assistance in return. In Europe, Taiwan has one diplomatic ally, the Vatican. In Africa, Taiwan maintains formal relations with Eswatini (where President Lai Ching-te visited in May), and conducts high-level diplomatic exchanges with the partially-recognized East African state, Somaliland. The Americas, meanwhile, hold seven of Taiwan’s 12 remaining embassies. These states challenge Beijing’s extensive efforts to isolate Taiwan diplomatically, demonstrating that Taipei can maintain and strengthen relations with sovereign nations.
Analyzing Taiwan’s relations with Africa and Latin America comparatively, we can see how and under what circumstances Taipei’s Global South engagement has prevailed against Beijing’s diplomatic efforts. Although economic assistance programs have been critical, Taiwan’s formal relations ultimately depend on political leverage drawn from diplomatic recognition rather than purely economic considerations. The recognition of Taiwan will therefore continue to serve as a political tool for smaller countries, independence movements, and breakaway states that find greater gain from Taipei than Beijing.
Until UNGA Resolution 2758 passed in 1971, Taiwan maintained widespread recognition throughout Africa. During decolonization in the 1950s and 1960s, most newly-independent African states were wary of Beijing’s  communist ideology and optimistic about their inclusion into the international community. Thus, incentivized by Taiwan’s foreign assistance, many African countries recognized the ROC over the PRC as the representative of China between 1960 and 1963. 
By 1971, the year of Resolution 2758, the PRC and Taiwan had an almost equal number of African countries’ recognition (Taiwan’s 20 to the PRC’s 22). Only five African countries recognized the ROC by 1979, highlighting the UNGA Resolution’s devastating impact on Taiwan’s international legitimacy. 
Since African decolonization, Taipei and Beijing have engaged in “dollar diplomacy,” leveraging favorable loans, technical knowledge-sharing, trade, and agricultural assistance to compete for support. Starting in 1960, Taipei began international development programs, trade incentives, and investments throughout Africa to preserve its influence despite being reliant on U.S. aid itself. Taiwan has become increasingly incapable of competing for African countries’ recognition as its economy has become dwarfed by the PRC in recent decades.
Burkina Faso was the latest African country to withdraw its recognition of Taiwan, doing so in 2018. Formerly known as Upper Volta, Burkina Faso first severed relations with Taiwan in 1973, along with much of the rest of the continent. In 1994, under coup-installed former president Blaise Compaoré, Burkina Faso reestablished relations with Taiwan in pursuit of a lucrative economic relationship. 
Due to China’s expanding economy, the Belt and Road Initiative, and chaotic power transfers, Burkina Faso eventually switched its recognition back to the PRC in 2018 after Compaoré lost power. 
Notably, Taiwan’s response solely blamed the PRC. Rather than condemning Burkina Faso’s decision to withdraw recognition of Taiwan, then-President Tsai Ing-wen attacked Beijing for its “serial acts of suppression against Taiwan in the diplomatic sphere” through economic coercion and political interference. 
A series of coups over the past decade has placed Burkina Faso firmly within the PRC’s sphere of influence, with Western counterterrorism forces being expelled and China’s economic and military investment in the country increasing.
Facing dwindling formal relations, Taiwan has adopted a “pragmatic diplomacy” approach, which prioritizes de facto economic influence over political recognition. In Africa, Taiwan operates trade and political representative offices in Nigeria, South Africa, Côte d’Ivoire, and Somaliland. Several quasi-governmental and non-state organizations expand Taiwan’s economic influence on the continent, such as the Taiwan External Trade Development Council, the International Cooperation and Development Fund, and the Taiwan-Africa Business Association. While these organizations have failed  to quell the rapidly expanding PRC influence across Africa, they highlight Taiwan’s capacity to maintain a diplomatic presence.
Eswatini’s continued support for Taiwan has resulted in both diplomatic condemnation and economic exclusion from Beijing. In 2026, the PRC prevented Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te from visiting Eswatini during celebrations of King Mswati III’s 40th year in power by pressuring Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar to revoke flight permits for Taiwan’s delegation. Lai clandestinely visited Eswatini the following month despite Beijing’s efforts to prevent the trip. However the episode illustrated how the PRC can use its political and economic clout against Taiwanese diplomacy.
Additionally, Eswatini’s exclusion from PRC investment through institutions like the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC) introduces an opportunity cost that harms the country’s economic competitiveness. Eswatini’s status as a monarchy, however, reduces the salience of political grievances tied to broader social, political, or economic conditions derivative of its adversarial relationship with the PRC.
Somaliland, the breakaway region of northern Somalia, has developed a unique relationship with Taiwan. Most countries deny Somaliland’s political status. Since declaring independence in 1991, Somaliland has lobbied the international community to recognize it as a fully autonomous state, with Israel being the only U.N. member state to recognize its independence in 2025. In similar states of de facto independence, Taiwan and Somaliland enhanced their bilateral relationship in 2020 to increase shared economic investment in East Africa and cement their political willingness to explore new, Western-aligned friendships.
Taiwan has implemented many development programs there for public health, education, government modernization, democratization, and humanitarian assistance. Taiwan’s ICDF currently facilitates six development programs in Somaliland, while Taiwan benefits from increased political and economic access to East Africa. While Somaliland has not officially established diplomatic recognition of Taiwan, the relationship could prove to be consequential for China-U.S. competition and rising insecurity in the Horn of Africa.
In its pursuit of legitimacy, Taiwan will see more success in diplomatic initiatives targeting smaller, less established, or more politically unique states. Countries that have already carved their places in the international community are less likely to have political environments conducive to recognition of Taiwan over the PRC, as they will prioritize economic opportunity and stability over Taiwan’s aspirations.
The PRC’s rapid economic growth and its “One China” principle” create a geopolitical competition stacked against Taiwan. Moving forward, Taiwan will likely have to leverage future relationships with breakaway movements, global pariahs, and peculiar governments to rebuild its international influence.
In Latin America, Taiwan’s diplomatic partnerships date back many decades. Unlike in Africa, where most countries were colonies until the 1960s, Latin American nations have been independent since the 19th century. Most established relations with the ROC before it relocated to Taiwan in 1949. Taipei then consolidated its diplomatic standing by establishing new relations with Haiti, Paraguay, and Uruguay in the mid-1950s. The ROC similarly established relations with newly-independent Grenada, Dominica, St. Kitts and Nevis, St. Vincent and the Grenadines, St. Lucia, and Belize in the 1980s.
The Cold War aided Taiwan, as Latin American governments could signal U.S. alignment by maintaining relations with the anticommunist ROC over the communist PRC. In fact, only Cuba and Chile cut ties with the ROC to establish relations with the PRC before 1971, both under leftist, Marxism-endorsing leaders. Although Mexico and most South American countries switched in the 1970s and 1980s, Taiwan continued commercial and cultural relations with these countries and still holds commercial offices in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico, and Peru.
As in Africa, Taiwan’s agricultural advisory missions significantly improved Latin American food production. One such mission more than doubled Dominican rice yields from 1972-82. Also like in Africa, Taiwan and China’s “dollar diplomacy” took off in the 1990s and 2000s, as Taiwan significantly increased economic donations to its allies, while China gave bountiful gifts in exchange for switching recognition, including stadiums in Dominica, Grenada, the Bahamas, and Costa Rica between 1997 and 2007.
Following the “diplomatic truce” with Beijing during Ma Ying-jeou’s 2008-16 administration, China resumed its diplomatic poaching after Tsai Ing-wen was elected in 2016. In 2017 and 2018, Panama, the Dominican Republic and El Salvador switched to China, reportedly securing hundreds of millions in Chinese funds in exchange.
Notably, the first Trump administration condemned El Salvador’s decision, and Trump signed the 2020 Taiwan Allies International Protection and Enhancement Initiative (TAIPEI) Act, which codifies U.S. support for Taiwan’s remaining diplomatic partnerships. The Biden administration rebuked Nicaragua’s dynastic dictatorship for ditching Taiwan and embracing China in 2021, and attempted to stop Honduras’ leftist government from doing the same two years later. 
Despite Beijing’s best efforts, however, seven countries in the Americas continue opting for relations with Taiwan over China: Belize, Guatemala, Haiti, Paraguay, St. Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines.
A country of 15 million, Guatemala has strengthened ties with both Taipei and Washington recently. Taiwan operates six developmental projects in Guatemala, spanning educational programs, medical technology, and agricultural assistance. These projects follow 26 completed ones, all through Taiwan’s ICDF. Taiwan has also signed commercial agreements, helping Guatemala become Taiwan’s fourth-largest coffee supplier. Taiwan boosts Guatemala’s human capital by giving several hundred scholarships to Guatemalan students studying in Taipei. 
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has commended Guatemala’s president for continuing to recognize Taiwan, and the U.S. and Taiwanese governments have jointly led development initiatives with Guatemala. With the United States being Guatemala’s largest export market and the source of 25 percent of its GDP via migrant remittances, Guatemala has pragmatic reasons to please Washington by recognizing Taipei.
Paraguay – Taiwan’s only remaining South American ally – has similarly maintained loyalty to Taipei. After its 35-year dictatorship fell in 1989, Paraguay maintained deep engagement with Taiwan. Economic engagements have solidified, with Taiwan becoming Paraguay’s second largest beef importer and largest pork importer. As agricultural exports generate 10 percent of Paraguay’s GDP and jobs, this commercial relationship is no trivial matter. 
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña’s visit to Taipei in May cemented this relationship by expanding chicken exports to Taiwan and obtaining pledges for AI computing center investments in Paraguay. Notably, with the exception of the 2008–12 Fernando Lugo administration, Paraguay’s executive has always been a member of the Colorado Party, which holds a multidecade close relationship with Taiwanese officials.
articles.summary: Taiwan’s formal relationships in Africa and Latin America point to the real factors driving recognition decisions – and it’s not “dollar diplomacy.”

articles.title: With Strict Agendas and Silent Corridors Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Is Muzzling the Press
articles.full_text:
Journalists covering the country’s parliament are pushing back against new rules that constrict their ability to question officials.
When Kazakhstan’s Kurultai convened in late August for the first time, there were new rules for the media. Journalists in the Kazakh capital’s parliament building were no longer able to question deputies in the corridors. The new rules set firm boundaries not only on where, but what, they could ask members of the country’s new unicameral parliament. 
At the opening of the Kurultai’s first session on August 28, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proclaimed the body would “radically modernize the system of government and provide a powerful impetus to the work of the entire state apparatus.” Later in his speech he urged the Kutultai to become “a platform for national dialogue to develop solutions to key issues in society.”
The boundaries of that dialogue, however, are to be set by the Kurultai itself. 
As explained by the Kurultai’s Deputy Chief of Staff Bolat Kalyanbekov in a September 2 Facebook post, “All interactions between journalists and deputies – as well as invited members of the Government – will now take place exclusively within the press center and strictly in relation to the Kurultai’s agenda.”
Kalyanbekov stated that briefings would be held on a regular basis and laid out the rationale behind the decision to bar off-topic questions.
“Our goal is to communicate the substance of the draft laws under consideration by the Kurultai to the public as clearly and comprehensively as possible – explaining the significance of each new legal provision and how the decisions being made may impact the lives of citizens,” he wrote.
Kalyanbekov also argued that the new rules were consistent both with Kazakh law and “established global practices.”
That’s not quite how Fiona O’Brien, the Europe and Central Asia regional director for the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), sees it. “Allowing journalists to informally approach and question deputies in the halls of parliament, and to ask questions not strictly related to the agenda of press conferences, are standard practices of established democracies,” O’Brien told The Diplomat.
Although Kazakhstan deems itself a democratic state, human rights organizations such as Freedom House, classify the country as “Not Free.”
“The kinds of restrictions on movement and questions implemented in Kazakhstan are more common in authoritarian or hybrid environments, where the authorities try to maintain an appearance of democracy while retaining strict control of the information sphere,” O’Brien explained.
On October 20, Otkir Kurek – an independent media outlet headed by Nazymgul Kumyspayeva, who also runs a YouTube channel – reported that a group of around 40 journalists accredited to the Kurultai had sent an appeal to Aibek Dadebay, chair of the body, demanding revision of the new media rules. 
Otkir Kurek means “sharp shovel” in Kazakh.
Dadebay is also leader of the Adilet party, into which the former ruling party Amanat (née Nur-Otan) merged earlier this year in the runup to the Kurultai elections on August 23. Until May 5, Dadebay headed Tokayev’s presidential administration.
In the recent appeal, as reported by KazTAG, the Kazakh journalists took particular issue with the restriction of questions to agenda-items only. 
Under the present rules, “For a question that the moderator deems off-topic, the journalist receives a warning. Two violations mean the loss of accreditation for six months… For a journalist who covers parliament, this is effectively a six-month ban from the profession.”
The appeal noted that the purpose of accreditation is to enable journalists “to inform the public broadly and promptly.”
“Kazakhstan’s parliament and other state organs have long tried to stop journalists asking ‘off-topic’ questions during press conferences,” CPJ’s O’Brien explained. “Introducing sanctions for doing so and preventing journalists from mixing freely with deputies in the halls of parliament essentially closes down the last avenues for journalists to freely question parliamentarians on issues not decided in advance by the authorities themselves.”
“A briefing that repeats what has already been said at the meeting provides no new information,” the journalists argued in their appeal, seeking a revision to the existing regulations to allow journalists to ask questions outside the strict agenda but within the purview of the featured speakers. 
“A minister or deputy can always refuse to answer a question, respond later, or respond in writing,” the appeal noted. The journalists characterized the existing policy as unjustified. Journalists, they argued, need to be free to question ministers, deputies, and other officials – who, the appeal pointed out, “rarely appear in public and for whom the public has many questions.”
Kazakh journalists have already run afoul of these rules. 
In early October, in the wake of a tragic accident on the Caspian Sea in which 14 servicemembers drowned during a military drill, journalist Asem Gumarova of Ulysmedia.kz asked questions related to the incident during a briefing with a member of parliament, Unzila Shapak, and Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs Sanjar Adilov. The brief was to cover a draft cybercrime law. 
Gumarova asked Shapak when the 146 million tenge that had been reportedly collected by Kurultai members would be transferred to the families of the fallen servicemen. She also asked Adilov about reports of pressure being exerted by mysterious callers masquerading as police demanding that the authors of critical posts related to the Caspian accident take their posts down. 
Ulysmedia said it received a warning letter threatening to strip Gumarova of her accreditation. The publication cited the “extraordinary nature of the incident and public demand” as justifying Gumarova’s questions.
The recent appeal to Dadebay cited the incident directly, noting that “[t]he question concerned police work online or crimes carried out under the guise of police – that is, the very topic of the briefing.”
Accreditation procedures vary country to country. But broadly speaking accreditation confers a degree of legitimacy on a journalist and their outlet and, importantly, provides access to official spaces and proceedings. In Kazakhstan, the Foreign Ministry handles foreign media and individual state bodies, like the Kurultai, as well as the Ministry of Culture and Information, deal with the domestic media. 
Kumyspayeva, the editor-in-chief and founder of Otkir Kurek, was earlier this month denied accreditation by the Kurultai. Kalyanbekov provided an official response, which The Diplomat has reviewed, stating that the reason was a mismatch in email addresses on her application materials.
“The official reason given for the denial was that I had provided my professional email address in the accreditation application rather than the email address listed on our media outlet’s website,” Kumyspaeva told The Diplomat. “In my view, this was merely a technicality used as a pretext to deny me accreditation. I suspect the real reason lies in my independent journalism.”
Kumyspayeva takes no government funding, and told The Diplomat that the outlet does not participate in government-funded media contracts. 
“As a result, government institutions have no leverage to dictate our editorial policy, determine what subjects we cover, or tell us which questions we are allowed to ask,” she said.
articles.summary: Journalists covering the country’s parliament are pushing back against new rules that constrict their ability to question officials.

articles.title: South China Sea Code of Conduct: A Deal Is Not Enough
articles.full_text:
A COC that lacks credible enforcement mechanisms would do little to address security challenges.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi delivers a speech on China-ASEAN relations at the ASEAN Secretariat in Jakarta, Indonesia, on July 11, 2022.
As ASEAN and China work toward concluding a Code of Conduct (COC) for the South China Sea in 2026, the central question is not simply whether an agreement can be reached, but whether it will meaningfully reduce tensions. A deal is not enough if it does not address the underlying drivers of tension and shape actors’ behaviors. 
The South China Sea is a contested maritime zone, involving China and ASEAN members Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. To address the overlapping maritime claims and disputes, ASEAN and China have been negotiating a COC to establish a rules-based framework to manage maritime disputes, reduce miscalculations, and prevent armed conflict. 
After nearly two decades of negotiations, Manila, as the current ASEAN chair, has recently signaled that agreement on the COC is at hand. A COC would represent an important diplomatic achievement. 
Yet an agreement that lacks credible enforcement mechanisms, preserves ambiguity over compliance, or constrains Southeast Asian countries’ strategic autonomy could do little to address the region’s underlying security challenges.
The substance of the agreement matters more than announcing its completion. A COC that primarily reiterates commitments to dialogue, restraint, and peaceful dispute resolution – like those contained in the existing Declaration of Conduct – would have limited practical value. The COC needs clear procedures for managing incidents, resolving disagreements, and addressing violations. 
The South China Sea has seen increased military activities. China has built a network of military facilities in the Spratly and Paracel Islands, some of which are now equipped to host bombers. In 2025, Vietnam commenced its own reclamation work on occupied features, building infrastructure to support a larger military presence. 
Naval confrontations between China and the Philippines continue, highlighting the fragility of stability in the contested waters. Diplomatic commitments alone cannot guarantee responsible behavior
If the COC is to improve regional stability, it must include practical measures to prevent escalation and hold parties accountable for their conduct.
This raises a second challenge: ASEAN’s ability to ensure compliance. Even if the agreement includes specific obligations, its effectiveness will depend on whether parties are willing to implement them when doing so conflicts with their strategic interests. ASEAN’s consensus-based approach, while essential to maintaining regional unity, can complicate collective responses to violations, particularly when member states have different economic and security relationships with China.
A credible COC should therefore establish transparent procedures for reporting incidents, conducting consultations, and addressing alleged breaches. Regular reviews and clearly defined dispute-management channels could help prevent disagreements from escalating. Without a meaningful accountability mechanism, the COC risks just becoming a declaration of intent.
The agreement must also protect Southeast Asian states’ strategic autonomy. China may seek arrangements that limit activities it considers destabilizing, such as joint military exercises with the United States. Provisions governing military exercises, defense partnerships, or cooperation with external powers could create constraints that extend beyond managing disputes in the South China Sea. If drafted too broadly, the COC could inadvertently restrict ASEAN members’ ability to pursue their own security interests.
The challenge is to distinguish between measures designed to prevent maritime incidents and provisions that limit legitimate defense cooperation. Southeast Asian states should retain the freedom to conduct exercises, modernize their armed forces, and establish partnerships with countries outside the region, consistent with international law. A COC that undermines these freedoms would risk weakening the very strategic independence ASEAN seeks to preserve.
The Philippines’ expanding defense cooperation with non-Southeast Asian powers such as Australia and Japan illustrates this tension. Manila’s partnerships strengthen its deterrence capabilities and provide additional options for responding to maritime pressure. However, Beijing may view these arrangements as contributing to strategic competition, complicating efforts to reach a mutually acceptable agreement.

Extra-regional powers’ participation in maritime security, however, should not obscure ASEAN’s central role in shaping regional norms.

articles.title: Why Durga Puja’s Celebration in West Bengal This Year Was Different
articles.full_text:
The BJP government in the state stripped the festival of its secular-cultural uniqueness to impose religious and ritualistic practices that are anathema to Bengalis.
An idol of the goddess Durga floats on a river after its immersion at the end of the Durga Puja festival.
Amid the festive fervor that engulfs India in autumn, the eastern Indian state of West Bengal is immersed in the 10-day celebration of Durga Puja.
Durga Puja, or the worship of the ten-armed goddess Durga, who slayed a demon king, symbolizes the victory of good over evil. It is the biggest festival for Bengalis and for the Bengali diaspora. It is much more than a religious festival and has metamorphosed into the largest public art festival in the world as well.
Given the significance of Durga Puja in the lives of Bengalis, ruling parties in the state have always leveraged the festival for political purposes. This was the first Durga Puja held under the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which came to power in Bengal just five months ago, after defeating the regional Trinamool Congress (TMC).
This year, however, the festival was in the news for all the wrong reasons. For the first time in Bengal, a stampede in a puja pandal (venue for worship) in north Kolkata left 19 dead and over 25 injured on October 17. The dead included 11 women and five children; the youngest was aged seven. A pall of gloom descended upon Bengal’s largest socio-cultural celebration. Kolkata has never witnessed such a tragedy during Durga Puja.
On the evening of the stampede disaster, there was another shock in store for Kolkata. Images of bulldozers demolishing bookstalls adjoining puja pandals in south Kolkata emerged.
For decades, leftist parties had set up bookstalls selling Marxist literature during the puja days. This time, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari declared that his government would not allow communist culture to flourish. His government used bulldozers to flatten the stalls. In north Kolkata’s Dum Dum area, Hindutva goons vandalized a leftist-run book stall and even tore great classics of Bengali literature. Kolkata is famous for its love for intellectual banter and books.
Although Durga Puja revolves around the worship of a Hindu goddess, in Bengal it is a cultural phenomenon rather than a ritualistic-religious one. Unlike North India, where Navaratri (nine days) is observed through strict fasting, prayers, consumption of only vegetarian fare, and worship of the Mata Rani (Mother Goddess), in Bengal the connection with Durga is more personal. She is perceived as a loving daughter coming to her parental home and is therefore pampered with the best food and sweet offerings, including sacrificial meat.
What makes the Durga Puja of Bengal unique is the pantheon of gods it includes — Saraswati and Lakshmi, the goddesses of learning and wealth, respectively – regarded as Durga’s children along with the male gods, Ganesh and Kartik. Her annual arrival on earth, accompanied by her children, is the rationale behind the celebration. This celebration is marked by cultural dance, music, theatrical performances, publication of literary magazines, new clothes, revelry, and feasting. It is an inclusive, secular approach to an ostensibly religious festival, which the Hindutva-dominated North Indian psyche cannot comprehend.
Under former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee of the TMC (2011-2026), the festival expanded both in scale and budget. Banerjee inaugurated thousands of community pujas every year in Kolkata, patronizing neighborhood clubs that organized the festival. Organizers would unleash their creativity and artistry through the pandal decorations and portrayal of Durga. Known as “theme pujas,” pandals depicted topical issues ranging from social problems to contemporary subjects like climate change, and even abstract concepts.
The dizzying creativity in the art installations attracted domestic and foreign tourists to Bengal during the puja season. As per a British Council study in 2021, the Durga Puja creative economy was worth around $4.53 billion, contributing 2.5 percent of the state’s GDP.
Bengal’s Durga Puja even earned the prestigious UNESCO tag for being an “Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity” in 2021. In its citation, UNESCO stated: “Durga Puja is seen as the best instance of the public performance of religion and art, and as a thriving ground for collaborative artists and designers.” Banerjee considered the UNESCO recognition a major achievement of her government and even started a Durga Puja Carnival to showcase the festivities.
Several ministers of Banerjee’s TMC became synonymous with their neighborhood pujas, which acquired political clout and prominence. Even prominent TMC leaders like former mayor Farhid (Bobby) Hakim, a Muslim, were famous for their patronage of the Durga Puja. In fact, this secular celebration of Durga Puja, where Muslims also participate, is what rankled the Hindutva organizations.  The TMC under Banerjee was known for its secular credentials and its patronage of festivals of all major religions, be it Durga Puja, Christmas or Eid.
In contrast, the BJP has always harped on retaining the purity of the “sanatan dharma” (literally, universal truth, i.e., Hinduism). It has always encouraged sectarian and communal politics with scant regard for minorities. Even before it came to power in Bengal, the BJP and its ideological mentor, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), had stoked the vegetarian versus non-vegetarian debate, projecting the Bengali tradition of offering meat to Durga as an aberration.
Not surprisingly, much before the festival, Adhikari issued a stern warning to puja organizers with a list of dos and don’ts, including strict adherence to religious rituals. Organizers were also given diktats not to take creative liberties with the idol and the pandal in any way that can defile the sanctity of the worship. Earlier Durga Puja pandal themes like taboos surrounding menstruation were anathema to the BJP government.
It was obvious that the BJP government in Bengal is intent on stripping Durga Puja of its cultural, secular, and artistic character and imposing a rigid ritualistic norm of worship in its stead. The state administration was more focused on such extraneous issues rather than basics like ensuring crowd management; this critical lapse led to the stampede on October 17. The Telegraph newspaper observed that the Adhikari government had replaced police personnel, who in the past were lauded for their efficient crowd control measures, with a new team of inexperienced officers.
Even the Left Front government, which ruled Bengal for 34 years (1977 to 2011) and was avowedly atheist, never interfered or restricted the festive celebrations of Durga Puja. Rather, it termed the puja as a “sharad utsav” (autumnal festival) and participated in it by setting up bookstalls at the venues.
The BJP’s victory in pluralistic Bengal surprised many. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah had been desperate to oust the proud Banerjee, who had publicly challenged the prime minister several times. Therefore, Durga Puja 2026 was, to many Bengalis, an attempt by the BJP to erase the TMC’s contributions to the Durga Puja spectacle.
Soon after forming the Bengal government, BJP leaders replaced TMC politicians heading prominent puja committees across Kolkata. Banerjee’s government used to give around $1,000 to puja committees. This year, the BJP government provided a grant of $1,000 as well as free electricity to each puja committee across Bengal.
The BJP, which valorizes the deity Ram, celebrates the Dussehra festival as Ram’s conquest of the demon, Ravana. In Bengal, the party had to make an uncomfortable compromise; it had to worship goddess Durga, and in the way Bengalis celebrate the festival.
In keeping with its communally divisive agenda, Chief Minister Adhikari announced on Wednesday that only those who believe in “sanatan dharma” will be allowed to touch the Durga idols during immersion in the river. The opposition has accused him of advocating untouchability.  But Adhikari is unperturbed.

articles.title: What States Make of Military Exercises: Ulchi and Beyond
articles.full_text:
Repeated military cooperation can help build predictability, trust, interoperability, and institutionalized relationships among participants.
U.S. Army soldiers advance forward during a live fire exercise as part of Ulchi Freedom Shield at Georgia Story Live Fire Complex, South Korea on Aug. 20, 2025.
Just before the South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise began in mid-August, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered a substantial reduction in its scale. Describing the drills as “costly” and an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea – a state he termed “unthreatening and respectful” – Trump also criticized what he described as Seoul’s lack of support for U.S. operations against Iran.
Trump’s sudden decision raised concerns about South Korea-U.S. defense readiness, alliance reliability, and Washington’s wider commitment to Asia. Several analysts warned that reducing exercises could weaken deterrence and alliance coordination, while others questioned whether the move would secure reciprocal restraint from Pyongyang. Such concerns are understandable: joint military exercises are a visible manifestation of the South Korea-U.S. defense commitment, while North Korea routinely denounces them as rehearsals for war. 
The reduction alone, however, does not carry a single, self-evident political meaning. U.S. commanders have since emphasized that other combined training continues and proposed changes to its frequency and geographic distribution. How audiences interpret these changes depends on the wider pattern of cooperation, established relationships, and political context.
Joint military exercises can serve two different but complementary strategic functions. They demonstrate capability and resolve to deter adversaries, but exercises also facilitate defense diplomacy. Repeated military cooperation can help build predictability, trust, interoperability, and institutionalized relationships among participants. 
Our research suggests that an exercise’s scale and scope alone cannot reliably distinguish between these functions. Deterrence and defense diplomacy often generate the same observable characteristics, making it difficult to determine where one ends and the other begins simply by examining an exercise’s material features.
Larger and more complex exercises – featuring tens of thousands of troops, sophisticated command-and-control systems, live-fire maneuvers, and complex scenarios – can demonstrate greater warfighting capability and resolve to deter. At the same time, however, those same characteristics may instead reflect years of accumulated defense cooperation and deeper levels of trust and institutional integration between the participating militaries. Their material features reveal what militaries practice and provide evidence of their capabilities but cannot by themselves establish the political messages governments intend or how different audiences will interpret them. Rather, as a political signal, joint military exercises ultimately depend on what participating states and other audiences make of them.
Different audiences will not necessarily derive the same meaning from the same exercise. Washington might intend a reduction in Ulchi as restraint toward Pyongyang, while North Korea might interpret it as a concession, Seoul as uncertainty over U.S. commitment to the bilateral alliance, and Beijing as evidence of Washington’s transactional approach to alliance management. Established relationships and political contexts are therefore essential to interpreting an exercise’s strategic meaning. 
Instead, established relationships and political contexts are more important in determining the strategic meaning of exercises than scale and scope alone. The history of Ulchi itself illustrates this. 
Ulchi’s scale and scope have seldom increased in tandem with the danger from North Korea. This divergence is significant. If Ulchi’s scale simply tracked the North Korean military threat, as one would expect for greater deterrence, participation should have risen relatively consistently alongside Pyongyang’s expanding nuclear and missile capabilities. Instead, exercise participation has repeatedly risen and fallen according to changes in the diplomatic environment. Participation declined during periods associated with the Six-Party Talks and suspended altogether to facilitate diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Trump’s first term.
The scale of South Korean participation also reflects domestic politics. According to publicly available data, South Korean troop numbers were generally lower under the progressive administrations of Kim Dae-jung and Roh Moo-hyun, increased substantially under conservative presidents Lee Myung-bak and Park Geun-hye, and were again affected by diplomatic engagement under Moon Jae-in. These patterns are consistent with progressive administrations’ greater emphasis on creating diplomatic space for negotiations with the North and conservative administrations’ stronger emphasis on deterrence and alliance cohesion.
Trump’s decision should therefore be understood within this broader political context. Indeed, his own explanations identified several purposes for the same reduction: reducing costs, signaling restraint toward North Korea, and expressing dissatisfaction with Seoul over Iran. The reduction’s material features cannot establish which purpose predominates or how different audiences will interpret it.
Recent developments illustrate why Ulchi’s reduction should also be understood within the wider pattern of South Korea-U.S. military cooperation. In an interview with the Financial Times, U.S. Army Pacific commander General Ronald Clark emphasized both displaying military capabilities to influence adversaries’ calculations and strengthening military partnerships. His account illustrates how the two functions can reinforce one another: military partnerships help sustain the access and cooperation through which forces demonstrate capability and resolve.
South Korea-U.S. cooperation has continued despite the reduction in Ulchi. Eighth Army commander Lieutenant General Joe Hilbert clarified that other combined training continued, although some activities affected by Trump’s order were conducted by South Korean forces alone. Continued trilateral training through Freedom Edge and South Korea’s observer participation in Keen Sword also demonstrate different forms of military engagement. Observation offers opportunities for familiarity and relationship building without active participation in training. These activities do not cancel out Ulchi’s reduction, but they complicate its interpretation as a broader withdrawal from military cooperation.
Exercise design can also change in response to operational requirements. U.S. Forces Korea commander General Xavier Brunson has proposed more frequent training and geographically dispersed operations, drawing lessons from Ukraine about the vulnerability of concentrated command posts. He suggested the possibility of expanding the scope of exercises from Jeju Island to Gyeonggi Province, while also adjusting the training schedule to include additional smaller-scale drills between the two large annual exercises, Freedom Shield and Ulchi Freedom Shield. Frequency, geographic reach, and the concentration of forces need not change together. Thus, the size of a single exercise therefore provides an incomplete picture of the training program. Whether audiences interpret such changes as reinforcing alliance commitments or altering priorities depends on their political context. 
Reducing Ulchi or cancelling a single amphibious exercise does not erase South Korea-U.S. warfighting capability. The institutional defense relationship between the two militaries established over decades – combined command structures, joint planning, interoperability, established procedures, and accumulated experience and “muscle memory” – remains in place. None of this is to suggest that exercises are irrelevant to preparedness; repeated reductions or cancellations over an extended period could eventually erode South Korea-U.S. interoperability and combined warfighting effectiveness. The effects, however, would be cumulative rather than instantaneous. A reduction or cancellation of a single iteration should not be conflated with the disappearance of capabilities built through decades of combined training.
Exercise scale and scope matter, but their strategic meaning is neither fixed nor self-evident. Rather than asking simply whether the United States is exercising more or less and with whom, the more pertinent questions are what particular exercises are intended to accomplish and how Seoul, Tokyo, Washington, Pyongyang, Beijing and other regional audiences interpret them. The deterrent or diplomatic value of an exercise ultimately lies not simply in how many troops participate, but in the political meaning that states attach to their participation – or absence.

Deterrence and defense diplomacy often generate the same observable characteristics, making it difficult to determine where one ends and the other begins simply by examining an exercise’s material features.
Larger and more complex exercises – featuring tens of thousands of troops, sophisticated command-and-control systems, live-fire maneuvers, and complex scenarios – can demonstrate greater warfighting capability and resolve to deter. At the same time, however, those same characteristics may instead reflect years of accumulated defense cooperation and deeper levels of trust and institutional integration between the participating militaries. Their material features reveal what militaries practice and provide evidence of their capabilities but cannot by themselves establish the political messages governments intend or how different audiences will interpret them. Rather, as a political signal, joint military exercises ultimately depend on what participating states and other audiences make of them.
Different audiences will not necessarily derive the same meaning from the same exercise. Washington might intend a reduction in Ulchi as restraint toward Pyongyang, while North Korea might interpret it as a concession, Seoul as uncertainty over U.S. commitment to the bilateral alliance, and Beijing as evidence of Washington’s transactional approach to alliance management. Established relationships and political contexts are therefore essential to interpreting an exercise’s strategic meaning. 
Instead, established relationships and political contexts are more important in determining the strategic meaning of exercises than scale and scope alone. The history of Ulchi itself illustrates this. 
Ulchi’s scale and scope have seldom increased in tandem with the danger from North Korea. This divergence is significant. If Ulchi’s scale simply tracked the North Korean military threat, as one would expect for greater deterrence, participation should have risen relatively consistently alongside Pyongyang’s expanding nuclear and missile capabilities. Instead, exercise participation has repeatedly risen and fallen according to changes in the diplomatic environment. Participation declined during periods associated with the Six-Party Talks and suspended altogether to facilitate diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Trump’s first term.
The scale of South Korean participation also reflects domestic politics. According to publicly available data, South Korean troop numbers were generally lower under the progressive administrations of Kim Dae-jung and Roh Moo-hyun, increased substantially under conservative presidents Lee Myung-bak and Park Geun-hye, and were again affected by diplomatic engagement under Moon Jae-in. These patterns are consistent with progressive administrations’ greater emphasis on creating diplomatic space for negotiations with the North and conservative administrations’ stronger emphasis on deterrence and alliance cohesion.
Trump’s decision should therefore be understood within this broader political context. Indeed, his own explanations identified several purposes for the same reduction: reducing costs, signaling restraint toward North Korea, and expressing dissatisfaction with Seoul over Iran. The reduction’s material features cannot establish which purpose predominates or how different audiences will interpret it.
Recent developments illustrate why Ulchi’s reduction should also be understood within the wider pattern of South Korea-U.S. military cooperation. In an interview with the Financial Times, U.S. Army Pacific commander General Ronald Clark emphasized both displaying military capabilities to influence adversaries’ calculations and strengthening military partnerships. His account illustrates how the two functions can reinforce one another: military partnerships help sustain the access and cooperation through which forces demonstrate capability and resolve.
articles.summary: Repeated military cooperation can help build predictability, trust, interoperability, and institutionalized relationships among participants.

articles.title: Karakoram 2026: Inside China-Pakistan Joint Military Training in Xinjiang
articles.full_text:
The deteriorating security environment in the region thus reinforces the importance of China-Pakistan military cooperation.
Chinese and Pakistani soldiers conduct a live-fire exercise as part of Karakoram 2026 in Xinjiang, China, held from Oct. 14-22, 2026.
On October 14, China and Pakistan began joint military training known as Karakoram 2026. According to official sources, the training’s opening ceremony was held in Korla city, Xinjiang, China. The main objective of this training is to focus on joint counterterrorism operations in high-altitude areas, according to China’s Ministry of National Defense. 
The nine-day exercise encompassed a range of operational and tactical training activities that are significant not only for bilateral military cooperation but also in the context of a changing regional security environment. 
Bilateral military exercises between Pakistan and China are a well-established and recurring feature of their defense cooperation. The two countries conducted the Sea Guardian IV naval exercise earlier this year to enhance interoperability and maritime cooperation. Joint counterterrorism drills are also a constant feature of their defense cooperation, with the previous example being Warrior IX held in December 2025. 
Karakoram 2026 particularly focused on joint counterterrorism in high-altitude areas, with “skills training in UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] operation, on-the-move target search and firing, and long-range sniping, and joint command and live-force exercises,” according to a Chinese Defense Ministry spokesperson. 
China Central Television’s military channel said that China provided all the equipment, including Type 191 rifles, Type 201 squad machine guns, Type 11 armored assault vehicles, Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles, artillery, and both unmanned and anti-unmanned systems. The use of Chinese equipment and subsequent Pakistani familiarization with equipment could boost the likelihood of future Pakistani procurement. 
However, the most notable feature of Karakoram 2026 is that this is the first time both countries are moving away from counterterrorism training by specialized units to regular army forces. This development will further strengthen defense cooperation and reinforce the broader all-weather strategic partnership between Pakistan and China. The main aim of this is to increase interoperability and joint cooperation on terrorism-related issues.  
Karakoram 2026 is a reflection of broader convergence between China and Pakistan over shared security concerns in the region. Their respective threat perceptions may not be identical, but they have a shared interest in preventing terrorist organizations from exploiting territorial vulnerabilities. Beijing continues to have concerns about the potential for attacks in China, while Chinese nationals operating in Afghanistan and Pakistan have faced attacks on occasion. Joint counterterrorism training provides an institutional mechanism to translate these shared concerns into practical military cooperation. 
One key component of these exercises was UAV operations. The motivation is obvious considering the emergence of drone warfare in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, especially the use of UAVs by terrorist outfits. Training in this domain will increase situational awareness while simultaneously supporting surveillance operations. At the same time, mobile target detection and engagement will strengthen coordination under dynamic battlefield conditions. 
Long-range sniping and live-force exercises further test tactical proficiency, decision-making, and interoperability. For participating forces, this exercise would be helpful in coordinating response and improving communication during complex operations.
Looking at all the capabilities involved in Karakoram 2026, it is evident that the exercises were specially designed in relevance to the difficult terrain of northern Pakistan and the bordering Chinese region of Xinjiang. The China-Pakistan border region has difficult, mountainous terrain with extreme weather conditions complicating security operations. However, one should not perceive these exercises as evidence of China and Pakistan preparing for a specific operation in the region. Rather, Karakoram 2026 is significant mainly due to improved preparedness for shared counterterrorism contingencies and strengthening military-to-military familiarity. 
Another major dimension setting the scene for these exercises is the fraught security environment between Afghanistan and Pakistan, which has complicated Pakistan’s counterterrorism efforts. Islamabad has repeatedly raised concerns about the presence of Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants on Afghan territory and their ability to conduct cross-border attacks. For Pakistan, the recent surge in drone attacks especially by the militants across the border raises another challenge that needs to be addressed. 
A 2026 report by the U.N. Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team documented escalating cross-border attacks involving Pakistan and Afghanistan and reported continued support for the TTP by Afghanistan’s de facto Taliban government. In this context, joint training in drone operations may help Pakistan improve both surveillance and defense. The value of such experience will greatly depend on whether the units and police forces bearing the brunt of these attacks, received practical training in counterdrone defense.           
The biggest implication of Karakoram 2026, however, is not the specific training received; it is the institutionalization of cooperation. With air, naval, and now army training exercises, China and Pakistan have developed a framework covering all three services. Pakistan used Chinese platforms during the May 2025 conflict with India, and army-level interoperability is a natural and logical next step in defense cooperation. 
Karakoram 2026 is not merely a military training but a broader reflection of evolving security priorities of China and Pakistan. With the resurgence of terrorist attacks, counterterrorism cooperation sits at the forefront of Islamabad’s national security concerns. On the other hand, Beijing remains heavily invested in Pakistan under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), and the security of Chinese nationals in Pakistan remains an important dimension of bilateral relations. 
The deteriorating security environment in the region thus reinforces the importance of China-Pakistan military cooperation. The UAV-related training, coordination in command, and realistic field exercises at Karakoram 2026 can be understood against the broader need to improve situational awareness, tactical coordination, and responsiveness to emerging threats. 
However, the effectiveness of military training cannot be measured solely by the completion of an exercise. Its lasting value will depend on the extent to which the participating forces incorporate lessons from joint training into their operational practices and adapt to emerging security challenges.

articles.title: Japan Needs Higher Interest Rates
articles.full_text:
Japanese exporters enjoy high demand and strong profit margins, but importers are under severe pressure. The weak yen also hurts Japanese consumers.
On a recent visit to Sapporo, the city on Japan’s northern island where my parents came from, my wife and I found gentle people, mild autumn days, and excellent food. As tourists who live and work in the United States, we also enjoyed very low prices: lunch at a high-quality restaurant cost only about $20 per person. While that was convenient for us, like so many other tourists who have headed to Japan to take advantage of favorable exchange rates, the cheap yen (yen yasu) has been hard on Japan’s economy.
To understand the pressure Japan is under, it is worth looking at the purchasing-power-parity equilibrium exchange rate – the rate at which a representative basket of goods and services would cost the same across two countries. This month, the OECD reports a PPP equilibrium exchange rate between Japan and the United States of around 93 yen per dollar. That is a far cry from the actual yen-dollar exchange rate, which has been hovering in the 150–160 range.
This means that goods produced in Japan cost much less than goods produced in the United States. As a result, Japanese exporters enjoy high demand and strong profit margins, but importers are under severe pressure. The weak yen also hurts Japanese consumers, as it creates strong incentives to raise prices: With imported goods more expensive, domestic producers know that their output will find buyers, and importers might pass their mounting costs on to buyers.
Japan used to have the opposite problem. In the early 1980s, it was a dominant economy experiencing strong growth. But the 1985 Plaza Accord, under which major economies agreed to take coordinated action to strengthen their currencies vis-à-vis the U.S. dollar, changed everything. After the accord was implemented, the PPP exchange rate was higher than the actual exchange rate, reaching almost double in 1995.
The strong yen (yen daka) persisted for decades, contributing to chronic deflation and stagnant growth. During this period, a visit to Tokyo strained tourists’ pocketbooks, Japanese goods found few customers abroad, and Japan’s once-formidable industries struggled. The situation deteriorated further around the 2008 global economic crisis, when the United States embraced monetary easing.
In the decades after the Plaza Accord, Bank of Japan (BOJ) governors (with the possible exception of Fukui Toshihiko) consistently failed to loosen monetary policy in line with changing economic conditions. Deflationary pressures intensified.
After returning to power in 2012, Prime Minister Abe Shinzo sought to turn things around with an economic-reform package, which came to be known as Abenomics.  (I served as an adviser to Abe.) This package included a recommendation for monetary expansion, which then-BOJ Governor Kuroda Haruhiko embraced.
Now, conditions have changed. After the COVID-19 pandemic, the United States experienced a surge in inflation, which forced the U.S. Federal Reserve to abandon monetary expansion and raise interest rates. As the dollar strengthened, and the Japan-U.S. interest-rate differential widened, the yen depreciated in value, and deflationary forces gave way to inflationary pressures.
When circumstances change, so, too, must policy. For the BOJ today, this means pursuing monetary tightening in order to reduce the domestic money supply, and raising the interest rate.
To some extent, Japanese policymakers seem to recognize this. After keeping the short-term interest rate around 1 percent for some time, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 percent last month. This is high for Japan – the highest in 31 years, to be precise. But with the U.S. short-term money market pushing the interest rate close to 4 percent, and more U.S. rate hikes likely, it is not nearly enough. Speculators continue to exploit the interest-rate differential via the so-called carry trade (borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets abroad).
Under the gold standard or a fixed exchange rate, if a major country pursued monetary expansion, another, weaker country might need to reduce its money supply and raise its interest rate. Under a flexible exchange-rate regime, however, an expansion in one country should be met with a (moderate) expansion in another, just as tightening should be met with tightening.
We know that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Japanese Finance Minister Katayama Satsuki are communicating about fiscal and monetary matters. Ultimately, however, monetary policy must be pursued autonomously, with BOJ Governor Ueda Kazuo doing what is best for Japan’s economy. Under the current circumstances, that means reducing the money supply and raising interest rates more aggressively.

articles.title: TenPayGo and China’s Digital Opening to Foreigners
articles.full_text:
Tencent’s new payment app shows how China’s tech companies can lower barriers for foreign users without fundamentally changing the systems behind them.
Attracting foreign visitors to China takes more than easing visa rules or improving transport links; visitors also need to navigate the country once they arrive. In an economy where much of daily life runs through digital platforms, seemingly small tasks – from paying for a meal to accessing everyday services – can become obstacles that shape how accessible the country feels to outsiders. 
China’s effort to make itself more welcoming to tourists has thus also extended into its digital ecosystem. Tencent’s TenPayGo offers a glimpse of how one of China’s largest technology companies is approaching that challenge.
TenPayGo is a standalone payment app built around Tencent’s existing Weixin Pay network. Tencent publicly launched the app on September 24, allowing foreign visitors to pay using supported international bank cards and overseas e-wallets, like Apple Pay. It also offers translation and travel-related features, with additional transport and lifestyle services being introduced gradually. 
The ability to pay with international bank cards on China’s digital platforms is not entirely new: WeChat Pay and Alipay have supported such payments for years. TenPayGo’s main distinction is that it gives foreign visitors a dedicated entry point to Tencent’s existing payment services. This could lower the barriers to using Tencent’s services and make them more visible to foreign visitors.
China recorded more than 150 million inbound visits in 2025, with spending exceeding $130 billion. Spending through mobile payment platforms reached more than $11 billion. Tencent reported that, between January and August 2026, the value of transactions made through overseas wallets in China rose 80 percent, while the volume increased 81.8 percent. These figures point to rapid growth in cross-border payment activity. 
Other Chinese fintech giants are already in this market. Ant Group, the parent company of Alipay, said in September 2024 that the number of international visitors using its mobile payment services in China had quadrupled over the previous six months. Both companies have already spent years adapting their payment services to foreigners. TenPayGo therefore looks less like the creation of a new payment service than a move to make Tencent’s existing network more accessible and competitive.
TenPayGo also arrives as Beijing seeks to address a problem its own officials have already acknowledged: Visitors still face barriers when navigating China’s digital services. On February 5, 2026, 11 government agencies issued a policy plan aimed at making these services more accessible. By 2027, China wants to significantly improve the convenience of digital services for visitors, largely removing barriers in areas including accommodation, healthcare, payments, tourism, and public services, while expanding the range of situations in which these services can be used. 
By 2030, it seeks to establish a more interconnected digital ecosystem aligned more closely with international practices. The plan also calls for multilingual services, integrated digital service platforms, more convenient digital payments and stronger data security and personal information protection. 
In July, authorities launched a year-long initiative in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Chengdu and Sanya to improve digital services for foreign visitors. 
TenPayGo reflects this broader effort, but it also illustrates the difference between making China’s digital ecosystem easier to access and making it more open. TenPayGo uses Tencent’s existing merchant network while simplifying the way outsiders enter it. This is a first step. But whether China can achieve digital openness will depend on how far it goes beyond the individual apps.

articles.title: Korean Dramas: Ukraine, Russia, and Where South Korea Begins
articles.full_text:
A diplomatic spat and a comment that caused controversy.
In this episode of The Diplomat’s Asia Geopolitics Podcast, hosts Katie Putz and Ankit Panda take stock of two tiffs: the recent diplomatic tensions between South Korea and Ukraine, sparked by the disclosure by the Ukrainian president that Kyiv had sent two North Korean POWs to Seoul; and the root of recent furor over comments made by the commander of U.S. Forces Korea regarding where South Korean territory begins. 
Putz and Panda put these diplomatic and rhetorical rows into the broader context of inter-Korean relations and the challenges of unification, highlighting the complex geopolitical dynamics in the region and the evolving perspectives within South Korean society regarding North Korea.
