articles.title: Xi’s Military Purges Make US Deterrence More Urgent
articles.full_text:
“If we are serious about the CCP as our foremost long-term strategic challenge, we should end the Iran war and rebuild depleted stockpiles, immediately.”
China’s top military command has been almost emptied out. Of the seven members chosen for the Central Military Commission in 2022, only Xi Jinping and one general remain active. Days before Xi met U.S. President Donlald Trump in Washington last month, Beijing formally expelled Gen. Zhang Youxia, Xi’s longtime ally and former top military deputy, and Gen. Liu Zhenli, the former chief of the Joint Staff Department.
We do not know why Xi is doing this or what he intends to do next. But the purge has further strengthened his hand over the military. Reuters reported that analysts see Xi’s grip on the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) as strengthened by the removal of senior commanders and their protégés even as the upheaval weakens near-term readiness. If Xi chooses to invade Taiwan, impose a blockade, or undertake another act of military aggression in the region, more of that decision now rests with him. We do not know whether he will. That freer hand adds risk.
The scale of the purge is extraordinary. The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that 41 of the 47 officers who held three-star rank in 2022 or were promoted afterward had been purged or potentially purged. Of the 35 three-star generals and admirals Xi promoted beginning in 2020, 32 had been investigated and 29 had been purged or potentially purged. Across the PLA, roughly 52 percent of senior leadership positions have been affected.
CSIS concluded that vacant posts and less experienced officers would complicate large-scale operations against Taiwan, including a blockade or amphibious assault. But we should not assume those complications will last. Taiwan’s defense ministry has warned of “rising unpredictability” in Chinese decision-making amid the purge. With this much upheaval in Beijing and more authority concentrated in Xi’s hands, steady, credible deterrence from Washington matters even more. Beijing should have no reason to believe an invasion, blockade or other act of aggression against Taiwan could succeed.
First, we should not answer upheaval in Beijing by creating upheaval at the Pentagon. One of America’s greatest military advantages is our professional officer corps, whose duty is to the constitution rather than a ruling party. Yet in 2025, Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. C.Q. Brown along with five other senior generals and admirals. In April, Hegseth abruptly removed Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George with more than a year remaining in his term while American forces were fighting in the Middle East. The Pentagon gave no public reason, and Reuters noted that removing a service chief during wartime is “extremely rare.” Experienced commanders who are prepared to give presidents unwelcome advice make our military stronger.
Second, our military resources have to match our priorities. The Iran war is draining weapons that matter for deterrence in the Indo-Pacific. In September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the war had cost the Defense Department about $38 billion through August 1, with another month costing $2 billion to $3 billion depending on the intensity of fighting. More importantly, CBO found that heavy use of missile-defense interceptors will leave U.S. inventories reduced for several years and warned that the shortfall would be especially problematic in a conflict with China over Taiwan. If we are serious about the CCP as our foremost long-term strategic challenge, we should end the Iran war and rebuild depleted stockpiles, immediately.
Third, deterrence requires communication as well as strength. After air and maritime safety talks in May, U.S. and Chinese military representatives agreed that better communication could reduce miscalculations and the risk of unsafe encounters. With this much turnover at the top of the PLA, those channels matter even more.
We do not know Xi’s objectives. We know he has strengthened his own hand amid the uncertainty created by his purge of the military. Without any meaningful check on his power, Xi has a freer hand to pursue potentially more aggressive military decisions, adding risk to our relationship with the CCP. 
Our job is not to guess Xi’s next move. It is to make sure Washington remains steady, with experienced military leadership, the weapons and forces needed to deter aggression, strong alliances, and reliable communication to keep a crisis from becoming a war.
China’s top military command has been almost emptied out. Of the seven members chosen for the Central Military Commission in 2022, only Xi Jinping and one general remain active. Days before Xi met U.S. President Donlald Trump in Washington last month, Beijing formally expelled Gen. Zhang Youxia, Xi’s longtime ally and former top military deputy, and Gen. Liu Zhenli, the former chief of the Joint Staff Department.
We do not know why Xi is doing this or what he intends to do next. But the purge has further strengthened his hand over the military. Reuters reported that analysts see Xi’s grip on the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) as strengthened by the removal of senior commanders and their protégés even as the upheaval weakens near-term readiness. If Xi chooses to invade Taiwan, impose a blockade, or undertake another act of military aggression in the region, more of that decision now rests with him. We do not know whether he will. articles.title: Rubio’s Unusual Visit to India Marks a Paradigm Shift in India-US Ties
articles.full_text:
The U.S. secretary of state’s itinerary skipped the corridors of power in Delhi for boardrooms and a refinery.
Since the February 2025 inauguration of the second Trump administration, New Delhi has struggled to find a way to deal with the constantly swinging moods in Washington. Although the still-emerging strategic partnership between the two has, at times, seemed to take center stage, on most occasions, U.S. President Donald Trump appears to have expressed very little affinity for India, his vice president’s matrimonial ties to the country notwithstanding.
The tariffs imposed on India – at one time among the highest for targeted countries – and the failure to arrive at a trade deal despite prolonged negotiations are among the many irritants that have seeped into the relationship. 
Beyond all else, there is the stark reality that in Washington’s calculations India appears to matter only to the extent it episodically can be played off against China. In this context, U.S. Secretary of State Mark Rubio’s two-day visit to India on October 20-21 may not have provided the positive breakthrough New Delhi was earnestly looking for, highlighting instead the contours of the changing strategic partnership and the increasingly erratic nature of U.S. foreign policy under Trump 2.0.
Rubio broke a protocol of sorts. His first stop was Mumbai, India’s financial capital. As a result, there was no meeting between him and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, which would have been a foregone conclusion had he included New Delhi in his itinerary. In Mumbai, he met the top two industrial chiefs of the country: Gautam Adani of the Adani Group and N. Chandrasekharan of the Tata Group. India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, who recently aired his grievances against the U.S., flew down to Mumbai to meet Rubio as well as visiting UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed. 
That the U.S. secretary of state could decide the venue of his meeting with his Indian counterpart while in India has been criticized by the opposition parties. It also dovetails squarely with emerging assessment that U.S. strategy is divorced from any cogent calculations, responding rather to rapidly shifting whims and fancies of a transactional leader. 
Following the meetings – bilaterally between Jaishankar and Rubio, another between Jaishankar and bin Zayed and finally, all three together – a readout of cooperation was issued. Curiously missing were two important initiatives involving all three countries: the I2U2 and the India-Middle East Economic Corridor (IMEC). 
The I2U2 was formed by the three countries along with Israel in 2021, and the IMEC was announced in 2023. Both projects have stalled due to a variety of reasons including the war in Iran. Jaishankar’s summation of the trilateral meeting as a “useful exchange of perspectives on energy, connectivity and contemporary developments” was a clear indicator of the limited outcome of the confabulation and served only to raise questions concerning U.S. intentions. 
Rubio and U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor did try to sound optimistic while predicting the future of the India-U.S. trade deal. Rubio said that the deal, which is allegedly 99 percent complete, could be only “weeks away” from being signed. This kind of temporal signaling is de rigor in Trump administration communications, but generally has little connection to real time. Rubio, in fact, uttered those same words on June 4 while testifying before the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee. “We can wrap up the negotiations on our trade agreement, which we think we’re a few weeks away from being able to conclude,” he said roughly 20 weeks ago.
The latest statement of reassurance comes amid pessimistic Indian assessments, including that of the country’s finance minister. Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting on October 5, Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said, “The negotiations are still ongoing but we would like to believe that both sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very difficult.” Trump’s October 20 prediction about a “much different” trade deal with India hasn’t cleared the air of the ambivalence surrounding the future of the deal. 
Rubio’s second and final stop was Jamnagar in the western Indian state of Gujarat, to visit the refinery of Reliance Industries to discuss energy cooperation and push for Indian imports of heavy Venezuelan crude. The latter may point to the true heart of the visit: seeking a way to involve India in transactional U.S. foreign policy by offering select Indian players a chance to profit from the questionable finances of ventures such as those in Venezuela. Jamnagar, which possesses the specialized high-capacity infrastructure required to process thick and high-sulfur heavy Venezuelan crude, is also the world’s largest single-location refining complex. A further tradeoff from the trip thus could also be to provide Rubio with a reason to claim, just before the impending U.S. mid-terms, that there is impending relief from high domestic diesel and energy prices.
Reliance Industries, led by Mukesh Ambani, is also embracing the prospect of such closer cooperation. Rubio and his wife were welcomed by the entire Ambani family, consisting of Mukesh’s wife, his sons, daughters, and their spouses. Apart from touring the oil-refining complex and Reliance’s emerging clean-energy manufacturing hub, Rubio also visited the Vantara, a controversial wildlife rescue and conservation center curated and led by one of Mukesh Ambani’s sons. 
Although Rubio explained his trip as a measure to strengthen bilateral trade ties, the thrust of the trip seems more focused on American domestic politics, a search for mid-term talking points by courting new buyers and markets for expanded Venezuelan oil production. The opaque finances of the entire Venezuelan escapade notwithstanding – it has been widely reported that there has been no public accounting of just where Venezuelan oil profits are going – Reliance Industries is also planning investment in a new refinery in Texas, which Gor tweeted is “an opportunity to expand U.S. energy production and create jobs.”
Indeed, during the visit, Rubio termed India the “refining superpower of the world.” This was music to select Indian media, owned by Reliance Industries, which doubled down on the point that India, which imports 89 percent of its energy requirements from different countries, is the fourth largest exporter of refined petroleum products. 
What India stands to gain out of the possible deal between Reliance Industries and the United States isn’t clear. Who will bear the cost if U.S. policies shift again remains an unanswered question. Given the fact that the U.S. is now importing Russian diesel against the will of the U.S. Congress – with its composition up for grabs in a matter of weeks – that would seem to raise questions concerning the rationale behind putting New Delhi’s import of Russian crude under permanent scanner and possible sanctions.
For decades, India has treated strategic, defense, and technology cooperation as the core of its partnership with the United States. But under Trump 2.0, the relationship is being recast as a transaction built on trade and energy, with India now viewed as buyer, refiner, and market. Rubio’s itinerary, which skipped the corridors of power for boardrooms and a refinery, made the point amply clear. articles.title: The Next Chapter of Africa-China Climate Cooperation
articles.full_text:
China’s climate cooperation with Africa is becoming more investment-led, with a focus on industrialization.
A solar power station near Clanwilliam in the Western Cape Province of South Africa.
Nearly five years have passed since the adoption of the Declaration on China-Africa Cooperation on Combating Climate Change at the Eighth Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC 8) in 2021. Since then, discussions have often centered on simple indicators to reflect on the progress made – for example, the number of projects announced, the size of new investments, and the scale of renewable energy commitments.
At first glance, Development Reimagined’s China-Africa Climate Action Tracker provides just this. The tracker captures 246 publicly announced climate actions across 50 African countries between 2022 and the first half of 2026, including nearly 49 GW of renewable energy in the development pipeline, clean technologies, clean transportation, and, more recently, critical minerals. However, while these results are important,  they capture only part of a partnership that has evolved significantly over the past five years.
Beyond the numbers, the tracker reveals three structural shifts that have been taking place since FOCAC 8: that cooperation is becoming more investment-led; more closely linked to green industrialization; and increasingly focused on building long-term institutions. As FOCAC 10 approaches in 2027, these shifts have important implications for how future Africa-China climate cooperation should be designed and evaluated.
From Infrastructure Delivery to Long-term Investment 
The first shift is a move from contractor-led cooperation toward longer-term investment partnerships.
For many years, Africa-China cooperation in the energy sector was largely associated with engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) projects. Often having bid and won procurement processes funded by African governments or banks, Chinese companies built power plants, transmission lines, and other infrastructure that supported African countries’ energy ambitions. That model remains important and continues to contribute to Africa’s energy transition.
However, the China-Africa Climate Action Tracker suggests that the partnership is evolving. Investment and equity-led projects, EPC-plus projects, and technology transfer are becoming increasingly prominent, while the share of traditional EPC-only projects is declining. And, although Chinese state-owned enterprises such as Power China and Energy China continue to play a dominant role in project delivery in Africa, a growing number of Chinese private firms are expanding their presence through investments in local manufacturing and production capacity. 
For example, in Zambia, a Chinese firm announced a lithium battery manufacturing project in 2024 with an investment of approximately $30 million. The facility, located in the Zambia-China Jiangxi International Economic and Technical Cooperation Zone, is now operational. This illustrates how Africa-China climate cooperation can extend beyond infrastructure delivery to support local green manufacturing and industrial development.
Climate Cooperation Is Becoming a Green Industrial Agenda
The second shift is even more interesting. Africa-China climate cooperation is increasingly extending beyond individual renewable energy projects toward the development of integrated green industrial value chains
Hence, although new solar, wind, and hydropower energy infrastructure continue to dominate Africa-China climate cooperation, the tracker also highlights the rapid emergence of critical minerals as an essential component of climate cooperation.
Development Reimagined began systematically tracking Africa-China critical minerals projects in 2025 and has already identified close to 20 projects involving lithium, graphite, rare earth elements, and other strategic resources. More significantly, eight of the nine countries hosting these critical mineral projects also have renewable energy projects. This overlap points to opportunities that Chinese and African firms are taking up to extend cooperation beyond mineral extraction. 
African countries are increasingly pursuing and implementing national industrial strategies that connect renewable energy, mineral processing, and manufacturing. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is developing battery value chains. Nigeria is expanding clean technology manufacturing. Tanzania is positioning itself as a multi-mineral processing hub. 
Looking at Africa’s green manufacturing progress, projects that involve Chinese stakeholders span electric vehicle assembly, battery manufacturing, energy storage, solar PV production, and related supply chains. These examples demonstrate growing interest among Chinese companies in localizing production in Africa markets rather than relying solely on exports of finished products. 
That said, some of this manufacturing pipeline remains at the memorandum of understanding, feasibility, planning or pre-construction stage. Announced projects don’t always become operational manufacturing capacity. In addition, feasibility studies often miss the opportunity presented by the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which could help make green manufacturing investments more commercially viable through access to the much larger continental market.
Cooperation Is Moving Beyond Individual Projects
The third trend is perhaps the least visible but could prove the most important. Climate cooperation is increasingly being built through and reinforcing African initiatives and institutions, not just project-by-project.
Since 2022, the tracker has recorded more than 40 climate “exchanges,” including strategic partnerships, technology cooperation, capacity-building initiatives, and industry collaborations. These initiatives receive less attention than utility-scale renewable energy projects, but they could prove fundamental in building the institutional foundations necessary for long-term economic transformation.
For example, pairing Chinese expertise in solar technology and energy storage with training for African engineers and technicians could do more than bring new clean-energy systems online. It could help build the local skills needed to operate and maintain these systems, support local businesses and expand access to reliable electricity over the long term.
So what do these three trends suggest for the next phase of Africa-China climate cooperation?
Our view at Development Reimagined is that while the number of megawatts installed will remain an important measure of progress – especially in the context of the 300 GW 2030 renewable energy goal announced by African leaders in the 2023 Nairobi declaration – the  next stage of Africa-China climate cooperation presents an opportunity for FOCAC 10 to do more than announce the next generation of projects. It can help shape the conditions under which these projects deliver lasting value.
The first priority could be turning a growing pipeline into projects that are delivered. The real test for any announced project comes afterwards – including the need to securing affordable finance, reach construction, begin operations and ultimately deliver economic and climate benefits. FOCAC 10 could place greater emphasis on this implementation journey, including clearer mechanisms to track progress and identify where policy, financing, or technical support is needed. This would help shift the focus from the volume of commitments towards the results they generate.
The second priority could be to continue to connect individual projects to the bigger opportunity of green industrialization. Investments in renewable energy, critical minerals, EVs, batteries, and solar PV are beginning to form the building blocks of new green industrial value chains across African countries. More energy projects need to be directed to support local production, technology transfer, skills development, and value addition. Chinese companies are already exploring this shift, while African countries are developing policies to attract and anchor these investments. FOCAC 10 can help strengthen this convergence, with the AfCFTA providing an important platform for linking national manufacturing investments to a larger continental market.
The third is to invest even after a project is built. A solar farm, manufacturing facility, or battery plant can create important economic and climate benefits, but its longer-term contribution depends on the capabilities around it, including skilled workers, local suppliers, research institutions, effective regulators, and access to finance. These foundations are less visible than a new project, but they determine whether investments can be sustained, replicated and scaled. 
Future Africa-China climate cooperation therefore has an opportunity to put greater emphasis on building these capabilities alongside physical infrastructure, while also responding more fully to African countries’ priorities on climate adaptation.
These three priorities, although they might be new, do not, in fact, require a departure from the progress made since FOCAC 8. Rather, they build on how the partnership is already evolving. 
FOCAC 10, to be held in 2027, can help move Africa-China climate cooperation into its next active phase: one where success is measured not simply by what is announced or built, but by what actual power is delivered, what industrial goods are produced locally and what industrial capabilities are growing on the continent. 
Nearly five years have passed since the adoption of the Declaration on China-Africa Cooperation on Combating Climate Change at the Eighth Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC 8) in 2021. Since then, discussions have often centered on simple indicators to reflect on the progress made – for example, the number of projects announced, the size of new investments, and the scale of renewable energy commitments.
articles.summary: China’s climate cooperation with Africa is becoming more investment-led, with a focus on industrialization.

articles.title: Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi Speaks With Son For First Time Since Military Coup
articles.full_text:
Kim Aris called for the release of all political prisoners in Myanmar and said that his mother “must never be held hostage or used as a bargaining chip.”
In this photo released by the Myanmar Presidential Spokesperson’s office, detained leader Aung San Suu Kyi speaks with her son Kim Aris by phone from Naypyidaw, Myanmar, Oct. 22, 2026.
The son of Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi says that he has spoken to his mother for the first time since the military coup of 2021, reiterating calls for her release.
“Today, I was able to speak directly with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, for the first time in more than five years,” Kim Aris said in a statement yesterday. “Hearing her voice again means more to me than words can express.”
The call came after the military-backed administration released two photos of Aung San Suu Kyi receiving two books and a sealed diplomatic pouch from Britain’s King Charles III.
Yesterday’s call was also publicized by Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson, who posted on Facebook that the “convicted prisoner” had spoken to her son with the assistance of the Myanmar embassy in London. It also released photos of the pair talking on the phone.
In this statement, Aris thanked all of those who had campaigned for his mother’s freedom, and those who facilitated the phone call, but said the conversation was no substitute for regular contact, let alone his mother’s freedom.
“This moment must not be mistaken for freedom,” Aris said, “My mother is 81. She remains unjustly detained, and a single conversation cannot restore the years taken from her or the rights she is still denied.”
As Aris detailed in an interview with my colleague Luke Hunt last month, he has waged an international campaign for his mother’s release since February 2021, when she was ousted in a coup and placed under tight military custody. She is currently serving an 18-year prison term for a host of criminal charges, including incitement, corruption, election fraud, and violation of Myanmar’s Official Secrets Act.
Despite spending most of the past five years in seclusion, with virtually no contact with the outside world, in recent months the authorities have loosened the terms of Aung San Suu Kyi’s detention and been more forthcoming about the activities of the Nobel laureate.
Shortly after coup leader Min Aung Hlaing took office as president in April, his pseudo-civilian administration announced Aung San Suu Kyi’s relocation from prison to house arrest at a “designated residence” in the capital Naypyidaw, alongside a broader amnesty of political prisoners. It also reduced her sentence by one-sixth. In August, the authorities also allowed her to meet with Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Myanmar, the first foreign official that she had met since the coup.
This recent “leniency” is clearly connected to Naypyidaw’s ongoing efforts to normalize its relations with important international partners, in particular the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
The 11-nation bloc has barred Myanmar from its summits since late 2021, over its failure to implement its Five-Point Consensus plan for resolving the country’s post-coup conflict, which involved pledges to cease violence, allow humanitarian access, and engage in political dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Recognizing that Aung San Suu Kyi’s international fame and status as a political symbol, the authorities in Naypyidaw have hoped that loosening the conditions of her detention will help pave the way to normalization with ASEAN member states and other governments. At the same time, it has ruled out (at least for now) any prospect of her release.
In his statement, Aris expressed an awareness of the role that his mother had long played in the Myanmar military’s diplomatic strategy.
“My mother must never be held hostage or used as a bargaining chip for diplomatic recognition, sanctions relief, or political advantage. Basic humanitarian rights cannot be exchanged for legitimacy,” he said.
“Regular, direct, and private family contact and independent medical access must be guaranteed. Above all, my mother and all political prisoners must be released immediately and unconditionally.”
The son of Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi says that he has spoken to his mother for the first time since the military coup of 2021, reiterating calls for her release.
“Today, I was able to speak directly with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, for the first time in more than five years,” Kim Aris said in a statement yesterday. “Hearing her voice again means more to me than words can express.”
The call came after the military-backed administration released two photos of Aung San Suu Kyi receiving two books and a sealed diplomatic pouch from Britain’s King Charles III.
Yesterday’s call was also publicized by Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson, who posted on Facebook that the “convicted prisoner” had spoken to her son with the assistance of the Myanmar embassy in London. It also released photos of the pair talking on the phone.
In this statement, Aris thanked all of those who had campaigned for his mother’s freedom, and those who facilitated the phone call, but said the conversation was no substitute for regular contact, let alone his mother’s freedom.
“This moment must not be mistaken for freedom,” Aris said, “My mother is 81. She remains unjustly detained, and a single conversation cannot restore the years taken from her or the rights she is still denied.”
As Aris detailed in an interview with my colleague Luke Hunt last month, he has waged an international campaign for his mother’s release since February 2021, when she was ousted in a coup and placed under tight military custody. She is currently serving an 18-year prison term for a host of criminal charges, including incitement, corruption, election fraud, and violation of Myanmar’s Official Secrets Act.
Despite spending most of the past five years in seclusion, with virtually no contact with the outside world, in recent months the authorities have loosened the terms of Aung San Suu Kyi’s detention and been more forthcoming about the activities of the Nobel laureate.
Shortly after coup leader Min Aung Hlaing took office as president in April, his pseudo-civilian administration announced Aung San Suu Kyi’s relocation from prison to house arrest at a “designated residence” in the capital Naypyidaw, alongside a broader amnesty of political prisoners. It also reduced her sentence by one-sixth. In August, the authorities also allowed her to meet with Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Myanmar, the first foreign official that she had met since the coup.
This recent “leniency” is clearly connected to Naypyidaw’s ongoing efforts to normalize its relations with important international partners, in particular the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
The 11-nation bloc has barred Myanmar from its summits since late 2021, over its failure to implement its Five-Point Consensus plan for resolving the country’s post-coup conflict, which involved pledges to cease violence, allow humanitarian access, and engage in political dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Recognizing that Aung San Suu Kyi’s international fame and status as a political symbol, the authorities in Naypyidaw have hoped that loosening the conditions of her detention will help pave the way to normalization with ASEAN member states and other governments. At the same time, it has ruled out (at least for now) any prospect of her release.
In his statement, Aris expressed an awareness of the role that his mother had long played in the Myanmar military’s diplomatic strategy.
articles.summary: Kim Aris called for the release of all political prisoners in Myanmar and said that his mother "must never be held hostage or used as a bargaining chip."

articles.title: Rubio’s India Visit Focuses on Energy
articles.full_text:
He visited Jamnagar, home to the world’s largest oil refinery, which is run by Reliance Industries. The latter plans to build a refinery in Texas.
Reliance Industry Ltd.’s oil refinery at Jamnagar in India.
During U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India on October 20-21, the two sides discussed stepping up energy cooperation and increasing procurement of American technologies and weapon systems as part of a stocktaking of their bilateral relationship.
Unlike his trip to India in May, Rubio did not visit the Indian capital, New Delhi. Instead, he visited India’s commercial capital, Mumbai, and Jamnagar, where the world’s largest oil refinery run by Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL) is located.
An Indian readout of Rubio’s visit to Mumbai said that “the two sides reviewed the entire gamut of India-U.S. relations and discussed ways to further strengthen the Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership.” They exchanged views on trade, defense, technology and energy security, and Rubio and Jaishankar welcomed “the progress made in negotiations on the India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) and reaffirmed their commitment to working towards its early conclusion.”
According to a U.S. statement on the talks between Rubio and his Indian counterpart S. Jaishankar, Rubio “reiterated that increased energy trade with the United States can play a transformative role in diversifying India’s supply chains while meeting its sizable consumer demand.” Commending recent progress in bilateral defense and civil nuclear cooperation, Rubio advocated the increased purchase of U.S. technologies and systems. No details were provided about which technologies the United States wants India to purchase.
In addition to Jaishankar, Rubio met representatives of three top Indian business houses – the Tatas, Adanis, and Reliance – in Mumbai. He also participated in a trilateral meeting with Jaishankar and the UAE’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan that focused on energy security and regional issues.
Rubio’s visit to Jamnagar was linked to the RIL-run refinery’s capacity to refine heavy crude oils and its plans to construct a refinery near the U.S. border in Texas.
The Rubio visit’s focus on energy is not surprising, as India is one of the top importers of petroleum products. The U.S. has been pressuring India to stop fuel imports from Russia, which surged after the outbreak of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, and to buy Venezuelan crude oil instead, especially after the Donald Trump administration took over Venezuela’s oil industry following its abduction of President Nicolás Maduro.
As Indian strategic affairs analyst C. Raja Mohan wrote in a recent opinion piece in Indian Express, “Washington wants greater energy cooperation with India and more Indian investment in the U.S. Reliance offers a substantial private-sector partner. The question is how Delhi can turn the company’s growing importance in American calculations into an asset for India-U.S. relations.”
Rubio’s latest visit to India came at a time when India-U.S. relations have plunged to their worst in several decades. In addition to imposing unprecedented levels of tariffs on India, the Trump administration has tightened immigration and visa rules that are likely to hit Indian professionals hard. Besides, it has cozied up to Pakistan.
Last month, the U.S. Congress passed a bill authorizing Trump to punish countries buying energy from Russia, which has major implications for India. However, days ahead of Rubio’s visit to India, U.S. President Donald Trump announced a waiver on sanctions and tariffs related to ‌Russian exports for a 60-day period, after he reached a deal on purchasing Russian diesel. The suspension of sanctions will give India some respite, albeit temporarily.
At a time when India-U.S. ties are strained, “Rubio’s visit seeks to shift the focus to energy security, corporate partnerships and resolving trade standoffs,” Indian analyst Brahma Chellaney observed in a post on X. By visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar rather than New Delhi, “Rubio is emphasizing pragmatic cooperation over diplomatic friction. The approach could help sustain momentum in energy, private-sector investment and economic ties, thus keeping the broader bilateral partnership productive,” Chellaney pointed out.
During his visit to India, Rubio made several statements that sought to reassure Delhi.
At an event to mark the 250th anniversary of American Independence, Rubio acknowledged differences between India and the U.S. “No two nations on Earth will ever be perfectly aligned on every issue, and of course there will be times and points of disagreement.” But on core issues “that define the national interest of both India and the United States – the alignment between our countries is extraordinary,” he said.
On the stalled India-U.S. trade deal that has cast a shadow over bilateral ties, Rubio said both countries were “incredibly close” to an agreement. “The way I would say it is we are weeks, not months away from I think, finalizing it.  I think 99 percent of the work is done… I feel very positive about the trajectory that it’s on.”
In an interview published in Indian Express, Rubio sought to assure India that improved ties with Pakistan would not be “at the expense of our relationship with India.” On the new immigration rules, he said that the regulations were “not unique to Indians or India; it is tied more broadly to the world… We are trying to fix 20 years of neglect of an immigration system that was simply not being enforced. And that’s not targeting India.”
Reassuring as Rubio’s statements may be, it will take a lot of work to bring the troubled India-U.S. relationship back to an even keel, especially since Trump is known for unpredictable policy changes. Therefore, Rubio’s visit may be the first step on a long and winding road to rebuilding trust.

articles.title: Indonesia’s Stock Market Crisis Is Self-Inflicted
articles.full_text:
Jakarta has serious questions to answer about the credibility of its capital markets and the effectiveness of the institutions responsible for regulating them.
The skyline of Indonesia’s capital Jakarta at dusk.
On Friday, October 16, Indonesia’s stock market suffered its worst one-day decline since the 1998 Asian financial crisis. The Jakarta Composite Index plunged 11.6 percent following the global index provider MSCI’s announcement that it was considering removing Indonesia from its Emerging Market classification and placing it directly into its Standalone Market category. The selling continued when markets opened on Monday, with the index falling another 3.9 percent, bringing the combined decline over the two trading days to approximately 15 percent.
For Southeast Asia’s largest economy, this is a serious development. However, the most important issue is not the decline in share prices or even the possibility of losing Emerging Market status. It is what this crisis reveals about the credibility of Indonesia’s capital markets and the effectiveness of the institutions responsible for regulating them.
MSCI’s concerns about concentrated share ownership, questionable free-float calculations, coordinated trading, and the reliability of market prices are not new. In January, MSCI restricted certain increases in Indonesian securities’ index representation, and announced that it was considering downgrading Indonesia from Emerging Market to Frontier Market status. By June, it had acknowledged reforms introduced by the authorities but emphasized the need for sustained implementation. However, MSCI was still concerned enough this month to propose removing Indonesia from both its Emerging and Frontier Market classifications.
Market Manipulation and Inflated Valuations
One of the main concerns is coordinated trading, where groups of investors work together to influence share prices rather than allowing them to be determined by genuine buying and selling. Such activities can involve transactions through multiple brokerage accounts, including accounts held by related parties or nominees, creating the appearance of greater trading activity and investor demand than actually exists.
The problem is especially serious when a company’s shares are concentrated among a small number of shareholders. With only a limited number genuinely available for trading, relatively modest transactions can have a disproportionate impact on the market price. If prices are pushed higher through coordinated buying, the resulting increase in market capitalization can give investors a misleading impression of the company’s value. Investors, including foreign institutions and index funds, may subsequently purchase shares at prices that do not reflect genuine independent demand.
For example, on October 16, Indonesia’s Financial Services Authority (OJK) announced that its investigation into trading in Dian Swastatika Sentosa (DSSA), a company associated with the Sinar Mas Group, had uncovered planned and structured market manipulation involving individual and institutional investors operating through several brokerage firms.
According to OJK, the investigation examined transactions between 2024 and 2026 and identified coordinated activities that significantly increased DSSA’s share price. The regulator questioned brokerage directors, individuals, and foreign legal entities, suspended certain individual licenses and announced penalties totaling Rp1.5 trillion (around $83 million) in connection with the case.
The regulator has not publicly established that the company’s controlling shareholders directed these activities, and it would be wrong to assume their involvement without evidence. However, the case demonstrates that trading on a regulated stock exchange can produce prices that do not reflect genuine independent demand.
There is also a broader concern about how inflated valuations affect the financial system. Higher share prices increase the apparent wealth of major shareholders and, where shares are accepted as collateral, may influence the financing available against those holdings. They can also affect index weightings and investment decisions by institutions relying on reported market prices and liquidity.
The obvious question is how such activities could continue over several years without being stopped earlier. Modern stock exchanges have surveillance systems designed to identify unusual trading patterns, concentrated ownership, and potentially coordinated transactions. Were these warning signs missed, were investigations delayed, or did the authorities lack the resources or willingness to intervene?
The Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX), OJK, and Central Securities Depository have taken steps to address these concerns. In response to MSCI’s first downgrade threat in January, the authorities have introduced measures to improve transparency, including reducing the shareholding disclosure threshold from 5 percent to 1 percent, expanding investor classifications from nine to 39 categories, and establishing a roadmap to increase the minimum free-float requirement from 7.5 percent to 15 percent. They have also introduced measures to identify companies with highly concentrated shareholdings, improve beneficial ownership disclosures, strengthen scrutiny of IPO allocations, and enhance market surveillance and enforcement.
These are all sensible reforms, but announcing new regulations and actually enforcing them are two different things. For instance, increasing the minimum free float means very little if shares supposedly held by independent investors are actually controlled through nominee arrangements, affiliated companies, or other parties connected with principal shareholders.
Indonesia’s listed companies have historically been dominated by family-controlled business groups, with various studies estimating that 60–70 percent of companies listed on the IDX are controlled by families. Many of these groups have played an important role in Indonesia’s economic development. While there is nothing inherently wrong with concentrated family ownership, the problem arises when complex ownership structures make it difficult to determine who actually controls publicly traded shares, whether transactions are conducted at arm’s length, and whether market prices reflect genuine trading between independent investors.
An example of this is Barito Renewables Energy. Following its 2023 IPO, the company’s market capitalization rose dramatically, at one point exceeding that of Bank Central Asia, one of Indonesia’s largest banks. The valuation attracted considerable attention, particularly given the company’s relatively limited earnings relative to its market capitalization.
In 2024, FTSE Russell excluded Barito Renewables from its global indices over concerns about concentrated share ownership. This should have been another warning that international investors were questioning whether the reported public shareholdings represented shares genuinely available for trading.
More recently, OJK announced penalties of Rp500 billion ($27.9 million) and Rp100 billion ($ 5.5 million), involving irregularities connected with the IPOs of Barito Renewables and Petrindo Jaya Kreasi, respectively, both associated with businessman Prajogo Pangestu. According to the regulator, shares intended for public investors had been allocated to parties associated with controlling shareholders, including through arrangements that obscured the identities of the ultimate beneficiaries. The penalties were directed at parties involved in the violations rather than the listed companies themselves.
Another example is the transaction involving Bayan Resources, in which founder Low Tuck Kwong and his daughter Elaine Low sold a combined 30.25 percent stake to PT Jhonlin Baratama, associated with businessman Haji Isam. According to regulatory filings, the shares were sold at Rp2,588 each, approximately 80 percent below the prevailing market price of Rp13,000–14,000.
There may be legitimate commercial reasons for selling such a large block of shares at a substantial discount. While this does not establish market manipulation, the difference between the negotiated price and the market price raises questions about whether the quoted share price accurately reflects its value.
The involvement of some of Indonesia’s most influential business families raises questions about whether financial regulators are sufficiently independent and willing to take action against powerful business interests.
Indonesia’s large conglomerates often have longstanding relationships with political figures, government institutions, and other influential groups. Such relationships are hardly unique to Indonesia and do not, by themselves, imply wrongdoing. However, they create concerns about whether regulators can operate without political or commercial pressure, particularly when enforcement actions could affect prominent shareholders or companies with political connections.
OJK deserves credit for pursuing the recent investigations and announcing substantial penalties, particularly given the prominence of the corporate groups involved. Although OJK maintains that its investigations were underway before MSCI’s announcement, it should explain why these problems persisted for so long and what steps it has taken to prevent them from happening again.
Investors should also be entitled to know who was responsible for the violations, what penalties have actually been collected, whether further proceedings are being pursued and whether those involved remain permitted to operate in the market.
Indonesia has considerable economic advantages, including its large domestic market, natural resources, and opportunities in infrastructure, energy, and manufacturing. However, international investors also value the reliability of financial information, minority shareholder protection, regulatory independence, and the predictability of government policies.
When confidence in these areas weakens, investors may demand higher returns or simply invest elsewhere. For Indonesian companies, this can mean lower valuations, a higher cost of capital, and greater difficulty raising funds for expansion.
The proposed MSCI reclassification could compound these problems. Funds required to track Emerging Market benchmarks may have to reduce their Indonesian holdings if the downgrade proceeds, while other investors may reassess their exposure because of concerns about governance and market integrity.
The government’s response should therefore concentrate on restoring confidence rather than simply supporting share prices. Danantara’s reported plans to invest $5 billion in domestic businesses may provide support during a period of market weakness. However, using public investment funds to support the market cannot resolve concerns about ownership transparency, coordinated trading, or regulatory enforcement. Such investments should be based on commercial considerations, with transparent investment criteria and proper accountability.
The IDX and OJK should concentrate on enforcing existing regulations rather than continuing to announce additional reforms. Beneficial ownership must be reliably identified, free-float requirements must reflect shares genuinely available to independent investors, and suspicious trading must be investigated promptly. The authorities should also publish regular reports identifying companies that remain in breach of the regulations, the corrective measures required and the outcomes of enforcement proceedings. Investors should not have to rely on general assurances that improvements are being made.
articles.summary: Jakarta has serious questions to answer about the credibility of its capital markets and the effectiveness of the institutions responsible for regulating them.

articles.title: Malaysian PM Anwar Bans Civil Servants From Using Israel-developed Navigation App
articles.full_text:
Anwar Ibrahim said that Waze, which was developed in Tel Aviv before being acquired by Google in 2013, could be “exploited by the Israeli regime.”
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim chairs a meeting of the National Cyber ​​Security Committee (JKSN) in Putrajaya, Malaysia, Oct. 20, 2026.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has prohibited civil servants from using Waze, a popular navigation app developed in Israel, warning that its use could compromise “national security and sovereignty.”
In a Facebook post on Wednesday, Anwar said that the ban was intended to “protect government information and users’ personal data from the threat of misuse by the Israeli regime.”
Anwar said his administration was looking into potential security risks arising from the use of Waze, which, despite now being a subsidiary of Google, remains subject to Israeli law. For the same reason, he urged Malaysians to stop using the app, and suggested that they switch to local alternatives including Tuju, an app developed by the Malaysian Highway Authority.
“The MADANI Government’s stance is firm and we will close any space that can be exploited by the Israeli regime to threaten the security of the country and the people,” Anwar stated.
Waze originated in 2006 as an open-source project called FreeMap Israel, created by Israeli software engineer Ehud Shabtai. It grew quickly and was subsequently acquired by Google for around $1 billion in 2013.
The prohibition on the app’s use was issued a day after Anwar chaired a meeting of the National Cyber Security Committee (JKSN), at which the potential risk of Waze being used to monitor Malaysian citizens’ data was discussed, Anwar said in a separate Facebook post on Tuesday.
The JKSN meeting also reviewed the development of cyber threats and efforts to strengthen Malaysia’s “digital preparedness and sovereignty.” It also discussed the security of MyDigital ID, Malaysia’s national digital identity verification platform, and efforts to implement the country’s Cyber Security Act 2024.
“This effort is crucial to ensure that the digitalization of public services continues to benefit the people, without neglecting the security, trust, and sovereignty of the nation,” he said.
Waze yesterday rejected Anwar’s allegations that it collects sensitive government information or allows users’ personal data to be exploited by third parties. In a statement to Reuters, a Waze spokesperson said that the company “operates under strict privacy policies that protect user data and comply with global legal data protection standards.”
The directive reflects the Malaysian government’s long-standing hostility toward Israel, with which it does not have diplomatic relations, and its support for the Palestinian national cause. Anwar has been particularly outspoken on this issue, condemning Israel’s assaults on Gaza in the wake of the militant group Hamas’ attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
Speaking at a large pro-Palestine rally in Kuala Lumpur several weeks after the Hamas incursion, Anwar described the Israel’s military response as “the height of barbarism in this world,” and called on Israel to end its occupation of Palestinian territories. Unlike other critical leaders, Anwar has also continued to engage publicly with Hamas, which Israel, the U.S., and many Western nations view as a terrorist organization.
Anwar also claimed that the U.S. government had brought diplomatic pressure to bear on his government to shift its position on Hamas, but that it would maintain “its independent position.”

articles.title: China, Djibouti Express ‘Serious Concern’ Over Threats to Red Sea Shipping
articles.full_text:
A joint communique ups the diplomatic rhetoric but offers no solutions.
A cargo ship in the Port of Djibouti, 2012.
Djibouti’s Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar is visiting China from October 19 to 25. On October 21, he held a meeting with his counterpart and host, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. According to a spokesperson from China’s Foreign Ministry, “They had an in-depth exchange of views on the Horn of Africa situation and the safety of shipping lanes across the Red Sea.”
The Red Sea is under siege – a major concern for Djibouti, which sits on the Horn of Africa, at the junction between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
For most of 2026, the world has been focused on another crucial waterway: the Strait of Hormuz, a transit route for around one-fourth of all global crude oil shipments and one-fifth of the world’s LNG. Israel and the U.S. began strikes against Iran on February 28; Iran retaliated in part by shutting down shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic through the strait has been constrained ever since.
In response, Saudi Arabia began rerouting some its oil via pipeline to the Red Sea. Saudi oil shipments on this route jumped nearly fivefold, going from 1 million to 4.9 million barrels per day. But new attacks by the Houthis, Iran-backed militants that occupy much of Yemen, are now jeopardizing that shipping. Starting in September, the Houthis began a concerted effort to seize control of the Bab al Mandeb Strait, the body of water between Yemen and Djibouti and a crucial chokepoint for shipping via the Red Sea.
While Yemeni government forces have taken back much of the territory, the threat to shipping remains high. A Washington Post article, citing “Iranian officials and diplomats in the region,” said that Iran saw the weeks before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3 as a “critical window” for weakening U.S. President Donald Trump. Iran is accordingly stepping up attack in the Strait of Hormuz – and may have the Houthis do the same in the Red Sea.
That leaves regional states like Djibouti to reckon with the fallout.
China, as the world’s largest exporter, has a direct stake in the outcome as well. Wang and Omar not only discussed the shipping threat during their talks but issued an entire joint communique on the subject.
Unfortunately, there’s not much new in the document. It serves more as a vehicle for both countries to express their concerns than an attempt to offer concrete solutions.
Djibouti and China agreed that “the recent escalation of tensions in the Red Sea poses a serious threat to the global economy, particularly to economic activities in the Horn of Africa region, including trade, investment, energy, and food security.” But they also made it clear that the onus is on other countries to solve the issue. “Both sides believe that easing tensions in the Middle East is key to resolving the security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea,” the statement declared. In other words, this is ultimately a problem for Israel, Iran, and the United States to tackle.
The joint statement called on “all parties” involved to “take concrete actions through dialogue and diplomacy to address the serious challenges facing the Middle East, the Red Sea, and the Horn of Africa, preventing the escalation or further complication of regional tensions.” There’s no indication that either China or Djibouti will take new steps to facilitate that “dialogue and diplomacy.”
“The Horn of Africa must never be used as a geopolitical arena, and the flames of war in the Middle East must never be brought to the Horn of Africa,” the statement avowed. How China or Djibouti plan to prevent exactly that outcome is left unsaid, other than Djibouti’s enthusiastic backing for China’s vague and largely unactionable peace plans for both the Middle East and “African hotspots.”
The reason for China’s concern is obvious. The Red Sea is a vital shipping link for Chinese exports to Europe, especially with the Strait of Hormuz looking increasingly unstable. That was highlighted during President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt in early September. Egypt controls the Suez Canal, which links the Red Sea to the Mediterranean – and Europe. China has already plowed over $5 billion into the Suez Canal Economic Zone in Egypt.
On the southern end of the Red Sea, China also has a lot invested in Djibouti specifically. The state-owned firm China Merchants Group helped build Djibouti’s Doraleh Multipurpose Port project, to the tune of $590 million. Separately, CMG has a 23.5 percent stake in the Port of Djibouti.
China also funded and built the Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway, to give landlocked Ethiopia another trading route for its exports. And let’s not forget that Djibouti hosts China’s first overseas military facility, whose stated purpose is to provide logistics for Chinese anti-piracy patrols in the region.
During their talks, Wang told Omar that China will “support” Djibouti “in building itself into a regional hub for trade, logistics, and connectivity.” But Djibouti’s ambitions – and China’s billions in investments – have little hope if the Red Sea is closed to shipping by militant attacks.
Djibouti’s Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar is visiting China from October 19 to 25. On October 21, he held a meeting with his counterpart and host, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. According to a spokesperson from China’s Foreign Ministry, “They had an in-depth exchange of views on the Horn of Africa situation and the safety of shipping lanes across the Red Sea.”
The Red Sea is under siege – a major concern for Djibouti, which sits on the Horn of Africa, at the junction between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
For most of 2026, the world has been focused on another crucial waterway: the Strait of Hormuz, a transit route for around one-fourth of all global crude oil shipments and one-fifth of the world’s LNG. Israel and the U.S. began strikes against Iran on February 28; Iran retaliated in part by shutting down shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic through the strait has been constrained ever since.
In response, Saudi Arabia began rerouting some its oil via pipeline to the Red Sea. Saudi oil shipments on this route jumped nearly fivefold, going from 1 million to 4.9 million barrels per day. But new attacks by the Houthis, Iran-backed militants that occupy much of Yemen, are now jeopardizing that shipping. Starting in September, the Houthis began a concerted effort to seize control of the Bab al Mandeb Strait, the body of water between Yemen and Djibouti and a crucial chokepoint for shipping via the Red Sea.
While Yemeni government forces have taken back much of the territory, the threat to shipping remains high. A Washington Post article, citing “Iranian officials and diplomats in the region,” said that Iran saw the weeks before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3 as a “critical window” for weakening U.S. President Donald Trump. Iran is accordingly stepping up attack in the Strait of Hormuz – and may have the Houthis do the same in the Red Sea.
That leaves regional states like Djibouti to reckon with the fallout.
China, as the world’s largest exporter, has a direct stake in the outcome as well. Wang and Omar not only discussed the shipping threat during their talks but issued an entire joint communique on the subject.
Unfortunately, there’s not much new in the document. It serves more as a vehicle for both countries to express their concerns than an attempt to offer concrete solutions.
Djibouti and China agreed that “the recent escalation of tensions in the Red Sea poses a serious threat to the global economy, particularly to economic activities in the Horn of Africa region, including trade, investment, energy, and food security.” But they also made it clear that the onus is on other countries to solve the issue. “Both sides believe that easing tensions in the Middle East is key to resolving the security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea,” the statement declared. In other words, this is ultimately a problem for Israel, Iran, and the United States to tackle.
The joint statement called on “all parties” involved to “take concrete actions through dialogue and diplomacy to address the serious challenges facing the Middle East, the Red Sea, and the Horn of Africa, preventing the escalation or further complication of regional tensions.” There’s no indication that either China or Djibouti will take new steps to facilitate that “dialogue and diplomacy.”
“The Horn of Africa must never be used as a geopolitical arena, and the flames of war in the Middle East must never be brought to the Horn of Africa,” the statement avowed. How China or Djibouti plan to prevent exactly that outcome is left unsaid, other than Djibouti’s enthusiastic backing for China’s vague and largely unactionable peace plans for both the Middle East and “African hotspots.”
The reason for China’s concern is obvious. The Red Sea is a vital shipping link for Chinese exports to Europe, especially with the Strait of Hormuz looking increasingly unstable. That was highlighted during President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt in early September. Egypt controls the Suez Canal, which links the Red Sea to the Mediterranean – and Europe. China has already plowed over $5 billion into the Suez Canal Economic Zone in Egypt.
On the southern end of the Red Sea, China also has a lot invested in Djibouti specifically. The state-owned firm China Merchants Group helped build Djibouti’s Doraleh Multipurpose Port project, to the tune of $590 million. Separately, CMG has a 23.5 percent stake in the Port of Djibouti.
articles.summary: A joint communique ups the diplomatic rhetoric but offers no solutions.

articles.title: This Time, the Korean Loudspeaker Standoff Is Different
articles.full_text:
Typically, South Korea has used loudspeakers to respond to North Korean provocations. Now Pyongyang has vowed to turn them on – and the prospects for de-escalation are dim.
In this image provided by North Korean state media, Kim Yo Jong visits the border area to inspect fortifications, Oct. 21, 2026.
On October 21, after inspecting fortification work along North Korea’s southern border, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, announced that “within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border.” (ROK refers to the Republic of Korea, South Korea’s formal name.) 
Two days earlier, Kim Yo Jong had said Pyongyang was considering the step, along with deploying more “tactical strike means” near the border. As a rationale, she cited the behavior of South Korean troops near the border, claiming they had issued 2,870 warning broadcasts and fired warning shots on 201 occasions between August 1 and October 17.
South Korea has no large loudspeakers left on the border; it took them down in August 2025 as a sign of goodwill. The Ministry of National Defense said that the warnings Kim referred to were issued by smaller speakers at guard posts as a defensive measure against North Korean soldiers crossing the Military Demarcation Line (MDL). 
If the North starts broadcasting, South Korea’s military said it would consider restarting its own loudspeakers on the principle of proportional response.
The loudspeaker broadcasts began in 1963, when North Korea began using the tool and South Korea responded in kind. The first bout lasted over nine years, with broadcasts only switched off in November 1972. North Korea resumed broadcasts in 1980; the loudspeaker contest lasted even longer this time, until 2004. 
But since then, loudspeaker use has settled into a pattern: South Korea resumed loudspeaker broadcasts in response to North Korean actions in 2015, 2016, and 2024. The latest round ended in 2025, with the Lee administration’s unilateral decision to dismantle South Korean speakers. This time, North Korea is the one resuming broadcasts, citing a growing dispute over the MDL.
Since 2015, Seoul has used loudspeakers when it wants to respond to North Korean provocations without resorting to force. In August 2015, South Korea’s defense minister called the broadcasts legitimate retaliation after mines that Seoul said the North had planted in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) seriously injured two South Korean soldiers. South Korea also used loudspeaker broadcasts to respond to North Korea’s nuclear test in 2016, and again in 2024 when North Korea sent balloons filled with trash and feces across the border.
There’s a reason South Korean governments turned to loudspeakers. A broadcast is non-lethal and can be switched off at will, yet it targets something Pyongyang guards closely: its control over information. South Korean broadcasts have carried news, weather forecasts, and pop music to North Korea’s front-line soldiers, and officials said in 2015 that the sound could carry 24 kilometers at night. In June 2017, a North Korean soldier who crossed to a South Korean guard post on the central front said the broadcasts had made him decide to defect.
While South Korea considered the broadcasts to be a proportional response, North Korea sees them differently. Pyongyang called the 2015 resumption “a direct provocation of war.” The North turned its own speakers on just days after Seoul did, though South Korean officials said they were so old that their messages were nearly impossible to understand. “It just sounds like a drone,” one official said.
On August 20, 2015, South Korea’s military said North Korean forces had fired toward a loudspeaker site in Yeoncheon, north of Seoul, and South Korean artillery answered with dozens of 155 mm rounds. Pyongyang denied firing, issued an ultimatum to stop the broadcasts and declared a “quasi-state of war.” The standoff closed on August 25, 2015 with a joint statement in which the North expressed regret over the mine blasts and the South agreed to stop broadcasting “unless an abnormal situation occurs.”
That “abnormal situation” came in January 2016, when North Korea conducted an underground nuclear test. Days later, South Korea restarted its loudspeaker broadcasts. This time, the broadcasts went on for over two years. Seoul only switched them off on April 23, 2018, four days before an inter-Korean summit. The resulting Panmunjom Declaration committed both sides to stop all hostile acts along the MDL, including loudspeaker broadcasts, from May 1. 
When Seoul turned the speakers back on in June 2024, after suspending the September 2018 inter-Korean military agreement. South Korea held that North Korea had already voided the agreement through its trash balloons and over provocations. South Korea’s broadcasts in 2024 included BTS songs, regional weather, and market prices, along with a message urging North Korean soldiers laying mines to escape what it called a life of slavery.
North Korea answered not with propaganda but with sheer noise: gunshots, screams, eerie laughter, and sounds like howling wolves. Noise levels on Ganghwa Island, about two kilometers from the North, reached 80 decibels late at night. To many, North Korea’s purpose was simply to torment South Koreans. 
South Korean law acknowledged the harm being done. A December 2024 amendment to the Framework Act on Civil Defense allows the state to compensate people harmed by enemy actions that fall short of a civil defense emergency. A decree issued in May 2025 included “noise broadcasting” among the “hazardous acts” it covers, alongside balloons, shooting or shelling, and drones. In July 2026, border counties began taking claims, with payments determined by the number of days residents lived with the noise.
Previously, North Korea and South Korea stopped their loudspeaker broadcasts through bilateral agreement, after discussions. But South Korea ended its last round unilaterally. New President Lee Jae-myung ordered the broadcasts stopped on June 11, 2025; the North’s broadcasts ended the next day. In August 2025, the military began dismantling its fixed loudspeakers in what the defense ministry called “a practical measure aimed at helping ease tensions with the North.” Seoul said it had not consulted Pyongyang.
Pyongyang rejected any suggestion of reciprocity. After South Korea’s military reported that the North was removing some of its own speakers, Kim Yo Jong said: “We have never removed loudspeakers installed on the border area and are not willing to remove them.” About a week later, in fact, two new North Korean speakers went up opposite the South Korean border counties of Cheorwon and Hwacheon. 
Now North Korea has declared that it will resume broadcasts. If so, the new round of loudspeaker use will be different from recent history. In 2015, 2016, and 2024, Seoul began broadcasting first; this time Pyongyang has declared its intention to do so, in response to alleged South Korean provocations. This is despite repeated efforts on the part of the Lee administration in Seoul to show its goodwill toward the North. 
Since Kim Jong Un declared the two Koreas hostile states in December 2023, North Korean troops have fortified the DMZ, laying mines and building roads, fences, and what appear to be anti-tank barriers. In September 2026, two mine explosions along the DMZ injured three South Korean soldiers. Seoul said the mines had been laid during the “so-called border fortification works” since 2023 – and that they were planted south of MDL that separates the two Koreas.
North Korean soldiers working near the line occasionally cross it, as evidenced by the recent mine incident. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff counted about 50 crossings in August and September 2026; South Korean troops responded with warning broadcasts and warning shots. 
Kim Yo Jong, however, insisted that “our soldiers have never crossed the border.” There may be disagreement over where, exactly, the MDL is situated. If so, it will be difficult to resolve; Pyongyang ignored Seoul’s November 2025 offer of military talks to set “a clear reference line for the MDL.”
Kim’s statements framed the loudspeaker broadcasts as about the border rather than propaganda. She also issued a threat, saying that North Korean troops would show “no mercy” if South Korean warning shots ever harmed a North Korean solider. Kim also reiterated her brother’s vision that the MDL is now “a permanent line never to be crossed.”
As long as North Korean troops keep working along – and crossing – the MDL, South Korean warnings are likely to continue. That means North Korea’s responses, including the broadcasts, will as well. Seoul has also reserved the right to carry out a “proportional response” to North Korean broadcasts, although no specific action has been selected yet. 
Over the longer term inter-Korean relations are likely to be shaped by interactions along the MDL, which Pyongyang now calls a permanent border and Seoul still treats as a temporary demarcation line set by the armistice. Preventing an accidental clash is now an urgent task. 
With inter-Korean hotlines silent since April 2023, South Korea’s Unification Ministry has called for reconciling the two sides’ understandings of the MDL and setting up a communication system to manage it. Thus far, however, Pyongyang has refused to engage. That leaves South Korea with few options for responding to North Korean escalations without raising the risk of conflict.

South Korea has no large loudspeakers left on the border; it took them down in August 2025 as a sign of goodwill. The Ministry of National Defense said that the warnings Kim referred to were issued by smaller speakers at guard posts as a defensive measure against North Korean soldiers crossing the Military Demarcation Line (MDL). 
If the North starts broadcasting, South Korea’s military said it would consider restarting its own loudspeakers on the principle of proportional response.
