Another pro-Duterte senator, who was a former police chief, went into hiding after an arrest warrant was issued against him by the International Criminal Court for his role in the bloody “war on drugs” during the previous administration of Rodrigo Duterte, the vice president’s father.
During the course of the trial, one member of the Senate Duterte bloc decided to join the majority. Another member went abroad to seek medical treatment, but it became an indefinite leave after a plunder complaint was filed against her. The absence of pro-Duterte senators has made it easier for the majority to lower the number of votes needed to convict the vice president. The Senate decision to lower the voting threshold was questioned by pro-Duterte lawyers at the Supreme Court, but the latter dismissed their petition on procedural grounds.
The prosecution’s presentation of evidence on the alleged unexplained wealth of Duterte and her husband provided the public with new information about the vice president’s undeclared assets and business dealings. Some of the suspicious financial transactions were traced to China, which prompted some Marcos officials to comment that it should be further investigated as a potential national security threat.
Duterte has denied ownership of the bank accounts and properties mentioned during her trial. She also insisted that doing business in China is legitimate. Nevertheless, she still needs to explain the mismatch and omissions in her statement of assets as a government official, and the large amount of earnings from her husband’s vague business operations in China.
The prosecution is confident that they can get a guilty verdict on the issue of Duterte’s unexplained wealth, and they made a bold move by dropping other charges in their presentation, including the grave threats against the First Family, misuse of confidential funds, and bribery.
This could also signal that there is now enough number of votes in the Senate to convict Duterte. The impeachment trial may last until the end of the year unless the defense panel decides to present additional witnesses to extend the sessions until early 2027.
The decision to limit the impeachment case to the issue of unexplained wealth has drawn mixed reactions. On one hand, it has been welcomed for expediting the trial and allowing the prosecution to focus on an issue with strong evidence. But it has also been criticized for its potential to undermine the public clamor for accountability, especially since the allegation about the anomalous spending of confidential funds was dropped from the charges. Critics said it could set a precedent by reducing the impeachment process to a transactional matter involving legislators and the presidential office, instead of upholding its role in exacting full accountability against erring officials.
Duterte’s political future will soon be decided by the Senate. Whatever happens, she can take comfort that she still leads in presidential election surveys. If she is convicted, her younger brother could run for president. So far, Marcos has no clear successor, which still makes the Dutertes the formidable team to beat at the 2028 presidential election.
In the meantime, the public awaits the counterarguments and evidence to be presented by Duterte’s legal team in the second half of the impeachment trial.
Recent political realignments in the Philippines suggest that a guilty verdict has already been secured in the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
The House of Representatives twice impeached Duterte, but it was only in July that a trial was convened by the Senate, which needs to deliver a verdict on the allegations that the vice president committed high crimes and betrayed public trust.
articles.summary: Four months into her impeachment trial in the Senate, the political winds are starting to turn against Duterte.

articles.title: Prabowo Accuses MSCI of Attempting to ‘Intimidate’ Indonesia After Downgrade Threat
articles.full_text:
“We possess strength, we have courage, we are willing to make sacrifices, and we refuse to surrender,” said the former general.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto takes part in an event marking the 81st anniversary of the founding of the Indonesian National Armed Forces (TNI) at their headquarters in Cilangkap, East Jakarta, Indonesia, Oct. 5, 2026.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has accused MSCI of attempting to “intimidate” Indonesia, after the global index provider threatened to downgrade the country due to serious stock market transparency issues.
In a statement on October 16, MSCI announced that it had launched “a consultation on a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status.” Among its concerns are coordinated trading practices, the high concentration of ownership in certain companies, and the limited “free float” of shares – i.e., those openly available for public trading.
Speaking to his cabinet yesterday, Prabowo said that MSCI “intended to intimidate us,” Reuters reported. “I simply say to the MSCI: the Indonesian nation fears no one and will not be cowed… We possess strength, we have courage, we are willing to make sacrifices, and we refuse to surrender.”
MSCI’s proposal was more serious than its threat in January to downgrade Indonesia to “frontier market” status due to the transparency concerns in its stock market. The “standalone market” category, which includes the likes of Argentina, Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine, and Zimbabwe, is a rung below “frontier market.”
MSCI said last week that it decided on a more serious downgrade because the long list of reforms announced by Indonesian policymakers to address its concerns had not achieved “sufficient progress.”
“Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement,” it stated. “Feedback from market participants suggests that a reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems.” MSCI said that it “expects to proceed with the proposed reclassification” barring clear evidence of “material improvements in market governance and functioning.”
The announcement prompted a bloodbath on the Jakarta Composite Index, which plunged by around 15 percent over two days of trading. The Indonesian stock market has been among the worst performing in the world in 2026, losing around 40 percent of its value, while the rupiah has fallen to levels not seen since the Asian financial crisis of 1997-1998.
The prospect of a further outflow of capital – a likely result of a downgrade to “standalone” status – has heaped pressure on Prabowo’s administration, which since coming to office in late 2024, has rattled markets with its centralized and free-spending approach to economic management. This has included both a multibillion-dollar free meal program and an increase in the state’s involvement in the Indonesian economy.
Perhaps less important than specific policies is Prabowo’s volatile, unpredictable and highly personalized style of economic governance, which represents a significant change from the conservative stewardship of the past few administrations. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for Indonesia, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.” George Xu, a Director in Fitch Ratings’ Sovereigns team, said in a statement on Tuesday that MSCI’s announcement and the subsequent market sell-off only “reinforce the risks” identified by Fitch during its downgrade in March.
Prabowo’s defiant remarks about the MSCI threat, which have also been echoed by other Indonesian politicians in recent days, are characteristic of his political style and nationalist leanings. They are also unlikely to do much to address the growing concerns about Indonesia’s investability, making it likely that Indonesia will face more economic turbulence during the remainder of his term.

articles.title: Inaccessible by Design: AIIB’s Complaint Mechanism
articles.full_text:
The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has yet to approve a single complaint involving its projects for dispute resolution or compliance review.
On September 28, the first day of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB)’s annual meeting in Doha, 108 Indigenous people from Lombok, Indonesia, filed a complaint with the bank’s grievance body, the Project-affected People’s Mechanism (PPM). They said the AIIB-financed Mandalika Urban and Tourism Infrastructure Project forced them from their homes, took their farming land, cost them their livelihoods, and ignored their right to be consulted. Many now struggle to make ends meet and fear future evictions.
Headquartered in Beijing, with China its largest shareholder, the AIIB began operations in 2016. In a decade, it has grown to 111 members and invested almost $70 billion in more than 350 projects across 40 economies. At the Doha meeting, AIIB President Zou Jiayi announced plans to double its annual financing to about $20 billion by 2030. A growing footprint in Asia and beyond demands an accountability and risk management system to match.
Like its peer multilateral development banks (MDBs), the AIIB has committed to “do no harm” and to offer people a route to seek redress when its projects cause harm. Independent accountability mechanisms, separate from bank management, exist at most MDBs and other development finance institutions. Complaints pass through an initial screening stage, known as admissibility, eligibility, or registration, to establish whether they fall within the mechanism’s mandate. The mechanism then offers dispute resolution or, if parties do not agree to it, examines whether the bank followed its environmental and social rules through a compliance review. 
Communities affected by AIIB-financed projects have never been able to test whether the PPM process works. Since the mechanism’s creation in 2019, none of the 45 complaints tracked on its website as of September 15 this year had passed the admissibility stage. By contrast, peer mechanisms at other development banks regularly take complaints into dispute resolution or compliance review. One of the largest handled more than 60 cases in each of the last two financial years.
The revised policy introduced in 2026 raised hopes that the PPM would become more effective and improve its track record. Since it took effect, however, the PPM has found 14 out of 16 complaints inadmissible. The remaining two, submitted in May, are still awaiting an admissibility decision. The Mandalika complaint would be the 17th complaint of 2026. 
The PPM’s entry requirements are significantly more restrictive than those of its peers. These “roadblocks to accountability” include referring complaints about co-financed projects to the lead lender, imposing narrow time limits on complaints about loans to governments, and requiring prior “good-faith efforts” to resolve grievances with both the project-level grievance mechanism and bank management. 
Complainants must also establish at the admissibility stage that their complaint concerns the AIIB’s failure to comply with its policies, while the complaint mechanism must conduct an assessment that other mechanisms carry out only in later steps. 
A central obstacle to accessibility is the requirement that complainants make “good-faith efforts” with both the project-level grievance mechanism and AIIB management. Under the PPM policy, complainants must explain why they could not resolve their concerns through these channels, and the PPM decides whether their efforts were sufficient. 
The rule has previously been used to reject complaints, including one regarding the Bhola gas power plant in Bangladesh, despite attempts to engage amid legitimate constraints and fears of retaliation. The two complaints filed in May 2026 remain pending while complainants have been asked to engage with the client and management.
Requiring prior engagement at both levels is unique among these mechanisms. Some peers require good-faith efforts with bank management, but not with the project-level grievance mechanism as well. Nor do they require complainants to explain why those efforts failed. The PPM’s approach places that burden on the people seeking redress.
There are legitimate reasons why such engagement may be impossible. A client’s grievance mechanism may be inaccessible or ineffective. The client or management may refuse to engage meaningfully. Restrictions on movement and the threat of retaliation can create further barriers. In many of the AIIB’s borrowing countries, restrictive civic space makes these risks particularly acute. 
The PPM policy lists risks of retaliation against complainants as a factor allowing the PPM to accept a complaint despite the absence of engagement with client and management. That provision has yet to be tested. It will only work only if the PPM trusts complainants’ accounts of why they could go no further and considers all relevant circumstances, including the risks they face. The Mandalika complaint will be an important test, as communities report continuing and increasing attempts at retaliation.
For complaints seeking a compliance review, the threshold is higher still. In addition to meeting the general criteria, they must relate their claim to the AIIB’s noncompliance with its environmental and social policy. The policy excludes complaints relating to actions “that do not involve AIIB’s failure to comply.” 
As we understand the rules, complainants must show the bank’s noncompliance at the outset and, on the strictest reading, that it caused their harm. The evidence for this sits in AIIB’s due diligence and supervision records, which communities cannot see. They cannot know whether the AIIB checked a resettlement plan or what its staff found on supervision visits. Establishing these facts is the purpose of an investigation. Unlike most of its peers, the PPM asks complainants to supply evidence that the mechanism itself should establish.
These restrictions raise doubts about whether any complaint could qualify for compliance review under a strict interpretation of the criteria. Without a compliance review there are no findings: nothing to establish what went wrong, to support remediation for affected communities, or to help the bank improve its procedures and practices.
These technical restrictions run counter to a simple principle: admissibility is a straightforward step to establish whether a complaint falls within the mechanism’s mandate. At peer mechanisms, apart from formal exclusions, the substantive screening focuses on the complaint’s connection to a bank-financed project and its environmental and social policies, and on indications of actual or potential harm. Detailed examination comes later. 
In a compliance review for instance, the mechanism must investigate whether the bank failed to comply with its policies and whether those failures relate to the alleged harm. That work can involve reviewing hundreds of project preparation and supervision documents, conducting field visits, and consulting intensely with affected people and other stakeholders. The admissibility phase is not the place for such an investigation. 
Yet the PPM Policy and Rules of Procedure complicate this initial step, impose unduly strict restrictions, and demand substantial work from both complainants and the mechanism before a case can proceed. It is little surprise that no complaint has cleared this hurdle.
At the AIIB’s annual meeting, Zou spoke of infrastructure “connecting people to opportunities” and of “people-centered development.” Carmen Nonay, the new managing director of AIIB’s Complaints-resolution, Evaluation, and Integrity Unit, which includes the PPM, can help turn that vision into practice by bringing the mechanism into line with its peers. There are 22 other mechanisms with established practices to learn from. 
The managing director has the authority and responsibility to interpret the PPM’s Rules of Procedure. The pending complaints offer an immediate opportunity to do so. We urge her to apply the policy and rules in line with established accountability practice: treat admissibility as a quick, straightforward first step; trust complainants’ accounts of their efforts and the risks they face; and hear them impartially before making a decision. The PPM should use its unrestricted access to management information to identify indications of noncompliance, rather than place that burden on complainants. This approach follows the PPM peers’ shared principles, reiterated this year, which put accessibility first: “A recourse mechanism is not effective if affected people do not know it exists or are unable to access its services.”
Because the PPM sits within the institution it reviews, its managing director may not feel sufficiently independent to pursue this approach. The AIIB board should make it clear that it expects the mechanism to follow its peers’ good practice. If the PPM still struggles to deliver on its mandate, the board should review the obstacles and require changes to the policy, particularly its accessibility provisions.
Almost eight years after the PPM’s creation, workers and communities affected by AIIB-financed projects deserve the same care and accountability as those affected by other MDBs. That is a matter of fairness and credibility for the AIIB and its shareholders. An accessible, effective complaints mechanism would strengthen the bank’s reputation and its ability to finance development sustainably.

articles.title: Why the China-US Naval Encounter at Sabina Shoal Is Different
articles.full_text:
It’s a new kind of close encounter. Will it become a new normal?
The Independence-class littoral combat ship USS Charleston approaches the Wasp-class amphibious assault ship USS Boxer (not pictured) for a fueling-at-sea, Nov. 1, 2025.
On October 20, China accused a U.S. naval vessel of “undermining regional stability” by entering waters near Sabina Shoal in the Spratly Islands. According to a spokesperson for the People’s Liberation Army’s Southern Theater Command Navy, the U.S. Littoral Combat Ship USS Charleston (LCS-18) “illegally ​intruded” into waters adjacent to Sabina Shoal “without approval from the Chinese government.” By contrast, a U.S.​ Navy 7th Fleet spokesperson maintained that the Charleston conducted “routine operations in international waters” consistent with international law.
This latest naval encounter reflects the long-standing legal dispute between China and the U.S. over the freedom of navigation of warships in the South China Sea. What makes it distinct is the location of the incident: unlike all previous U.S. Freedom of Navigation Operations (FONOPs) targeted at China in the South China Sea, the encounter occurred near Sabina Shoal, a maritime feature not occupied by China. Thus, this is also the first time that the PLA Navy (PLAN) officially admitted that it “dispatched forces to track and monitor the U.S. vessel” near a feature China doesn’t occupy. 
This new kind of close encounter may reveal that the Chinese government is upgrading its strategy to respond to perceived U.S. naval intrusions in the South China Sea. At the same time, the incident may also serve as a warning to the Philippines, which considers Sabina Shoal to be a part of its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). These interpretations remain tentative, and non-exclusive, but they make the encounter worth examining beyond the immediate exchange of official statements.
Disputes Between China and the U.S. over “Freedom of Navigation” of Warships 
The United States holds that the right to sail and operate its military vessels “wherever customary international law allows” is “a long-standing national interest.” The U.S. military uses FONOPs to challenge maritime claims and restrictions that it considers excessive. 
China, by contrast, argues that freedom of navigation cannot be invoked to justify activities that it views as threatening its territorial integrity or security, including foreign warships’ operations near maritime features over which China asserts sovereignty. Beijing considers the intentional “intrusion” of warships into its claimed territorial sea to be “hegemonic freedom of navigation.” China argues U.S. FONOPs have no place in contemporary international law. 
A semi-official research report published by the China Institute for Marine Affairs under the Ministry of Natural Resources in August 2025 highlighted this issue. The report concluded that the “U.S. Freedom of Navigation lacks a basis in international law and seriously distorts the interpretation and development of international law.” These competing positions have underpinned repeated Chinese protests against U.S. naval operations in the South China Sea.
Notably, news reports of the Charleston’s October 20 operation did not officially describe it as a FONOP. The U.S. spokesperson’s statement instead emphasized that “all nations enjoy freedom of navigation and other lawful uses of the sea in this area.” That language is consistent with Washington’s broader position on maritime access, but it does not establish that the operation was a formally designated FONOP or identify the specific legal claim, if any, that the vessel intended to challenge. 
The distinction matters: a naval transit, a routine operation, and a FONOP may overlap in practice, but they are not necessarily interchangeable descriptions of an operation’s purpose.
U.S. FONOPs generally identify a particular maritime claim or restriction they seek to challenge.  For instance, the United States explicitly labeled a previous operation that took place on August 13, 2025, near Scarborough Shoal as a FONOP intended to challenge Chinese domestic legislation requiring prior authorization for foreign warships to enter China’s territorial sea. In such cases, the stated legal objective provides a relatively clear basis for interpreting the operation and anticipating a Chinese response. In the August 2025 case, the PLA said it had “organized forces to lawfully track, monitor, issue warnings, and expel the U.S. warship.” 
Sabina Shoal presents a different situation for a number of reasons. First of all, unlike Scarborough Shoal, Sabina Shoal was not among the contested maritime features in the 2016 South China Sea Arbitration Award. 
At the same time, there is no mutual understanding between China and the Philippines on the legal status of the shoal and its surrounding waters. The United States and the Philippines regard Sabina Shoal as a low-tide elevation that cannot, in its own right, generate a territorial sea. They thus regard the surrounding waters as part of the Philippines’ EEZ. 
By contrast, the Chinese government disputes that Sabina Shoal (known in Chinese as Xianbin Jiao) is a low-tide elevation. In fact, a “Survey Report on the Coral Reef Ecosystem of Xianbin Jiao” published by the Ministry of Natural Resources of China in August 2024, said that there are at least three naturally formed cays above water at high tide. Accordingly, China considers Sabina Shoal to be a rock that can claim a territorial sea. This may explain why China accused the Charleston of an “illegal intrusion” into the “adjacent waters” of Sabina Shoal. 
Nevertheless, the most peculiar scenario at Sabina Shoal is that this maritime feature has never been formally occupied by China, thanks to the 2002 Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC), which prohibits “inhabitation” on previously unoccupied maritime features. 
Yet in Beijing’s view, Sabina Shoal is part of the “Nansha Qundao” (Spratly Islands), which as a whole belongs to China. That might be the reason that China never formally claimed any territorial sea around its occupied maritime features such as Johnson Reef (Chigua Jiao), Fiery Cross Reef (Yongshu Jiao), or Cuarteron Reef (Huayang Jiao). Instead, Beijing claims “indisputable territorial sovereignty, sovereign rights and interests” within the whole of the Spratly Islands group.
The ambiguity surrounding the nature of the Charleston’s operation makes it difficult to interpret. It’s unclear if the United States intended to challenge a Chinese claim to maritime entitlements around Sabina Shoal or a requirement for prior authorization of transiting its territorial sea. If, however, the operation was instead intended to demonstrate support for the Philippines, the significance would lie less in a specific legal challenge than in the strategic signal conveyed by a U.S. naval presence near a flashpoint in the China-Philippines dispute.
The encounter occurred amid heightened tensions between China and the Philippines. On October 14, Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan reportedly remarked that China could “easily win a conflict” against the Philippines if it chose to use force. The remark followed a serious confrontation between a Chinese Coast Guard vessel and a Philippine government vessel at Sabina Shoal on September 18. 
In fact, since the beginning of October, at least eight close encounters between China and the Philippines have occurred across the South China Sea and Luzon Strait, according to Reuters. This wider context helps explain why the Philippines might view the Charleston’s presence at Sabina Shoal as a sign of U.S. support, even if the operation was not formally identified as a FONOP against Chinese maritime claims.
China’s response, on the other hand, could be interpreted as a fresh warning to the Philippines. By dispatching naval forces to track and monitor the U.S. warship at an unoccupied maritime feature for the first time, China showcased its determination to protect its claimed rights and interests at Sabina Shoal. 
This upgraded response also sends a straightforward warning to the Philippines that any further provocation at Sabina Shoal, with or without support from the U.S., will predictably receive an escalated Chinese response.
The Outlook of China-U.S. Naval Encounters in the South China Sea 
While international law provides a common framework for maritime conduct, its interpretation and application remain deeply contested by major powers. The United States advocates its naval operations as a defense of freedom of navigation, whereas China views U.S. naval operations near South China Sea maritime features as challenges to its territorial sovereignty and security. Without a shared understanding of the legal and strategic implications of such operations, similar encounters are likely to recur.
The outlook is therefore one of persistent competition accompanied by risks of unintended escalation. As both navies maintain a significant presence in the South China Sea, close encounters – including, as in this case – China-U.S. naval encounters at maritime features not occupied by China, may become increasingly frequent, particularly amid intensifying Philippine-U.S. security cooperation. Even when neither side seeks confrontation, miscalculation, communication failures, or domestic political pressure could turn a “routine operation” into a serious crisis.
Yet confrontation is not inevitable. Both China and the United States have strong incentives to prevent tactical incidents from escalating into broader military conflict. Maintaining effective military communication channels, strengthening incident-management mechanisms, and clarifying operational protocols should therefore remain priorities. Equally important is a willingness to address maritime disagreements through diplomacy and international law rather than relying exclusively on military assertions such as the FONOPs.
Ultimately, the significance of the Sabina Shoal naval encounter lies not simply in the actions of the two navies, but in what it reveals about the future of maritime order in the South China Sea. Whether such encounters become catalysts for escalation or opportunities for improved crisis management will depend on the strategic choices made in Beijing and Washington.

articles.title: New Zealand’s Climate Report Tests Its Pacific Leadership
articles.full_text:
Wellington’s latest environmental assessment highlights the growing economic risks of climate change, raising questions about whether government policy can keep pace.
New Zealand’s latest climate assessment presents a challenge that extends beyond environmental protection, raising questions about whether the country can translate growing evidence of climate change into policies that protect its economy and strengthen its standing in the Pacific.
Published October 7, “Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026” documents rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns and mounting pressure on infrastructure, ecosystems and communities. New Zealand’s annual average temperature has risen 1.36 degrees Celsius since records began in 1909, while seven of its 10 warmest years occurred between 2016 and 2025. Concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide also reached record highs in 2025.
The report’s significance lies in what these trends mean for government policy. New Zealand must reduce emissions while preparing for climate impacts that are already occurring. How effectively it manages that balance will affect not only its economic resilience but also its credibility as a partner to Pacific island countries confronting similar challenges.
The government’s accompanying publication, “Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026: The Stories Behind the Numbers,” examines how communities and organizations are responding to climate-related risks. Read alongside the government’s “Second Emissions Reduction Plan for 2026–30,” the publications highlight the gap policymakers must bridge between documenting environmental change, reducing emissions, and preparing for its consequences.
Efforts to reduce emissions must be balanced against the economic importance of key industries and the livelihoods of those who depend on them. Agriculture accounted for 53 percent of New Zealand’s gross greenhouse gas emissions in 2024, according to the assessment, while remaining central to its export economy. Reducing agricultural emissions therefore presents difficult choices involving competitiveness, rural livelihoods, and the pace of economic transition.
Climate impacts add to those economic pressures. Drought and changing rainfall patterns threaten agricultural production, while flooding and landslides can damage roads, disrupt supply chains, and increase infrastructure costs. Coastal hazards create additional risks for homes and communities. The extent of the damage will depend partly on how effectively the government incorporates climate projections into land-use planning, infrastructure investment, and public spending.
The emissions reduction plan addresses the government’s approach to cutting emissions. But reducing emissions does not eliminate the need to adapt to further climate change. New Zealand must also decide which infrastructure to protect, where new development is appropriate, and how to distribute the costs of preparing for future hazards.
These decisions have consequences beyond its borders, as across the Pacific, rising seas, coastal erosion, and extreme weather threaten communities, infrastructure, and freshwater resources. Many island countries have limited financial capacity to respond, despite contributing relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions.
New Zealand has a direct interest in the region’s resilience through its economic, social, and security relationships with Pacific countries. Supporting adaptation, disaster preparedness, and resilient infrastructure can strengthen those relationships. But effective cooperation requires more than emergency assistance after disasters; it depends on sustained investment and respect for the priorities of Pacific governments and communities.
New Zealand’s domestic response will also shape its regional credibility. Wellington cannot control global emissions or eliminate every climate risk, but it can demonstrate that environmental evidence informs its own infrastructure decisions, economic planning, and emissions policies. A disconnect between international commitments and domestic implementation would weaken the force of its regional advocacy.
The new publications provide a foundation for that work, not proof that it is already being done effectively. The companion report’s case studies may offer practical lessons, but their broader value depends on whether those lessons influence government decisions. Similarly, an emissions reduction plan must be judged by implementation and outcomes, not simply by the existence of published targets.
New Zealand’s latest climate assessment therefore presents a test of governance as much as an environmental warning. The government has consolidated evidence of a changing climate and published a plan for reducing emissions. The next step is to ensure that those efforts translate into practical adaptation, more resilient infrastructure and sustained cooperation across the Pacific.
For Wellington, the stakes are clear: its ability to manage climate risks at home will help determine the strength of its economy and the credibility of its leadership in a region where climate change is already a defining concern.

articles.title: China’s AI Industry Brings Both Gains and Challenges for Its Fragile Economy
articles.full_text:
China’s exports are surging, driven by AI-related technologies. National security-driven export bans could change that.
China is attracting global interest and achieving record-breaking export growth as a trailblazer in the field of artificial intelligence (AI). However, the sector’s growing importance for China’s economy is a double-edged sword. The delicacy of the ongoing AI race, coupled with its national security implications, could lead to curbs on the sharing of certain technologies, casting new doubt on the frontier as an economic driver. 
China’s exports are growing at a phenomenal rate, recording a 36.3 percent year-on-year boost in September to reach $447.18 billion. That’s the highest growth level for Chinese exports since 2021, and even then figures were somewhat unreliable due to the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. 
September’s figures extended a positive run. China’s exports grew 25 percent year-on-year in August. In both months, high-tech trade was a critical contributor to the surging growth. China’s semiconductor exports grew more than 108 percent over the past month, and automatic data processing machine shipments, recorded a boost of 55 percent. 
The AI industry has been providing economic tailwinds for China, bolstered by government initiatives to support the development of the technology domestically. In turn, China’s tech-focused exports have helped to support the national economy. However, it appears that China is mulling placing new bans on exports focusing on emerging technologies. That includes AI as well as biotechnology and solar power. 
In recent days, China has unveiled a draft plan to establish a fresh series of export bans that will impact 14 different forms of technology. The notice, issued by China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology, proposes bans or restrictions that cover 40 technologies in total. The Ministry of Commerce has claimed that the implementation of export bans is necessary to reinforce security while preventing misuse and abuse. 
If implemented, those curbs could significantly impact the nation’s ongoing export boom. Critically, the restrictions would see domestic AI models with parameter counts of 2 trillion or more excluded from exports. Parameter counts are important measures of the learning capacity of models, and controlling higher-end models is likely to be China’s way of maintaining an edge in a highly competitive buildout. Both of China’s leading AI models – Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8-Max – exceed parameter counts of 2 trillion, meaning that their export could be banned entirely. 
However, it’s worth noting that foreign businesses and users would still be able to use AI models via front-end software like APIs, websites, or cloud apps, just so long as the underlying core technology remains hosted securely inside China. 
There’s also the potential for foreign-owned businesses to enter foreign-trade zones like Beijing to maintain their access to Chinese AI technology. However, the intricacies of market entry in China mean that higher degrees of access to domestic AI tools aren’t assured forever. 
As China’s government considers tighter restrictions on technology-related exports, it will have to confront the economic implications. The nation has secured significant growth off the back of its strength in AI. Alongside the nation’s export strength, growing interest in Chinese AI from overseas is helping to transform both trade and the economy on a fundamental level. It’s also supporting China’s economic ties with other countries in a way that boosts global integration. 
Chinese exports of integrated circuits surged 99.1 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters of 2026. Other sectors of technology, such as computer parts and accessories, have seen Chinese exports more than triple over the same period. 
Even so, the latest figures show that China’s economy expanded 4.4 percent in the third quarter. That’s below the government target of between 4.5 percent and 5 percent GDP growth for the year – China’s lowest growth target in decades. 
Although AI exports have helped to support the economy, Beijing is still struggling to address its sinking real estate sector in the post-pandemic landscape. Multiple geopolitical stresses and macroeconomic headwinds linked to both trade rows and global conflicts have stifled growth in a way that has absorbed China’s high-tech export success story. The prospect of tighter controls over AI exports could create fresh pressures for an economy that’s already facing severe challenges. 
At this stage, it’s important to note that China’s AI export bans would largely be limited to the distribution of its high-end models, meaning that we can still expect a sustained upturn in high-tech exports throughout the final quarter 2026. But with AI helping to strengthen China’s international ties with other countries, stronger restrictions on its frontier technology could stunt its growth at a time when the economy appears set to miss its annual targets. 
For a nation that’s still seeking to plot its recovery from a deep real estate crisis, AI has emerged as a major economic opportunity. However, China’s strong stance on protecting national security could create more economic disruption, making the road to 5 percent growth even more challenging.

articles.title: The China-US Quantum Computing Contest
articles.full_text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Matt Kinsella – the CEO of Infleqtion, a leading U.S. quantum technology company – is the 531st in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Briefly describe U.S. advancements in quantum computing technology.
The United States is moving from experimental quantum systems toward logical, fault-tolerant computing. The key measure is no longer the number of physical qubits, but whether those qubits can be organized into reliable logical qubits and used for meaningful applications.
Infleqtion is at the forefront of that shift. Our neutral-atom platform has demonstrated 12 logical qubits with error detection and loss correction, a 99.73 percent two-qubit gate fidelity, and arrays of up to 1,600 neutral-atom sites. With Nvidia, we published a materials-science demonstration in which logical encoding reduced error approximately sixfold compared with physical-qubit execution.
Our roadmap achieves 30 logical qubits later this year, 100 by 2028, and 1,000 by 2030. We see approximately 100 high-quality logical qubits as the threshold for outperforming classical systems on selected valuable problems.
Hardware alone will not get us there. As our CTO, Pranav Gokhale, has emphasized, hardware-aware software can force-multiply quantum performance. Infleqtion is developing the complete stack – from atoms, photonics, and control systems to error correction, Superstaq compilation, resource estimation, and integration with GPU-accelerated computing. That full-system approach is how quantum computing becomes useful.
In what ways is the U.S. collaborating with partners in the Asia Pacific in developing quantum computing technology?
The United States is building a trusted quantum ecosystem with Asia-Pacific partners through joint research, technology development, workforce training, and access to advanced systems.
Japan provides a strong example. Japan’s Science and Technology Agency selected Infleqtion as the first foreign company – and the only foreign quantum-computing partner – to participate in its Quantum Moonshot program. In a consortium led by Professor Kenji Ohmori of the Institute for Molecular Science, we are contributing neutral-atom technology, photonics expertise, and systems engineering to the development of a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer based on atomic qubits.
This is more than a research exchange. It combines an American commercial platform with Japanese leadership in ultrafast atomic control and aligns both countries around a shared technical objective. To this end, Infleqtion has delivered neutral-atom systems, helping researchers build the practical experience required to operate and develop applications for advanced quantum machines.
In Australia, Infleqtion has established an Asia-Pacific presence at Swinburne University of Technology and worked with the Australian Army and Australian industry on trustworthy quantum computation. One collaboration with Australian quantum company Diraq explored quantum physically unclonable functions intended to help verify the identity and integrity of remotely accessed quantum computers.
We are also engaging Australian leaders on the future use of quantum computing in energy and infrastructure. This application-led approach is essential: allied programs should begin with consequential problems and jointly determine the hardware, software, and classical resources required to address them.
These partnerships expand the talent, facilities, test environments, and applications available to the United States. Our alliances are not simply diplomatic relationships; they are a practical technology advantage.
Analyze the scope and scale of the U.S.-China quantum computing competition.
The U.S.-China quantum competition is not a single race. It spans computing architecture, logical reliability, software, photonics, manufacturing, talent, supply chains, data-center integration, and applications.
China can concentrate substantial state resources behind selected national programs. The United States operates through a more distributed system of companies, universities, federal laboratories, private capital, and international partners. That diversity supports several technical pathways while creating strong pressure to demonstrate practical results.
Infleqtion represents the strength of the American model. We are advancing a vertically integrated neutral-atom platform while expanding from research milestones into deployed systems and application centers. Our technology is operational in national institutions, and our teams are working with government and industry on energy, materials, AI, and scientific discovery.
We have delivered a 100-physical-qubit system to the U.K. National Quantum Computing Centre, announced a fault-tolerant system for Illinois, opened a Chicago Quantum Innovation Center, and expanded our U.K. engineering and manufacturing presence. These are signs of an industry developing the infrastructure to scale – not merely producing individual experiments.
The competition will be decided by sustained execution: who can build dependable logical systems, reduce resource overhead, manufacture them, connect them to classical supercomputers, and solve consequential problems. The United States has a powerful innovation network, and Infleqtion is rapidly converting that advantage into operating capability.
Examine China’s quantum computing technology developments.
China has demonstrated credible progress in superconducting and photonic quantum computing, supported by centralized programs that coordinate across universities, national laboratories, and state-linked companies. In particular, the University of Science and Technology of China’s Zuchongzhi 3.0 superconducting processor and Jiuzhang 4.0 photonic system have now achieved world-leading results.
These are technically impressive demonstrations, but more consequential questions concern logical error rates, programmable circuit depth, application performance, system availability, and the resources required to outperform the best classical alternative. Of note, China’s leading results in neutral atom quantum computing have lagged developments here in the U.S., though there have been recent accelerations in China’s efforts over the past year. 
China is also building domestic control electronics, cloud platforms, software, and industrial capacity. Its 2026-2030 planning framework treats quantum technology as a strategic emerging field, so the United States should expect continued progress.
The appropriate response is disciplined acceleration. We should measure China’s achievements accurately while investing in the capabilities that determine practical advantage: logical qubits, efficient error correction, hardware-aware software, advanced manufacturing, and application deployment. Those are the areas where Infleqtion is concentrating its computing roadmap.
Assess how quantum computing technology is integrated into U.S. national security and defense systems and its implications for the U.S.-China tech race.
Large-scale quantum computers are not yet embedded in operational defense systems. Current integration is occurring through research programs, independent technical validation, hybrid computing infrastructure, and development of mission-relevant applications.
An exemplar is DARPA’s HARQ program exploring heterogeneous systems that combine different quantum processors with classical resources. To meet that demand, Infleqtion is developing Multistaq, a software layer designed to compile and coordinate workloads across multiple qubit technologies.
Infleqtion is also supporting three Department of Energy Genesis Mission projects involving AI-optimized quantum circuits for nuclear applications, fusion research, and deployable atomic sensing. Our planned Illinois system will connect a neutral-atom QPU with Nvidia GPU infrastructure, providing a test environment for quantum-classical workflows and real-time error correction. The associated Chicago center is initially focused on energy-grid and nuclear optimization problems with direct implications for national resilience.
Quantum sensing and timing are closer to field deployment than fault-tolerant computing. Infleqtion’s work in GPS-independent navigation, spectrum awareness, precision timing, gravity sensing, and space systems gives the company operating experience with government missions while strengthening the shared photonics, controls, software, and manufacturing base behind our computers.
For the U.S.-China competition, the objective should be clear: move quantum computing from scientific potential to trusted national infrastructure. Infleqtion is helping the United States do that by combining technical progress, deployed systems, application development, and allied partnerships on one scalable neutral-atom platform.
articles.summary: Insights from Matt Kinsella.

articles.title: The Indian Government’s Job Statistics Are Misleading
articles.full_text:
Behind the surge in EPFO numbers lies an uncomfortable question: is Delhi measuring new jobs or merely recording existing workers differently?
The Indian government claims that the formal job market in the country is booming. It cites as proof payroll data from the Employees’ Provident Fund Organization (EPFO).
The Employees’ Provident Fund is a mandatory government-backed retirement savings scheme in India for salaried workers. The question, however, is: does a rising EPFO count really amount to more good jobs?
The official story goes as follows. The Economic Survey 2023-24 reported that net EPFO payroll additions more than doubled, from 6.11 million in FY2018-19 to 13.15 million. The survey called it “healthy growth in formal employment.” The Union Labor Ministry hailed it as a “growing formal employment landscape.”
The Indian government has now gone further and linked formalization of employment directly to “quality jobs.” In August 2026, it promoted the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana as a scheme to expand formal employment, designed to encourage first-time employment and to reward employers for creating new formal jobs through EPFO.
Formalization is valuable. A worker brought under EPF coverage gains access to an institutional mechanism for retirement savings and social security. An enterprise complying with labor regulations represents progress over one that does not. 
However, these claims ignore reality. An EPFO “net subscriber addition” is not a net new job. It can include a person moving from one EPFO-covered employer to another; an existing worker newly brought into EPFO coverage; a worker previously outside formal coverage becoming covered; workers rejoining after an employment break; changes resulting from EPFO administrative coverage; and, importantly, formalization of an already existing informal job.
September 2026 EPFO data showed contributors in 12 traditionally labor-intensive sectors (garments, textiles, leather, jute, beedi, tea, brick-making, cashew, coir, cotton ginning, diamond cutting, and others) fell 1.3 percent, from 5,536,000 in 2023-24 to 5,464,000 in 2025-26. These are precisely the sectors India must expand to absorb workers leaving agriculture.
There is a further fundamental statistical problem. 
EPFO payroll statistics measure movements into and out of the EPF system. The monthly payroll series records first-time subscribers, members exiting coverage, and earlier members who rejoin. The government itself cautions that the numbers are provisional because employee records are continuously updated. 
The Economic Survey 2025-26 carried the government’s claims further: organized manufacturing added 5.7 million jobs. This is potentially more interesting because it is not based on EPFO figures. 
The National Sample Survey or NSS Survey uses Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) data and says organized manufacturing employment increased by more than 5.7 million between FY2015 and FY2024; grew at about 4 percent compounded annual growth rate (CAGR); and increased by more than 1 million in FY2024 alone, a 6 percent year-on-year increase. 
This is probably the strongest official evidence currently being cited for actual employment expansion in the organized sector, rather than simply formalization. But there is a major definitional qualification: The ASI’s “persons engaged” category includes working proprietors, family members, and unpaid workers, as well as employees. So it is not synonymous with regular wage/salaried formal jobs. 
The government is also pointing to the rise in regular salaried employment. Regular wage/salaried employment increased from 22.4 percent of workers in 2024 to 23.6 percent in 2025. That is a meaningful movement toward wage employment, although it is still very far from the claim that most new employment is formal.
In fact, what takes the wind out of the government’s claims is that the increase in organized manufacturing has been accompanied by growing contractualization. According to ASI, contract workers accounted for only about 13 percent of the formal manufacturing workforce in 1993-94. However, this share rose sharply to 20 percent by 1999-2000 and further to 37.8 percent in 2018-19. As per the latest ASI data (2022-23), it has reached 40.7 percent. So much for the claim of formalization – the ILO defines it as work with social security, and contract work does not offer that.
The percentage share of contract labor in capital-intensive industries has increased from 19.5 percent in 1999-2000 to 46 percent in 2018-2019, whereas it has increased from 22 percent in 1999-2000 to 33 percent in 2018-2019 in labor-intensive enterprises. 
As though that is not enough, if EPFO was really creating so many new jobs, how is it that India’s Periodic Labor Force Survey (PLFS) continues to show that India’s share of informal workers without social insurance (i.e. pensions, death/disability insurance, maternity benefits, etc.) was 90 percent in 2004-5, 90 percent in 2017-18, and still 90 percent in 2024. 
Job quality also matters: duration, earnings, working conditions, social protection, security of tenure, and prospects for advancement. India’s employment challenge has historically been not only unemployment but also underemployment, low productivity, and poor-quality work.
The latest PLFS data illustrate this complexity. Even after the increase in regular wage employment, 56.2 percent of workers in 2025 remained self-employed (mostly own-account and unpaid family labor) and another 20.20 percent were casual wage laborers. Agriculture still accounted for 43 percent of employment in 2025 (42 percent in 2019). The largest addition to the workforce since 2020 has been in agriculture (rising from 200 million to 280 million in 2024). 
This matters most for the young. A graduate in a low-paid, insecure job is technically employed but not upwardly mobile. As we estimate in our new book, “India Out of Work,” real wages for casual and regular workers, and for the 53 percent of workers who are self-employed, have stagnated for 12 years. If non-farm jobs have grown at half the required rate (12 million a year) for a dozen years the Modi government has been in power, leaving youth unemployment double its 2012 level, from 6 percent to 12 percent in 2024, how can real wages rise, however loudly the government touts its low inflation?
The real test of India’s labor market is not how many names enter an EPFO database but whether the economy creates enough stable, productive, and decently paid jobs. If it did, the youth (those aged 15-29 years) not in education, employment, and training, would not have jumped from 50 million in 2012 to 100 million in 2024.  Clearly, many became “discouraged workers” who stopped looking for work.

articles.title: Is China Getting Involved in the Japan-Russia Territorial Dispute?
articles.full_text:
Amid deepening China-Russia ties, a Chinese delegation visited one of the disputed Southern Kuril Islands.
According to information released by the government of Russia’s Sakhalin Oblast on October 13, a delegation from China’s Heilongjiang Province, including government officials and entrepreneurs, recently visited Iturup Island (Etorofu in Japanese). The island is part of the Southern Kuril Islands, known as the Northern Territories in Japan, which are currently under Russian de facto control, though Japan claims sovereignty over them.
The Chinese group’s visit led to an immediate expression of dissatisfaction from Tokyo, with Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu declaring it “absolutely unacceptable.” In response, Beijing stated that it “consistently advocates for respecting and upholding the outcomes of the victory [of World War II].” A Japanese media outlet suggested that this reflects “a coordinated stance between China and Russia regarding the Northern Territories issue and a joint approach in dealing with Japan.”
The islands in question were under Japanese control until they were occupied by the Soviet Union at the end of World War II. The Japanese government has maintained its claim ever since. Tokyo has made repeated attempts to advance negotiations on the territorial issue with Russia by leveraging economic cooperation and investment. Ultimately, however, these efforts have not yielded satisfactory results.
Despite possessing abundant fishery and mineral resources, the economic potential of these islands remains largely untapped due to the lagging economic development of the Russian Far East, inadequate infrastructure, and high transportation costs. In 2022, Russia announced the establishment of a special economic zone on the islands to foster economic growth. If Chinese enterprises become more involved in the economic development of the Southern Kuril Islands in the future, it would not only exert political pressure on Japan but could also strengthen Russia’s de facto control over these islands.
Although maps currently published in China label these islands as Japanese territory under Russian occupation, Beijing generally avoids taking an explicit stance on their sovereignty. In August 2026, following Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Iturup Island, the Chinese and Russian ambassadors to Japan co-authored an article stating: “The preservation of historical memory of World War II and its outcomes is particularly important for our countries.” This appeared to imply China’s acknowledgment of the status quo without an overt declaration. Some Japanese media outlets perceive Beijing as shifting away from the position it held during the later Mao era and moving toward the Russian side.
It remains unclear whether this delegation’s visit was intentionally orchestrated by Beijing. However, given that the delegation included officials from the Heilongjiang provincial government, the visit clearly had at least the tacit approval of the authorities. 
Over the past few months, Japanese lawmakers from various political parties have visited Taiwan, and most notably, a group of 27 Japanese parliamentarians arrived in Taiwan around the same time as this delegation’s visit. Beijing typically views such actions as an infringement upon China’s territorial sovereignty. Consequently, this visit by the Chinese delegation may well be a countermeasure by Beijing against Japan.
One disadvantage for Japan is that it is involved in territorial or maritime disputes with nearly all of its neighbors. These disputes currently remain largely a matter of bilateral relations between Japan and the respective countries involved. However, the Chinese delegation’s visit to the Southern Kuril Islands against the backdrop of deteriorating China-Japan relations may signal that Beijing has deployed a diplomatic card against Japan that had previously received little attention.
The deepening of China-Russia relations has further complicated this issue. In recent years, the frequent joint patrols conducted by Chinese and Russian military aircraft and naval vessels in the vicinity of Japan have drawn concern from Tokyo. 
Concurrently, China and Russia have aligned their historical narratives. In May 2025, the two nations issued a joint statement commemorating their respective victories in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the Great Patriotic War, while also pledging to strengthen bilateral cooperation and uphold the authority of international law. The statement characterized both China and Russia as “pivotal forces in the fight against militarism and fascism” and asserts their commitment to “defending the outcomes of the Second World War” and resisting any “resurgence of militarism.” This aligns with Beijing’s accusations that Japan is pursuing a “new-type militarism.” 
Given these shared historical perceptions, China and Russia can be expected to coordinate more closely on historical and security-related issues in their diplomatic approaches toward Japan.
However, it remains highly likely that Beijing will continue to avoid formally recognizing Russian sovereignty over the islands. This is not only because China needs to maintain diplomatic maneuvering room vis-à-vis Japan, but also because it seeks to avoid becoming entirely tethered to Russia’s interests.
Japan’s response, meanwhile, is constrained by both its own policy toward Russia and the state of its relations with China. Japan’s continued imposition of sanctions against Russia makes any substantive improvement in its relations with Moscow in the near term highly unlikely. At the same time, there are no signs of any meaningful improvement in Tokyo’s relations with China. Against this backdrop, it is difficult for Japan to effectively counter the activities of China and Russia in the region.
More significantly, should China begin to actively engage in economic activities or even pursue military cooperation with Russia on the islands, the issue could gradually evolve from a bilateral dispute between Japan and Russia into a new variable affecting China-Japan relations and, by extension, the security landscape of Northeast Asia.

articles.title: Afghanistan’s Wakhan Transit Road Is a Long Shot to Connect with China
articles.full_text:
The road has been officially inaugurated, but China and the Taliban have very different views of its function.
The mountainous terrain of the Wakhan Corridor, the thin strip of Afghanistan that shares a border with China.
On October 4, Taliban officials inaugurated the 121-kilometer-long Wakhan Transit Road connecting Afghanistan to China via the Wakhan Corridor after approximately three years of construction work. The road stretches from Afghanistan’s Broghil border area, on the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, along Badakhshan province’s Wakhan district, finally reaching the border with China. According to Afghanistan’s de facto government under the Taliban, beyond China, the road will connect the country with third parties like Central Asian countries and global markets. 
This corridor is expected to play a significant role for Afghanistan’s trade as well as its regional transit. Its opening marks an important milestone for the Taliban since the corridor was ignored for years due to security concerns. 
A remote region in northeast Afghanistan, the Wakhan Corridor is 350 kilometers long and 13 to 65 km wide. The corridor, which shares borders with Pakistan (through the Durand Line, which the Taliban has started referring to as a “hypothetical” line), Tajikistan, and China, was created as a buffer zone between the Russian and British empires in 1895-96 when the Anglo-Russian Boundary Commission awarded the area to Afghanistan. Once a part of the famous Silk Road trade route, the Wakhan Corridor has been closed for regular transit for almost a century now.
Taliban Minister of Rural Rehabilitation and Development Abdul Latif Mansour, speaking at the inauguration ceremony, said that the road held “political, economic, and strategic significance” for Afghanistan. “The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan has prioritized such public projects, especially in provinces that are most in need,” Mansour said, according to Tolo News. He further emphasized the homegrown nature of the project, saying, “There are no foreign engineers or advisers; all the engineers are Afghans.” 
Governor of Badakhshan Rahmatullah Najib highlighted the road’s opening as a milestone. “After 45 years of war in the country, the Afghan people are witnessing the completion of such a major project in one of Afghanistan’s most remote areas,” Tolo News paraphrased Najib as saying. 
This project is said to have cost 365 million Afghanis ($5.6 million) and was funded by the Taliban’s Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development.
According to Afghanistan’s Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs’ website, this trade route will benefit Afghanistan by providing direct access to imports from and exports to China. The minister highlighted that China is Afghanistan’s largest trading partner, with annual trade exceeding $1 billion between the two countries. The website claimed that the Wakhan Corridor is now the “closest, safest, and most reliable” route for China to export its goods not only to Afghanistan, but to the Central Asian countries, and beyond: to the Arab world, Turkiye, Iran, and the European countries. 
That assumption is questionable; China has direct borders with three Central Asian countries – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan – and has invested millions in upgrading its trade and transit infrastructure to the region. China already has well-developed rail links with Kazakhstan. The Khorgos Gateway, which opened for operations in 2012 on the China-Kazakhstan border, is the world’s largest dry port. And construction on the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway is underway. It’s unclear why China would choose to route exports to Central Asia via Afghanistan. 
The benefits for Afghanistan are more obvious. Due to the ongoing conflict between Afghanistan and Pakistan, trade across their border has come to a halt. That cuts off landlocked Afghanistan’s primary trade and transit route for reaching third countries. If the Wakhan Corridor route becomes fully operational, it will provide an alternative route for Afghanistan to trade with the regional countries, particularly with China. Afghanistan could then connect directly with China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), rather than linking itself to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) as previously discussed. 
In 2016, Afghanistan – then under the Republic government – and China signed a memorandum of understanding to integrate Afghanistan into the BRI. The following year in December, foreign ministers from Afghanistan, China, and Pakistan agreed to discuss ways to extend the CPEC to Afghanistan. In 2023, Afghanistan – now ruled by the Taliban – again reiterated its intention to join CPEC. This was also discussed during last year’s trilateral foreign ministers’ dialogue in Kabul. However, there has been no further progress in this regard due to the ongoing conflict between Pakistan and Afghanistan.
The Taliban government views the new road via the Wakhan Corridor as an opportunity to lessen Pakistan’s leverage. Islamabad has a history of closing the border crossings between the countries, affecting trade and inflicting heavy losses on Afghanistan’s economy. Thus, the de facto regime is jubilant with the inauguration of the Wakhan transit road. 
As per Afghanistan’s Deputy Minister for Economic Affairs’ website, “With the opening of the Wakhan Corridor, Afghanistan will be forever freed from the pressure of neighboring countries, which often exploit the Karachi route, Gwadar Port, and Chabahar for political purposes and cause heavy financial losses to our traders and compatriots every year.”
Even though the inauguration of the route is expected to alleviate the transportation challenges for the residents of Pamir and Wakhan, its role as a trans-regional route, or even just connecting Afghanistan to China, seems to be a distant dream.
Despite the Taliban regime’s completion of the road, China still has not opened its border with Afghanistan, arguably due to security concerns vis-à-vis the crossing. Moreover, China neither sent its representative to the inaugural ceremony on October 4, nor did it acknowledge the road’s completion diplomatically. 
China built the road that the Taliban’s Wakhan transit road aimed to link up with over a decade ago. The goal wasn’t to increase trade, but to secure its militarized border with Afghanistan by advancing access for its armed patrols. The Taliban refer to the transit route as a trading link to gain access to Chinese markets; Chinese media refers to this approximately 76-kilometer-long border as a “major counterterrorism front line.” This media framing aligns with Chinese officials’ narrative that Uyghurs in the region have frequently visited the corridor in order to “return to Xinjiang for Jihad.”
China’s major security concern in Afghanistan is the potential threat from the members of the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM), a group that seeks self-determination for the Uyghurs and independence of Xinjiang province from the Chinese government.
According to some estimates, there are over 3,000 Uyghurs living in Afghanistan. China has asked the Taliban to ensure that Uyghur separatists would not be allowed to use Afghan soil as a base for their activities in Xinjiang. Besides this, China wants the Taliban to extradite Uyghurs affiliated with ETIM to China.
China’s lukewarm reaction to the Taliban’s completion of the Wakhan transit route emanates mainly from its security concerns. Until the Taliban completely secure the route and convince Beijing that it will not be used as a route by ETIM members to infiltrate Xinjiang, the use of the Wakhan Corridor as a trade route between the two countries will remain a distant dream.

articles.title: The US Army Looks to the Pacific – and Space – for Future Relevance
articles.full_text:
Army leadership has focused on developing tools to contribute to a potential fight against China, a fight in which space assets will be critical.
Soldiers assigned to the 7th Infantry Division (Multi-Domain Command – Pacific) conduct unmanned aerial systems tests during exercise Bayonet Quest 2026 in Alpena, Michigan, Oct. 5, 2026.
The U.S. Army sees its future as preparing for a fight in the Pacific, and it’s taking lessons from both the current fight in the Middle East and Russia’s ongoing war with Ukraine. In addition to missiles, drones, and electronic warfare, that means an increasing presence for the land service in the space domain. The effort represents an attempt by the Army to maintain its relevance under geographical constraints that are less than ideal, and in an institutional context that increasingly favors long-range, high-end unmanned systems. 
Both the U.S. Navy and the U.S. Air Force have experienced embarrassing setbacks in the present war against Iran, the former because of an overcommitment of its aircraft carrier fleet and the latter because of the loss of several key assets in combat. Nevertheless, both services have contributed immensely to ongoing operations. The contribution of the U.S. Army has been more limited and less visible, in large part because of the reluctance of the Trump administration to develop serious plans for an invasion of Iran. 
Given the geography and the strategic issues at stake, a war in the Pacific is likely to resemble the Iran War much more than the Wars on Terror, which highlighted the Army’s strengths. Given this, Army leadership has focused on developing tools to contribute to a potential fight against China. The most recent and notable of these efforts is the stand up of a new Indo-Pacific task force, designed to conduct long-range missile combat and defeat area denial networks. The 4th Multi Domain Task Force is expected to integrate long-range strike with intelligence gathering and air defense capabilities in an effort to threaten and defeat efforts to impede the entry of the U.S. Navy and the U.S. Air Force into the Western Pacific. The 7th Infantry Division Multi-Domain Command has concentrated on developing plans for long-range drone and electronic warfare (EW) combat in the Western Pacific, assisted by AI tools that will manage data flow and the sequencing of targets. 
These efforts build upon the Army’s work to establish itself in space and to institutionalize networked warfare. Space assets act as the connective tissue for all of the elements that the Army is attempting to integrate into a cohesive whole with a standard operational logic. The steadily increasing profile of the U.S. Space Force complicates the institutional landscape by creating overlapping claims of bureaucratic authority. 
All of this is an artifact of the way that the U.S. military does business. Although the geography of the Western Pacific (like the Persian Gulf) favors air and sea power, the Army must be involved because its funding and future depend on its ability to contribute in critical sectors. That Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has made reforming the Army’s senior leadership a focus of his tenure only makes the situation more urgent for the organization. In a sense, what the Army is preparing to fight in the Western Pacific in order to preserve its ability to fight in the halls of Congress and the Pentagon. 
Arguably, the Army’s relatively low level of commitment in the Middle East may work to the Army’s advantage, as it can commit its focus and attention to fighting the next fight instead of an intractable slog against Iran. But new technological realities always require time, experience, and a careful negotiation with institutional reality. Whether Hegseth’s Army is capable of that negotiation remains open to question.
