articles.title: Saudi Arabia Executes Two Bangladeshi Nationals
articles.full_text:
Dhaka says it learned of their execution only after it happened.  Its diplomacy is under scrutiny
On October 13, Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court set aside the death sentence of Sri Lankan migrant worker Anojan Sivarasa. Sivarasa had been sentenced to death over a Facebook post deemed insulting to Prophet Muhammad and blasphemous against Islam.
The following day, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Suety Akhter (Sweety Akhtar, according to family), in the holy city of Makkah. According to their families, both had moved to Saudi Arabia for work nearly four years earlier. They had been convicted of what Saudi authorities described as an “immoral act” inside a mosque.
The two cases put Bangladesh’s protection of migrant workers in Saudi Arabia under scrutiny. Sri Lanka organized legal and diplomatic support for Sivarasa, winning a reprieve for its citizen. Bangladesh said it learned of the execution of its nationals only after it happened.
Sri Lanka’s success does not mean Bangladesh could have secured the same outcome; the allegations in the two cases were different. But the fact that Dhaka claimed not to know about the sentences until it was too late to intervene is concerning.
Saudi authorities described the death sentences of the Bangladeshis as ta’zir, a discretionary punishment, and said judicial review and a royal order preceded execution. The public statement did not explain the precise “immoral act,” identify the mosque, or disclose the arrest dates.
What evidence supported the conviction of the two Bangladeshis? Did the defendants have lawyers and interpreters? Could they understand the proceedings and challenge the charges?
Bangladesh’s claims are hard to accept without scrutiny. Media reports said the Bangladesh consulate general in Jeddah had sought prisoner information in September. Saudi authorities supplied a list containing the two names on September 30, but no details of their death sentences.
The Jeddah consulate sent a report to Bangladesh’s Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment on October 18. The Daily Star, a Bangladeshi daily, which obtained the report, says that the two Bangladeshis had been detained since August 2023. The list recorded cybercrime allegations against Nazrul and adultery allegations against Akhter.
The report also listed 306 Bangladeshis held in prisons across Saudi Arabia’s western region. Of them, 147 had received sentences ranging from one month to 15 years of jail time.
A Bangladeshi official said the consulate received no requests for assistance from the pair or their family members. Another official said following every case was impossible.
What the government said after the executions has also drawn criticism. Speaking to reporters on October 17, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam described the executions as a lesson for Bangladesh and urged citizens abroad to follow their host countries’ laws. “When a law is violated, there is not much I can do for a Bangladeshi citizen,” she said.
However, Bangladesh could still have sought lawyers’ help and engaged in diplomatic discussions to help the two citizens appeal their sentences.
Did Bangladeshi officials ask for details of the charges or copies of the court records? Were cases that involved potentially severe punishment referred for legal advice? Who was responsible for following the cases? Bangladesh needs to explain what its officials did and when. The claim that the two citizens did not ask for help does not resolve questions about its own consular response.
Sri Lanka’s response shows what Bangladesh could have done. Sivarasa was arrested on July 1. A court initially imposed five years in prison and a fine of 3 million riyals (about $800,000) on him. On September 17, an appeals court increased the punishment to death. Amnesty International said he lacked access to a lawyer before his initial sentencing.
On September 18, Sri Lanka’s Foreign Ministry publicly confirmed that it was pursuing his case through diplomatic channels. Ambassador O. L. Ameer Ajwad visited him in prison on October 8 and provided contact details. A specialist Sri Lankan legal delegation supported the Supreme Court appeal.
The court overturned Sivarasa’s death sentence. That did not guarantee that he would be acquitted or could return home. Media reports also give little detail about why the court ruled in his favor. It is unclear how much the outcome was due to the legal appeal or Sri Lanka’s diplomatic efforts.
Still, Sri Lanka provided legal support, pursued the case through diplomatic channels, and visited its citizen in prison. Bangladesh has yet to provide evidence of comparable efforts in these two cases.
Saudi Arabia also needs to explain what happened. Both countries are parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. Article 36 requires authorities to inform detained foreigners promptly of their consular rights. If a detainee requests it, the consulate must be notified without delay. Consular officers have the right to visit, communicate, and arrange legal representation.
The convention does not expressly mention a duty to warn an embassy before every execution. Therefore, the absence of an advance warning alone cannot establish that Article 36 was breached. Even so, Saudi authorities could have taken greater care to inform Bangladesh of the death sentences while there was still time to seek legal help. Saudi authorities need to explain what the prisoners were told about contacting the Bangladeshi consulate. They also need to clarify what happened to any requests for help, and if consular officials were allowed to visit.
Bangladesh has strong reasons to preserve relations with Riyadh. More than 3 million Bangladeshis live in the kingdom. Protecting such a large community requires a large consular staff and a system for following serious criminal cases. Officials need to know which prisoners face severe punishment and when legal help is needed. That work cannot depend entirely on prisoners or their families knowing whom to contact.
Sri Lanka’s efforts helped its citizen challenge his death sentence. In Bangladesh’s case, it is still unclear whether officials could have acted in time. The executions have left Bangladesh’s diplomats facing a difficult question about whether they could have done more before they were executed.
On October 13, Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court set aside the death sentence of Sri Lankan migrant worker Anojan Sivarasa. Sivarasa had been sentenced to death over a Facebook post deemed insulting to Prophet Muhammad and blasphemous against Islam.
The following day, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Suety Akhter (Sweety Akhtar, according to family), in the holy city of Makkah. According to their families, both had moved to Saudi Arabia for work nearly four years earlier. They had been convicted of what Saudi authorities described as an “immoral act” inside a mosque.
The two cases put Bangladesh’s protection of migrant workers in Saudi Arabia under scrutiny. Sri Lanka organized legal and diplomatic support for Sivarasa, winning a reprieve for its citizen. Bangladesh said it learned of the execution of its nationals only after it happened.
Sri Lanka’s success does not mean Bangladesh could have secured the same outcome; the allegations in the two cases were different. But the fact that Dhaka claimed not to know about the sentences until it was too late to intervene is concerning.
Saudi authorities described the death sentences of the Bangladeshis as ta’zir, a discretionary punishment, and said judicial review and a royal order preceded execution. The public statement did not explain the precise “immoral act,” identify the mosque, or disclose the arrest dates.
What evidence supported the conviction of the two Bangladeshis? Did the defendants have lawyers and interpreters? Could they understand the proceedings and challenge the charges?
Bangladesh’s claims are hard to accept without scrutiny. Media reports said the Bangladesh consulate general in Jeddah had sought prisoner information in September. Saudi authorities supplied a list containing the two names on September 30, but no details of their death sentences.
The Jeddah consulate sent a report to Bangladesh’s Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment on October 18. The Daily Star, a Bangladeshi daily, which obtained the report, says that the two Bangladeshis had been detained since August 2023. The list recorded cybercrime allegations against Nazrul and adultery allegations against Akhter.
articles.summary: Dhaka says it learned of their execution only after it happened.  Its diplomacy is under scrutiny

articles.title: China Capitalizes on America’s Scientific Brain Drain
articles.full_text:
For generations, the flow of global talent was almost entirely one directional. Now China is increasingly attracting top researchers from U.S. institutions.
This summer, the departure of more than a dozen established scientists from American universities to China caused a stir in the international press. They were established figures across a variety of disciplines – mainly in the sciences – from quantum computing to biochemistry to artificial intelligence. In one high-profile example, Nobel Prize winner Omar Yaghi left the University of California, Berkeley to lead an AI research institute at Tsinghua University. Several National Academy members also left U.S. universities for positions in China. Many had spent more than a decade, and in some cases several decades, building long careers in the United States.
These departures had been long in the making. Fueled by frustration with the Trump administration’s stringent immigration and national security policies in both its first and second terms, an unprecedented number of researchers say they are considering leaving the U.S.  
“Actually, I have been thinking about returning to China for the past few years, especially in the last year or two, due to some geopolitical issues and the state of Sino-U.S. relations,” Zhang Yitang told Phoenix TV in August 2025. Zhang, a renowned mathematician, joined Sun Yat-sen University in 2025 after more than a decade in the United States. “Many Chinese scholars and professors in the United States have already returned, and many others are currently considering it.”
Like Zhang, several of these departing scholars are ethnically Chinese academics who earned their initial degrees on the mainland before rising to build elite careers in the United States. 
For generations, the flow of global talent was almost entirely one-directional: “China trained the foundational talent while the United States absorbed the top tier,” explained Dai Mingjie, a scholar at South China University of Technology’s Institute of Public Policy. American institutions, which have long led the world in research funding, facilities, and influence, were highly coveted destinations for foreign talent. Researchers also had ample pathways to enter the domestic workforce after graduation through the H-1B visa, while U.S. universities offered early career researchers levels of independence that were rarely found in the more hierarchical academic systems of Europe or East Asia.
This arrangement supplied the United States with a deep well of scientific talent for over half a century. In 2021, foreign-born scholars accounted for 43 percent of the U.S. science and engineering workforce holding doctoral degrees. Chinese-origin researchers in particular showed exceptionally high stay rates: among those who earned doctorates on temporary visas at American universities, 81 percent were still in the country a decade later. 
But the current is now beginning to flow in reverse. The change began with the first Trump administration, when the Department of Justice launched the China Initiative in 2018. Though the program’s ostensible purpose was to investigate suspected spying and theft of trade secrets, it resulted in few successful espionage prosecutions – instead largely indicting academics for minor mistakes on administrative forms. Several prominent cases, including that of MIT professor Gang Chen – who was arrested in 2021 over non-disclosure of Chinese affiliations on federal grant applications before prosecutors dropped all charges a year later – drew widespread condemnation from Asian American organizations for racial profiling. “The community was concerned that the initiative was reinforcing the perpetual foreigner stereotype,” said Dr. Jeremy Wu of APA Justice.
Although the Biden administration nominally ended the China Initiative in 2022, the chilling effects on the academic community were clear to see. In a survey of U.S.-based scientists of Chinese descent, 72 percent reported feeling unsafe conducting academic research, and 61 percent indicated they had considered leaving the United States. By the advent of the second Trump administration, experienced Chinese-origin researchers were returning to China at an annual rate several times higher than they had two decades prior. 
Under the second Trump administration, the federal government has pressed forward with an aggressive “America First” agenda. Against a backdrop of escalating China-U.S. tensions, the administration has restricted visas, increased scrutiny of foreign scholars, and limited federal research funding – all meant to curb foreign influence at U.S. universities. In May 2025, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced plans to “aggressively” revoke visas held by Chinese students with ties to Chinese Communist Party (CCP) institutions, or those enrolled in technology fields with sensitive national security applications. 
One affected student was Xiaotian Liu, a computer science doctoral researcher at Dartmouth, whose status was terminated that spring. Although a federal judge restored his status after Li sued the Department of Homeland Security, the enforcement action caused widespread anxiety among international students. “Who knows if they’ll be hit by the iron fist tomorrow?” one student told Chinese media.
The anxiety has only been compounded by the uncertain state of federal research budgets. For the 2026 fiscal year, the administration proposed to cut several billion dollars across federal science agencies, including a nearly 57 percent cut to the National Science Foundation (NSF). Although Congress ultimately rejected the most severe funding reductions, the threat alone was enough to alter plans for early-career researchers. Han Fu, a biomedical doctoral applicant who spoke with Chinese media, said he started eyeing Singapore and Europe early last year. “I originally wanted to choose the United States because of its leading position in biomedical research,” said Han. “But if the broader environment is unfavorable, I have no choice but to look elsewhere.”
Meanwhile, Beijing has deliberately moved to capitalize on this mass exodus of talent. Speaking at a national science and technology conference over the summer, President Xi Jinping urged China to “seize the window of opportunity created by global talent flows and actively attract outstanding young talent and teams from overseas.” Ahead of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan – which launched this year with a heavy emphasis on technological self-reliance – the country’s annual spending on research and development reached 3.63 trillion yuan, or approximately 2.7 percent of GDP in 2024. Beijing also offers incoming researchers generous perks, including startup capital, housing subsidies, and up to 800,000 yuan directly in research grants for eligible scholars. 
Such incentives have been frequently cited by returning academics as a decisive factor in their relocation. Jiaming Chen, a former Duke University professor who spent over three decades working in the United States, told China Science Daily: “In recent years, the overall research environment in China has changed enormously… investment in science and technology has increased substantially, and research conditions are comparable to those of world-leading institutions.”
Chinese universities are also trying to tackle their notorious reputation for neijuan – the hypercompetitive culture of “involution” that has long plagued mainland academia. In August 2023, the State Council and the Central Committee issued a joint directive seeking to alleviate burdens on early-career faculty by curbing administrative tasks and mitigating the pressure to “publish or perish.” The directive mandates that early-career scientists spend over 80 percent of their working time directly engaged in active research. 
Several new research institutes are implementing these operational changes to a seemingly positive effect. Neuroscientist Dan Yang, who left UC Berkeley in 2025 to join the Shenzhen Medical Academy of Research and Translation, highlighted its “research-without-worries” model designed to minimize administrative overhead and grant application burdens. As Yang told China Science Daily: “I can now confidently devote all my energy to research.”
For others, the attraction of China lies less in government subsidies than in the chance to apply their work more quickly to its large and rapidly-expanding industrial base. “The rapid development of China’s biomedical industry allows me to translate my research results into clinical applications more quickly, benefiting more people,” said Ma Shixin, an immunologist who joined the Shenzhen Medical Academy of Research and Translation last year. “This was the most important reason that prompted me to choose to return to China.”
Whatever their individual motivations, the influx of returning scholars has made a significant impact on Chinese scientific output, as researchers bring back the expertise and connections they established during their time in the United States. In 2023, China surpassed the United States for the first time on the Nature Index, which tracks contributions to papers in a set of leading natural science journals.
A study analyzing scientific publications estimated that returnees contributed to 38 percent of China-addressed papers, while Chinese diaspora scholars accounted for 27 percent of U.S.-addressed papers. Papers involving either group also received more citations on average than other papers from their respective countries, a sign of the lasting value of those international networks. 
All this jockeying for talent sits within a larger great power competition over who will control crucial technologies ahead. Washington seeks to preserve its edge in the race, while restricting Beijing’s access to advanced technologies such as high-end semiconductors crucial for training frontier AI models. Beijing, for its part, aims to achieve breakthroughs that bypass foreign chokepoints and close the gap in key industries. Both powers are also keeping an eye on the future, seeking to gain early ground in frontier fields like quantum computing.
China and the United States are fishing in the same pool of talent, particularly in fields both countries see as top priorities, like AI research. A report from the Carnegie Endowment found that 57 percent of elite AI researchers in its 2025 sample earned their undergraduate degrees in China. The United States is ultimately still a net importer of this talent, while China still suffers a net loss. But the U.S. edge depends heavily on its ability to keep drawing foreign-trained talent – a questionable assumption as more researchers decide to stay in their home countries or leave the U.S., driven in no small part by tighter immigration rules.
For the United States, the long-term cost of this slow attrition could prove much harder to reverse than the departure of any single star researcher. Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, explained: “If fewer top Chinese students come to the U.S. for Ph.D.s, fewer stay for postdocs, and faculty become less funded… then the U.S. loses not just top talents today, but a large part of the mechanism through which it has historically replenished its scientific pipeline.” As key research hubs once concentrated in the United States are dispersed globally, foreign institutions gain greater influence over the trajectory of global science, threatening the dominant position U.S. universities have long held in shaping future research frontiers.
But for many, nativism will always be the enemy of scientific progress. In an interview with Chinese media, Director of Carnegie China Ma Yang warned against politicizing scientific research. “So far, humanity has not found a better way to continuously generate breakthrough innovation than bringing together large numbers of talented people from different backgrounds and allowing them to openly exchange different ideas,” Ma said.
He added: “If the movement of people were to stop completely, both countries would suffer enormous negative consequences.”

articles.title: Rubio Gets a Medal. Russia Gets Military Drills. Karakalpakstan Gets Silence.
articles.full_text:
Washington celebrates closer ties as Tashkent strengthens its Russian alliance—and offers no announced relief for Karakalpak political prisoners.
On October 19, Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev awarded U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio the Order of Outstanding Merit. On October 20, UzDaily reported the arrival of Russian troops for joint military exercises in Uzbekistan. For Karakalpak families awaiting the release of political prisoners, neither announcement offered relief. Uzbekistan celebrated American investment and welcomed Russian soldiers while making no publicly announced commitment to people imprisoned for exercising and defending their rights.
Mirziyoyev’s office announced $12 billion in agreements, while Rubio participated in the C5+1 ministerial meeting and witnessed Uzbekistan’s signing of the Artemis Accords on peaceful space exploration. Sustained American engagement with Central Asia serves legitimate interests, and investment can create opportunities across the region. But announced agreements must still become functioning projects. 
The more immediate political benefit went to Mirziyoyev, who received the public appreciation of America’s top diplomat. Rubio wrote that he was “deeply honored to be awarded the Order of Outstanding Merit by President Mirziyoyev” on X. The public results of the visit offered no hint of discussion on Karakalpak prisoners or accountability for the July 2022 massacre in Karakalpakstan.
The Russian exercises make it harder to mistake American access for a strategic shift in Tashkent. According to UzDaily, citing Russia’s Central Military District, servicemen from the 201st Guards Military Base – a Russian base in Tajikistan – arrived for Hamkorlik-2026, scheduled for October 20-27 in Uzbekistan. The report described the participation of assault units, reconnaissance and strike drones, robotic systems, and Mi-24 helicopters. These drills need not have been organized as a message to Washington to illustrate Tashkent’s position. Uzbekistan could welcome an American secretary of state and Russian military personnel in the same week without treating either relationship as a concession to the other.
Mirziyoyev had already explained that position in his own words. During an October 7 birthday call with Putin, he praised the Russian president’s “historic role” in modern Russia and his contribution to their countries’ “comprehensive strategic partnership and alliance.” That same day, he received a delegation led by Denis Manturov to advance cooperation in industry, energy, metallurgy, nuclear energy, and industrial zones. Earlier, Putin had authorized negotiations to amend military-technical agreements with Uzbekistan. RFE/RL reported in August that the proposed changes remained undisclosed. 
Uzbekistan has been equally adept at cultivating other partners. Mirziyoyev signed the charter of President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace in January. His Interior Ministry has described cooperation with Huawei, including plans for “intelligent video surveillance.” In September, an institute under the Agriculture Ministry announced a memorandum with Iran’s Sirang UAV covering agricultural drone training and service centers. That agreement concerns agricultural applications and does not establish military cooperation or imply sanctions evasion, but it does illustrate a developing relationship. Washington should judge its own successes by the commitments it obtains, rather than assume that a warm reception will translate into influence.
The commercial relationship requires the same scrutiny. In April, the EU imposed sanctions on Uzbek companies over their Russia links, citing cotton-cellulose supplies to Russian gunpowder manufacturers. Those findings give U.S. officials concrete reasons to insist on rigorous screening of counterparties, beneficial ownership, and supply chains before promoting investment. Uzbekistan’s political system presents additional concerns: Freedom House rates it “Not Free,” with a score of 12 out of 100, while the Human Rights Foundation classifies it as a fully authoritarian regime. Freedom House reports that no opposition parties operate legally and that the legislature and judiciary effectively serve the executive.
American investors have encountered the consequences of weak institutional protections before. In 2006, Newmont disclosed approximately $48 million in tax claims against its Uzbek joint venture despite written confirmation from Uzbekistan’s Justice Ministry that a relevant tax decree applied for the venture’s lifetime. Access to the venture’s bank accounts was restricted, its assets placed under legal restraint, and bankruptcy proceedings initiated. A 2007 settlement provided for $80 million in payments and the transfer of Newmont’s interest to Uzbek parties, without an admission of liability. These events occurred when Shavkat Mirziyoyev was Uzbekistan’s prime minister.
The OECD’s 2025 investment review identifies continuing concerns about executive influence over courts, inconsistent decisions in technically complex cases, and overlapping rules that undermine predictability. Investors therefore have reason to ask whether commitments will survive a change of leadership, a reshuffle of influential officials, or a dispute involving politically connected interests. Official assurances offer limited protection unless institutions can enforce them.
The U.S. also has a strategic lesson to remember. After the May 2005 Andijan crackdown, the United States supported calls for an independent international investigation. That July, Uzbekistan ordered American forces out of the Karshi-Khanabad airbase, which supported operations in Afghanistan. Years of security cooperation failed to preserve American access once accountability became a source of bilateral tension. If Washington now avoids difficult questions to protect its agreements, Tashkent again holds considerable leverage over the relationship.
For Karakalpak people, those questions are urgent. Dauletmurat Tajimuratov, a Karakalpak lawyer and journalist, received a 16-year sentence after opposing proposed constitutional changes affecting the Sovereign Republic of Karakalpakstan’s status. The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found his imprisonment arbitrary and called for his immediate release. Another two and a half years were added to his sentence this year. Before Rubio’s visit,  Kaitie Holland and Sergei Korotkov, both international legal associates at the Human Rights Foundation, urged him in an article published by Just Security to demand freedom for Uzbekistan’s political prisoners, detailing Tajimuratov’s reported beatings, degrading prison conditions, and attempts to force him to renounce his Karakalpak identity.
In June, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer reaffirmed strong support for Uzbekistan’s World Trade Organization (WTO) accession. Further discretionary benefits should accompany published commitments on prisoner protection, accountability, and predictable legal treatment. Washington should press for Tajimuratov’s release, independent medical and monitoring access pending release, and an independent international investigation into the 2022 massacre. Independent courts and limits on executive interference would also protect the American businesses the administration is encouraging to invest.
Tashkent played its hand well. Mirziyoyev secured American recognition and commercial support while strengthening ties with Russia and maintaining an iron grip at home. Rubio must now explain what Washington obtained in return. Until commercial promises become enforceable commitments and American influence helps secure freedom for political prisoners, the medal around Rubio’s neck offers clearer evidence of Mirziyoyev’s diplomatic success than America’s.

articles.title: Weapons to Russia, Wigs to China: How North Korea Balances Its Allies
articles.full_text:
A clear division of labor ensures North Korea’s alliances with Russia and China are complementary, not competitive with each other.
North Korea’s balancing act is back in the spotlight. In September, it opened its first road bridge with Russia. Just last week, North Korea opened a similar one with China. Pyongyang’s land bridge with Russia will strengthen the bilateral arms trade while the one with China will provide it with energy products, raw materials, and heavy equipment for domestic consumption. 
The two bridges are a microcosm of how North Korea seeks to benefit from improved relations with Moscow and Beijing. North Korea is looking for military assistance from Russia and economic help from China. The clear division of labor ensures North Korea’s alliances with Russia and China are complementary, not competitive with each other.
North Korea has decades of experience when it comes to managing relations with Moscow and Beijing for its own benefits. In July 1961, the country signed two separate alliance treaties with the Soviet Union and China by exploiting the Sino-Soviet Split. The more bitter Moscow and Beijing were toward each other, the more willing they were to meet Pyongyang’s demands. 
The combined Soviet and Chinese economic aid meant North Korea enjoyed a relatively higher living standard compared to its communist peers China and North Vietnam in the 1960s and 1970s. Its military was also on par with that of South Korea thanks to generous Soviet and Chinese transfers of weapons and technologies. 
However, North Korea’s balancing act failed when the Soviet Union encountered economic trouble and began to amend ties with China in 1986. Moscow was no longer interested in competing with China for influence over North Korea and began to cut back economic and military aid. China in turn reduced the amount of military and economic support due to Soviet retrenchment. 
Without a split to leverage, Pyongyang could not demand that Moscow and Beijing maintain a generous level of aid. North Korea went bankrupt in the 1990s, and its military slipped behind South Korea’s.
North Korea has now crafted a new playbook on how to get Russia and China to support Pyongyang’s goals – even in the absence of a split. In the past, North Korea handled Moscow and Beijing by having them compete over both military and economic aid. Now, North Korea balances between its two patrons by assigning them a separate domain of cooperation suitable to their specific needs. 
North Korea’s outreach to Russia revolves around military exchanges to get Moscow to assist in the development of its weapons of mass destruction program. North Korea leverages Russia’s need for weapons, troops, and ammunition for the war against Ukraine in exchange for Russia’s military technology. In return, Russia has been vocal about its support for North Korea’s nuclear program and even pledged to defend Pyongyang under the 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty. 
North Korea-Russia arms trade nearly doubled from 2023 to 2025, growing from $7.7 billion to $14.4 billion. This amount overshadows the food and fuel trade, which reached a record high of $34 million in 2024. North Korean laborers in Russia work in drone factories or in warzones along the Russia-Ukraine border. Pyongyang is also stressing its blood sacrifice for Russia’s war to remind Moscow of its military debt. 
North Korea’s outreach to China takes on a completely different tone. Pyongyang emphasizes economic cooperation with China because it understands Beijing desires political and economic stability on the Korean Peninsula. In 2026, bilateral trade increased to $1.5 billion, up 19.6 percent compared to the first half of 2025. This marks a record high since China imposed sanctions on North Korea for its nuclear test in 2017. Noticeably, weapons made up little of the trade rebound. Unlike their peers in Russia, North Korean laborers in China mostly work in the food service and textile industry.
When Chinese President Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June, he and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un agreed to bolster ties in politics, economy, and culture. The military aspect of the Kim-Xi summit was largely absent from public view although the visit corresponded with the 65th anniversary of the signing of the 1961 Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance. Unlike Russia and North Korea, China and North Korea didn’t publicly praise the mutual defense clause in the treaty. However, Pyongyang got Beijing to quietly drop “denuclearization” in its North Korea policy and to stop enforcing international sanctions. 
Russia and China have been comfortable with North Korea’s division of labor. Neither Moscow nor Beijing sees each other’s expanding cooperation with North Korea as a threat. China accepts Pyongyang sending troops to Russia’s war in Ukraine so long as North Korea’s participation doesn’t undermine China’s desire for stability in Northeast Asia. China even harbored a Russian ship involved in the North Korea-Russia arms trade, which had to be conducted by  air and sea  routes before the new land bridge was opened. 
For its part, although Russia’s 2024 alliance treaty with North Korea mirrors the 1961 treaty, Moscow doesn’t treat it as a rival to China’s 1961 alliance treaty. Russia even supports trilateral dialogue with China and North Korea over Chinese vessels’ use of the Tumen River for access to the Sea of Japan. Russia’s support for North Korea’s nuclear and conventional forces modernization doesn’t come at China’s expense as North Korea doesn’t plan on invading South Korea anytime soon. 
From North Korea’s perspective, selling weapons to Russia and wigs to China means its alliances with both are complimentary instead of competitive. Pyongyang can secure long-term support from Russia and China not through their spite toward each other but through their genuine interest in fostering a stable ally in the Asia-Pacific. 
Thanks to Russian and Chinese backing, North Korea’s economy is booming and its military is undergoing the most comprehensive modernization program since 1991. Russia’s and China’s support also gives North Korea stronger diplomatic leverage in case it decides to restart dialogue with the United States. Importantly, North Korea doesn’t base its foreign policy on the state of Beijing-Moscow relations like it did during the Cold War. If either Russia or China loses interest in bolstering North Korea’s economy and military at some point in the future, the other patron will not reduce aid just because it has “won” the competition.
North Korea’s balancing act is back in the spotlight. In September, it opened its first road bridge with Russia. Just last week, North Korea opened a similar one with China. Pyongyang’s land bridge with Russia will strengthen the bilateral arms trade while the one with China will provide it with energy products, raw materials, and heavy equipment for domestic consumption. 
The two bridges are a microcosm of how North Korea seeks to benefit from improved relations with Moscow and Beijing. North Korea is looking for military assistance from Russia and economic help from China. The clear division of labor ensures North Korea’s alliances with Russia and China are complementary, not competitive with each other.
North Korea has decades of experience when it comes to managing relations with Moscow and Beijing for its own benefits. In July 1961, the country signed two separate alliance treaties with the Soviet Union and China by exploiting the Sino-Soviet Split. The more bitter Moscow and Beijing were toward each other, the more willing they were to meet Pyongyang’s demands. 
The combined Soviet and Chinese economic aid meant North Korea enjoyed a relatively higher living standard compared to its communist peers China and North Vietnam in the 1960s and 1970s. Its military was also on par with that of South Korea thanks to generous Soviet and Chinese transfers of weapons and technologies. 
However, North Korea’s balancing act failed when the Soviet Union encountered economic trouble and began to amend ties with China in 1986. Moscow was no longer interested in competing with China for influence over North Korea and began to cut back economic and military aid. China in turn reduced the amount of military and economic support due to Soviet retrenchment. 
Without a split to leverage, Pyongyang could not demand that Moscow and Beijing maintain a generous level of aid. North Korea went bankrupt in the 1990s, and its military slipped behind South Korea’s.
North Korea has now crafted a new playbook on how to get Russia and China to support Pyongyang’s goals – even in the absence of a split. In the past, North Korea handled Moscow and Beijing by having them compete over both military and economic aid. Now, North Korea balances between its two patrons by assigning them a separate domain of cooperation suitable to their specific needs.

North Korea leverages Russia’s need for weapons, troops, and ammunition for the war against Ukraine in exchange for Russia’s military technology. In return, Russia has been vocal about its support for North Korea’s nuclear program and even pledged to defend Pyongyang under the 2024 Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty. 
North Korea-Russia arms trade nearly doubled from 2023 to 2025, growing from $7.7 billion to $14.4 billion. This amount overshadows the food and fuel trade, which reached a record high of $34 million in 2024. Pyongyang is also stressing its blood sacrifice for Russia’s war to remind Moscow of its military debt.

articles.title: Bougainville Needs a Credible Timetable for PNG’s Independence Vote. Australia Can Help.
articles.full_text:
Canberra should stay out of what Port Moresby decides on Bougainville, but it can push for a concrete timeline for the decision.
PNG Prime Minister James Marape (right) and Bougainville’s President Ishmael Toroama hold up the Melanesian Agreement, which recognized the legitimacy of the 2019 independence referendum, June 26, 2025.
In September, Kokoda constituency in Bougainville declared itself “independence ready.” At the ceremony, Ishmael Toroama, president of the Autonomous Bougainville Government, pledged funding for a hospital and a police station. 
Similar ceremonies are being held across Bougainville, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG). Each carries the same message: the long road from civil war to self-determination is nearing its end.
97.7 percent of Bougainvilleans voted in favor of independence in 2019, but that referendum was not binding. PNG’s parliament has the final say, and seven years later, the wait for a parliamentary decision continues. 
This year, Prime Minister James Marape had proposed holding a vote on August 30. Parliament formally received the result on August 27, then adjourned without voting. 
Now Peter Tsiamalili Jr, Bougainville’s regional MP and the leader of government business, has announced a two-day debate for October 20-21. That is progress. But it remains unclear whether the sitting will end in a vote, or what will follow if parliament adjourns without one.
Australia has been careful on the issue of Bougainville, with good reason. In 2022, Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said Canberra’s job was to “support Papua New Guinea.” Bougainville’s leadership took that as a retreat from neutrality, and Canberra had to clarify that it would support whatever the two sides agreed. 
Australia is right to keep its distance on what parliament decides, but it can – and should – help nudge PNG to make a decision. 
The 2001 Bougainville peace agreement required a referendum within 10 to 15 years after the election of Bougainville’s first autonomous government. The agreement also gave PNG’s parliament authority to make the final decision on independence – but did not set a deadline for parliamentary action. 
The 2022 Era Kone Covenant set 2027 as the outer limit for implementing independence or another settlement, but again it failed to fix a date for parliament to vote. The covenant’s one interim deadline – tabling the result in parliament by the end of 2023 – was missed by almost three years.
The lack of a deadline lets Port Moresby postpone a politically difficult decision; meanwhile Bougainville’s leaders must keep persuading supporters to accept the wait. Many who sustained the peace are former combatants who staked their credibility on the promise that politics would produce an answer. Toroama himself was once a rebel commander. He now warns that trust is under strain even as he urges Bougainvilleans to stay patient. Each postponement makes that appeal harder to sustain. 
The approaching PNG election compounds the problem. Under the provisional timetable, voting will be held from June 26 to July 9 of next year. If PNG’s parliament does not vote before the election, the decision will pass to a new parliament, which may first need to decide how much of its predecessor’s groundwork it accepts. Bougainville’s leaders have set September 1, 2027, as the “firm timetable” for a further stage of self-government. At that point, the new PNG parliament would be barely a month old. 
Without an agreed timetable, Bougainville and PNG are heading back toward potential conflict. “Trust is the foundation of every agreement. Where agreed processes have been departed from, concerns have naturally arisen,” Toroama said while announcing his timetable in June. He added that “recent events violating these existing understandings cannot be ignored or downplayed,” even as he urged the people of Bougainville to “remain patient.”
Australia has a stake in avoiding a new rift between PNG’s central government and Bougainville. Canberra witnessed the 2001 agreement and led the Peace Monitoring Group that helped hold the ceasefire. Under the Pukpuk Treaty that entered into force in July, Australia and the PNG are formal allies, with an obligation to consult on threats to either country’s sovereignty, peace, or stability. 
If Bougainville moves on its own timetable in 2027 and Port Moresby treats that as a challenge to its sovereignty, Canberra might be asked to consult as an ally on the dispute. It’s better for Australia to press for a credible timetable now than be forced to take sides later.
Port Moresby may resent even that level of Australian involvement. Marape’s government frames the referendum as a matter for PNG’s constitutional process, and an ally’s question about parliamentary scheduling can easily be heard as pressure on parliament. 
But in asking for a concrete deadline, Canberra would merely be aligning itself with voices from within the PNG. When the result was tabled in August, opposition leader James Nomane told parliament the government should “not kick the can down the road” and pressed it to say when MPs would vote. The PNG and Bougainville have already agreed that Marape and Toroama will jointly determine the date. Canberra would simply be holding them to their word.
A hurried vote under contested procedures could deepen mistrust. In June, parliament set the bar for ratification at a three-quarters majority: 89 of 118 members. Bougainville’s leaders dispute the threshold and how the rule was adopted. However, leaving the vote date open-ended risks pushing the issue past the election – and conflicting with Toroama’s timetable. 
That is where Canberra can help. Its role is not to shape the outcome, but to help ensure the process does not drag on indefinitely. Through existing ministerial talks, it should seek a date for the vote and a timetable for addressing the disputed voting rules. A deadline alone is not enough; the covenant had one. What matters is what happens if the next deadline is missed. Both governments should then say publicly why it slipped, who must act next, and when parliament will return to the issue. 
If a pre-election vote proves impossible, a joint record of what has been agreed, what remains contested, and when talks resume would at least protect the handover to the next parliament. Australia, already a backer of the transfer of powers, could help maintain that record with both sides’ consent.
Kokoda says it is ready for independence. If Bougainvilleans are asked to keep waiting for parliament to act, their governments owe them a clear account of what comes next.
In September, Kokoda constituency in Bougainville declared itself “independence ready.” At the ceremony, Ishmael Toroama, president of the Autonomous Bougainville Government, pledged funding for a hospital and a police station.

articles.title: Taiwan’s Tech Diplomacy Has a Labor Problem
articles.full_text:
Migrant worker recruitment debt threatens the island’s access to Western markets and its ties with Southeast Asia.
Foreign migrant workers often gather in the square in front of Taipei Station during their day off. Photo taken Sep. 24, 2023.
In an investigation published this October, three migrant workers at a Garmin factory in Taiwan said recruiters had forced them to sign documents falsely denying the mandatory fees they had paid to get jobs. Two reported that the recruiters threatened to retaliate and deport them if they disclosed the charges. These workers were making products for a U.S.-based electronics company.
The nonprofit Transparentem interviewed 24 workers at seven manufacturers operating in Taiwan and documented recruitment fees totaling $6,400 each. Compal, the laptop maker, and Garmin claimed they had long prohibited worker-paid fees. But they only reimbursed current migrant workers after investigators contacted them, and excluded former workers from compensation. Despite corporate promises, these exploitative charges continued.
These findings expose a blind spot in Taiwan’s economic diplomacy. Taipei and Washington should stop treating their technology partnership and Taiwan’s Southeast Asian labor relationships separately. Recruitment abuse threatens Taiwan’s Western market access and regional goodwill. Fair recruitment is just as integral to supply chain security as factory investment.
A framework for reform already exists. The February 2026 Taiwan-U.S. trade agreement compels Taiwan to prohibit worker-paid recruitment fees and related costs in manufacturing and fishing within three years of entry into force. Yet on October 6, Premier Cho Jung-tai said unresolved U.S. trade measures were delaying ratification in Taiwan’s legislature. Tariff negotiations cannot excuse delaying recruitment reform.
Taiwan’s Labor Ministry counted more than 910,000 migrant workers at the end of August, including approximately 100,000 lacking valid work permits. Among permit holders, 515,000 worked in manufacturing, with 127,000 of those in the electronics industry. These numbers reveal just how critical migrant labor is to Taiwan’s technology sector.
Rather than stopping at a recruitment fee, the brokerage system often continually exploits workers. Agencies abroad initially charge workers to secure jobs in Taiwan, and Taiwanese brokers then skim recurring service fees off worker bank accounts that they control. Taiwan also restricts migrant workers from changing employment, requiring extensive paperwork and official authorization. Debt and restricted mobility thus reinforce each other.
My fieldwork has revealed what is at stake. In May 2024, I interviewed a Filipino worker at a Hsinchu semiconductor supplier. The worker described 12-hour night shifts, six days a week, and a broker who deducted fees from her wages. Only Catholic missionaries and more experienced migrants offered the worker reliable support.
While debt alone does not establish forced labor, the International Labor Organization (ILO) recognizes debt bondage as an indicator of it. For a worker still repaying heavy recruitment fee loans, the cost of reporting abuse could be exceptionally high. Losing their job could not only force them to default on the loan that secured it, but also threaten their family’s very livelihood. Such fear of whistleblowing also makes buyers and regulators less aware of actual factory conditions.
The commercial consequences are stark. In September 2025, U.S. Customs and Border Protection detained imported Giant bicycles and related products manufactured in Taiwan over forced labor concerns. Giant subsequently expanded recruitment fee reimbursements. By September 2026, companies comprising over 80 percent of Taiwan’s bicycle exports had joined an industry human rights initiative. Customer access restrictions accelerated reform.
Electronics manufacturers should take notice. The European Union will automatically block products made with forced labor by December 2027. Exporters will soon face significant overseas scrutiny and potential import bans. Continued broker charges could then lead to shipment delays and loss of customer trust. Taiwanese electronics firms cannot continue offloading their due diligence responsibilities.
The diplomatic stakes are just as important. Launched in 2016, Taiwan’s New Southbound Policy promised a “people-centered” partnership with its Southeast Asian neighbors through trade, education, and closer social ties. The Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, and Thailand are key partners in that initiative; they are also the home countries of virtually all migrant workers in Taiwan. With the world’s lowest birth rate, Taiwan’s reliance on Southeast Asian workers will only grow. Since Taiwan has no formal diplomatic relations with any of these countries, properly treating their migrant workers is especially important.
Taiwan’s electronics sector would particularly benefit from improved ASEAN-Taiwan relations. Filipinos account for nearly 83 percent of migrant permit holders across electronic components and computer, electronics, and optical manufacturing. Properly treating Taiwan’s Filipino workers is thus integral to sustaining the U.S.-Taiwan technology relationship. 
Recruitment costs have already generated bilateral friction. In 2020, Taiwan’s Labor Ministry rejected Indonesia’s demand that employers cover recruitment expenses and said it would consider recruiting elsewhere. In February 2026, the Philippines’ envoy in Taipei suggested Taiwanese authorities crack down on exploitative brokers and encouraged direct hiring. These governments want Taiwan to treat their citizens better.
While worker exploitation may not determine an ASEAN government’s policy toward Taipei, it can definitely sabotage Taiwan’s New Southbound Policy. Taiwan cannot credibly offer a people-centered partnership with ASEAN countries while exploiting their citizens’ labor. Protecting these almost 1 million migrant workers would thus strengthen the New Southbound Policy much more than limited business delegations or university exchanges.
Labor reform stalls partly because its beneficiaries lack political influence. Migrant workers diffusely spread all over Taiwan cannot vote, while concentrated employers and brokers can organize to defend their interests. A petition against employer-paid recruitment drew 5,929 endorsements. The Labor Ministry rejected demands to halt the planned ban, but such opposition reveals why external pressure is so helpful for reforming Taiwan’s migrant labor system. When access to export markets requires reform, employers are more incentivized to remedy an exploitative recruitment model they previously embraced.
Not all hope for internal reform is lost. Just on October 2, Labor Minister Hung Sun-han described preparations to end certain overseas recruitment charges from the end of 2026 into 2027.  The challenge is turning those promises into actually enforceable protections.
Opponents rightly point out that recruitment costs money. Someone must screen applicants, process visas, arrange travel, translate contracts, and resolve disputes. Small factories cannot operate their own overseas recruiting offices. So banning worker-paid fees alone would simply push them underground. Policymakers must more narrowly focus on freeing workers from broader recruitment burdens.
However, there are successful examples of alternative models. On September 14, Taiwan welcomed 35 Indonesian hotel workers into its first foreign skilled hospitality worker program. Indonesia’s representative to Taipei celebrated the program, stressing that employers paid all associated recruitment expenses. Fairer hiring thus directly contributes to more diplomatic goodwill toward Taiwan.
Taiwan should align with ILO principles in having employers cover all recruitment and related costs throughout the hiring chain, including payments abroad. Beyond simply promising reimbursement, Taiwan should ensure that these workers do not have to advance the money. Otherwise, workers may still have to borrow money and wait for a nebulous reimbursement. 
Taiwan should also block brokers from leveraging wage deductions to evade recruitment fee bans. Workers who document prohibited payments should receive restitution from their employer, which should be obligated to sanction the responsible recruiter.
But Taiwan cannot wait for its ASEAN partners to crack down on local agency fees. Taiwan should provide temporary transition funding to smaller suppliers, along with separate financial aid for low-income families to hire migrant household caregivers. These measures would help relieve immediate employer cost concerns.
In addition, Taiwan should make direct hiring more compelling. Taiwan’s Direct Hiring Service Center already assists firms with worker selection, applications, and multilingual services. But for employers to actually use these services, direct hiring must be as fast and reliable as their brokerage competitors. Alongside improving direct hiring services, Taiwan’s Labor Ministry should more regularly audit private brokers.
Taipei should engage the Philippines, Vietnam, Indonesia, and Thailand on fee ban enforcement. Taiwan could strengthen these critical ASEAN relationships through shared fee disclosures, joint recruiter investigations, and more accessible reporting channels. Migrant workers and their advocates should help shape enforcement measures. Those running Taiwan’s industries should also have a stake in their governance.
Finally, workers in Taiwan must be able to leave. Workers should be allowed to change employers if faced with coercion, wage theft, or unsafe conditions. Labor Ministry investigators should confidentially interview these reporters outside their workplaces and in their own languages. Additionally, Taiwan should work toward making work permits transferable within certain sectors. Otherwise, migrant workers would be perpetually vulnerable to potential employer coercion.
Washington should backstop these changes. U.S. officials could monitor fees repaid and mandate anti-retaliation requirements into subsequent trade agreements. Furthermore, U.S. buyers should bake fair recruitment conditions into Taiwanese supplier contracts and help shoulder remediation costs.
Congress and the administration should also mandate that new semiconductor subsidy recipients and their suppliers fairly recruit. Juggernauts like TSMC could thus pressure their vendors to improve migrant labor conditions. After all, federal procurement contracts already include an anti-trafficking clause that prohibits contractors and subcontractors from charging recruitment fees. Incremental funding releases should reward worker repayment and compliance while punishing continued violations. Domestic grants, tax incentives, and purchases could thus further the Taiwan-U.S. trade agreement’s labor provisions.
Some may argue that protecting Taiwan from China is more important than strengthening Taiwan’s labor laws. But detaining Taiwanese exports and alienating Taiwan’s essential migrant workforce weaken the island’s industrial base. Taipei is better off preemptively strengthening its own labor laws than letting customs officials and overseas customers set them.
Still, U.S. customers should avoid broadly abandoning Taiwanese suppliers, which may leave more workers jobless and indebted. Instead, buyers should encourage worker repayment while selectively punishing companies that conceal abuse.
articles.summary: Migrant worker recruitment debt threatens the island’s access to Western markets and its ties with Southeast Asia.

articles.title: North Korea Wants Security Talks With the US, Not Nuclear Talks
articles.full_text:
For decades, Washington tried to change Pyongyang’s nuclear policy. Now North Korea is trying to do the reverse: use its nuclear weapons to change U.S. policy.
In this Feb. 27, 2019, file photo, U.S. President Donald Trump shakes hands with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at the Sofitel Legend Metropole hotel in Hanoi, Vietnam, for their second summit meeting.
Since the start of his second administration, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly proposed renewed talks with North Korea. Pyongyang has said that relations could improve if Washington respected its nuclear status and abandoned what it calls its “hostile policy.” But what would North Korea be willing to talk about if discussions resumed? 
Pyongyang increasingly seeks talks on its security concerns, particularly U.S. military policy and the regional security environment, while treating its own possession of nuclear weapons as non-negotiable. It may even demand a halt to U.S. military exercises with its allies as a precondition for talks.
The failure of the 2019 North Korea-Trump summit in Hanoi may have prompted Pyongyang to reassess its negotiating strategy and strengthen its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons. At the summit, North Korea sought partial relief from United Nations sanctions in exchange for dismantling its Yongbyon nuclear facilities. Washington, however, sought denuclearization measures extending beyond Yongbyon in exchange for a broader package of economic benefits. The summit ended without an agreement. 
Why did North Korea not accept Washington’s “big deal”? Shortly after the summit collapsed, North Korean Foreign Minister Ri Yong Ho explained that security guarantees mattered more to Pyongyang than sanctions relief. North Korea had nevertheless proposed partial sanctions relief in return for dismantling Yongbyon because it believed Washington would find it difficult to take military measures at the time.
North Korea may have recognized the limits of what the United States could offer in terms of security guarantees. U.S. military strategy in Northeast Asia is not solely a response to the North Korean threat. It also reflects Washington’s alliance commitments to South Korea and Japan and its broader strategic competition with China. Even if North Korea gave up all its nuclear weapons, Washington might not be able to offer the security guarantees Pyongyang wants, given its regional interests and alliance commitments. From this perspective, North Korea’s attempt in Hanoi to exchange partial denuclearization for partial sanctions relief may have been a realistic approach. The failure in Hanoi appears to have convinced Pyongyang that giving up its nuclear weapons would not secure the guarantees it sought. After Hanoi, North Korea reinforced its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons through legislation and constitutional changes. In September 2022, it adopted a new law on nuclear forces policy. Kim Jong Un declared that North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state was irreversible and ruled out further negotiations on giving up its nuclear weapons or on denuclearization.
North Korea did not begin identifying itself as a nuclear weapon state in 2022. It had already codified that status in a 2013 law “consolidating the position of nuclear weapons state for self-defense.” Article 9 of that law, however, expressed support for international nuclear disarmament efforts. The omission of that provision from the 2022 law was therefore significant. 
The 2022 law not only entrenched nuclear possession as a permanent foundation of national strategy but also called for qualitative and quantitative improvements in nuclear forces in response to external threats and changes in the international nuclear balance. In this context, a freeze on nuclear weapons production or a reduction in its nuclear arsenal could conflict with this policy if North Korea’s security environment remained unchanged.
North Korea’s recent statements on relations with Washington indicate that it expects changes in U.S. policy before talks resume, while treating its nuclear possession as non-negotiable.
In October 2025, Trump publicly expressed his desire to meet Kim Jong Un again during his trip to Asia. That didn’t eventuate, but Trump is reportedly looking at the possibility of a meeting with Kim during his next trip to Asia in November 2026.
At the Ninth Workers’ Party Congress in February 2026, Kim Jong Un stated that relations with the United States could improve if Washington respected North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state and abandoned its hostile policy. He thus linked improved relations to a change in Washington’s attitude toward a nuclear-armed North Korea and its policy toward Pyongyang.
In August, Trump again expressed interest in meeting Kim and ordered a reduction in South Korea-U.S. military exercises. Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s sister and an authoritative voice for the regime, dismissed the move as insufficient. She argued that holding the exercises at all demonstrated Washington’s hostility. Kim Yo Jong’s response suggested that Pyongyang wanted the exercises halted altogether, rather than merely scaled back, before agreeing to talks. In the same statement, she also criticized South Korea’s push to acquire nuclear-powered submarines.
In September, Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui reaffirmed that North Korea’s nuclear status was irreversible. She rejected the coexistence of confrontation and dialogue in relations with North Korea and argued that a geopolitical realignment centered on a nuclear-armed North Korea was inevitable. Her statement reinforced the message that Washington could not maintain policies Pyongyang regarded as hostile and expect dialogue to follow.
North Korea has long sought security guarantees and an end to Washington’s hostile policy. The difference now is that Pyongyang treats its nuclear possession as non-negotiable and expects changes in U.S. attitudes and military policy before talks resume. A reduction in South Korea-U.S. military exercises alone appears insufficient to meet its demands. Its criticism of South Korea’s nuclear-powered submarine plans also suggests concern about potential U.S. support for such capabilities. 
This departs from the Singapore agreement, which paired a commitment to denuclearization with improved relations and the establishment of a peace regime. Pyongyang now seeks U.S. policy changes as the starting point for diplomacy, rather than as part of a bargain over giving up its nuclear weapons.
North Korea’s strategy notwithstanding, its ability to change U.S. policy is not guaranteed. Despite Trump’s efforts to engage Pyongyang, the United States, South Korea, and Japan continue to reaffirm the goal of North Korea’s denuclearization, while Washington maintains its defense commitments to its allies.
Pyongyang may see no need to rush into talks. It continues to build up its nuclear forces, citing security threats, while strengthening ties with its partners.
In September 2026, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported signs of a new uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon and indications of expanded operations at Kangson. North Korea has also recently increased the frequency of its missile tests. Meanwhile, expanding military cooperation with Russia and improving relations with China are giving Pyongyang greater room to resist international pressure, including sanctions. Both countries oppose further sanctions on North Korea and have become quieter on its denuclearization.
North Korea may believe that time is on its side: As its nuclear capabilities grow and its diplomatic options expand, Washington may eventually have no choice but to enter talks on the basis that North Korea will retain its nuclear weapons.
Washington’s first task is to clarify the conditions under which North Korea is willing to negotiate and the agenda it is prepared to discuss. Some experts argue that a nuclear freeze or reductions should serve as interim goals if complete denuclearization cannot be achieved in the short term. This may be a realistic alternative for the United States, but Washington should not assume that Pyongyang will accept it as a topic for negotiation. North Korea may instead demand that negotiations focus on regional security issues or insist on changes in U.S. policy before agreeing to talks.
To clarify these issues, working-level meetings should precede any new North Korea-U.S. summit. Washington must coordinate closely with Seoul and Tokyo before negotiating measures that affect their security. If Pyongyang raises concerns about U.S. military activities on the Korean Peninsula, Washington should assess whether its demands can be addressed through reciprocal military measures. 
Discussing regional security does not necessarily mean recognizing North Korea as a nuclear-weapon state or weakening allied military readiness. With South Korea’s agreement, for example, the United States could consider adjusting the scale or format of joint exercises in exchange for limits on North Korean exercises in specific areas, with arrangements for both sides to verify compliance. Once military crisis-management measures are in place and the security environment improves, Washington could argue that Pyongyang should move toward a nuclear freeze or reductions.
The United States must also challenge North Korea’s calculation that time is on its side. Maintaining existing sanctions and deterrence alone is unlikely to change Pyongyang’s strategic judgment. The United States should make clear that North Korea’s continued nuclear buildup could lead South Korea and Japan to strengthen their military capabilities and fuel calls in both countries for nuclear weapons of their own. An offer to discuss regional security should accompany that message. The aim should be to create incentives for diplomacy without triggering another arms race.
Washington should use security talks to pursue reciprocal military measures and build a path toward limits on North Korea’s nuclear capabilities. Knowing what each side is willing to offer before the next summit would improve the chances of reaching an agreement.
Since the start of his second administration, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly proposed renewed talks with North Korea. Pyongyang has said that relations could improve if Washington respected its nuclear status and abandoned what it calls its “hostile policy.” But what would North Korea be willing to talk about if discussions resumed? 
Pyongyang increasingly seeks talks on its security concerns, particularly U.S. military policy and the regional security environment, while treating its own possession of nuclear weapons as non-negotiable. It may even demand a halt to U.S. military exercises with its allies as a precondition for talks.
The failure of the 2019 North Korea-Trump summit in Hanoi may have prompted Pyongyang to reassess its negotiating strategy and strengthen its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons. At the summit, North Korea sought partial relief from United Nations sanctions in exchange for dismantling its Yongbyon nuclear facilities. Washington, however, sought denuclearization measures extending beyond Yongbyon in exchange for a broader package of economic benefits. The summit ended without an agreement. 
Why did North Korea not accept Washington’s “big deal”? Shortly after the summit collapsed, North Korean Foreign Minister Ri Yong Ho explained that security guarantees mattered more to Pyongyang than sanctions relief. North Korea had nevertheless proposed partial sanctions relief in return for dismantling Yongbyon because it believed Washington would find it difficult to take military measures at the time.
North Korea may have recognized the limits of what the United States could offer in terms of security guarantees. U.S. military strategy in Northeast Asia is not solely a response to the North Korean threat. It also reflects Washington’s alliance commitments to South Korea and Japan and its broader strategic competition with China. Even if North Korea gave up all its nuclear weapons, Washington might not be able to offer the security guarantees Pyongyang wants, given its regional interests and alliance commitments. From this perspective, North Korea’s attempt in Hanoi to exchange partial denuclearization for partial sanctions relief may have been a realistic approach. The failure in Hanoi appears to have convinced Pyongyang that giving up its nuclear weapons would not secure the guarantees it sought. After Hanoi, North Korea reinforced its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons through legislation and constitutional changes. In September 2022, it adopted a new law on nuclear forces policy. Kim Jong Un declared that North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state was irreversible and ruled out further negotiations on giving up its nuclear weapons or on denuclearization.
articles.summary: For decades, Washington tried to change Pyongyang’s nuclear policy. Now North Korea is trying to do the reverse: use its nuclear weapons to change U.S. policy.

articles.title: Japan Has Considered Nuclear-Powered Submarines Since 1958. Why Has It Never Built One?
articles.full_text:
From a 1958 design study to reported approaches to the U.S. Navy, Japan has repeatedly examined nuclear-powered submarines without making an acquisition decision.
JS Sogei, the sixth Taigei-class diesel-electric submarine, entered the water in a ceremony held at KHI’s shipyard in Kobe City, Japan, Oct. 14, 2025.
Japan is once again considering acquiring nuclear-powered submarines. As Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s government prepares to revise its three key national security documents by the end of 2026, proposals have emerged to include further research into their acquisition. On October 14, Takaichi told parliament that her government would deepen its “concrete and realistic consideration” of the issue. Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro has said no options should be ruled out.
Yet Japan has been here before. Parliamentary records and contemporary newspaper reports reveal that nuclear-powered submarines have repeatedly been considered for nearly 70 years, without Japan ever acquiring one.
The earliest evidence of Japan’s consideration dates to May 1958, less than four years after the USS Nautilus, the world’s first nuclear-powered submarine, entered service. A preliminary design document bearing the name Kawasaki Heavy Industries examined a nuclear propulsion system for a 2,500-ton submarine. The 1958 study concluded that the submarine concept was technically feasible but acknowledged that Japan could not independently manufacture its reactor and would need extensive U.S. technology.
The document’s existence was revealed in February 1974, when Japan Socialist Party lawmaker Narazaki Yanosuke questioned the government in parliament. The government and Kawasaki maintained that the document represented an individual engineer’s work rather than an official corporate development project. Narazaki challenged that explanation, but institutional involvement was never conclusively established.
In June 1964, a government-industry advisory group concluded that nuclear-powered submarines would provide the most effective means of countering foreign nuclear submarines’ superior underwater speed and endurance. However, legal obstacles remained. 
In April 1965, then-Science and Technology Agency chief Aichi Kiichi stated that using nuclear propulsion aboard Self-Defense Forces vessels was impermissible under Japan’s Atomic Energy Basic Act because nuclear propulsion had not become generally established for civilian maritime use. At the same hearing, then-Defense Agency chief Koizumi Junya declared that Japan had no intention of building nuclear-powered submarines “at the present stage.”
On November 14, 2025, the Takaichi Cabinet reaffirmed that longstanding legal interpretation in a formal written response to a parliamentary question
The issue resurfaced in 1986. The Mainichi Shimbun reported that the Maritime Self-Defense Force had informally approached the U.S. Navy about acquiring nuclear-powered attack submarines. Japanese naval officers reportedly believed conventional submarines could no longer match U.S. nuclear submarines in speed and endurance.
According to a 2011 investigative report by the Sankei Shimbun, Defense Agency officials also secretly examined the possibility of developing nuclear-powered submarines domestically or acquiring them from the United States while preparing Japan’s 2004 defense guidelines. The idea was abandoned as premature.
Across these episodes, recurring obstacles included legal restrictions, technological challenges, substantial costs, and public opposition shaped partly by the 1974 radiation leak aboard Japan’s experimental nuclear-powered ship Mutsu.
Today’s strategic environment is markedly different.
China is expanding its naval presence across the western Pacific. The U.S. Department of Defense’s 2025 report on China’s military power assessed that Beijing aims to field nine aircraft carriers by 2035. China is already building a fourth carrier that is widely believed to be nuclear-powered.
North Korea has announced construction of a nuclear-powered submarine, while South Korea is pursuing its own acquisition plans.
Japan, meanwhile, is studying a next-generation submarine equipped with vertical launch systems (VLS) for long-range missiles. Incorporating VLS would require design modifications, potentially including a larger hull. Advanced sonar systems and unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) would further increase power demands. Conventional submarines, however, face limits on the electrical energy available while submerged, particularly because of their finite battery capacity.
Nevertheless, VLS does not necessarily require nuclear propulsion: South Korea already operates conventionally powered submarines equipped with such systems.
Nuclear propulsion could enable Japanese submarines to remain submerged for extended periods and maintain high underwater speeds, strengthening their ability to monitor Chinese naval movements and support deterrence.
But nuclear-powered submarines are no panacea. They entail major financial and technical burdens, while conventional submarines can offer acoustic advantages under certain conditions. Japan must also address the need for nuclear safeguards, specialized crew training, maintenance infrastructure, and public acceptance.
At a September government advisory meeting, one expert urged Tokyo to commit to acquisition, warning that reactor development and crew training would take a decade or more. Others argued that it was too early to decide.
In 1965, Koizumi Junya said Japan had no intention of building nuclear-powered submarines at that stage. Sixty-one years later, his grandson, Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro, says no options should be ruled out. But keeping an option open is not the same as making a decision. Another open-ended study risks repeating a familiar pattern: identifying the advantages, recognizing the obstacles, and postponing a decision.
Long development timelines justify timely decisions. They do not, however, establish which decision is correct. Japan needs a clear timetable, defined responsibilities, and a rigorous assessment of the legal, technological, financial, and operational questions. Deciding against acquisition after such an assessment would itself constitute a decision.
Nearly seven decades after the first documented study, Japan’s forthcoming security strategy revision will test whether Tokyo is finally prepared to move beyond perpetual consideration.
